Clause 6.5.4 of EN 1990 states that the partial safety factor applied to material properties should generally be 1.0.

The properties of the materials which are normally significant in serviceability calculations are the modulus of elasticity of the reinforcement, the modulus of elasticity, the creep coefficient, the shrinkage strain and the tensile strength of the concrete. All this information is given in Section 3, but is summarized here for convenience.

For ordinary reinforcement this may be taken as 200 kN/mm2 (clause 3.2.7(4)). For prestressing steel, 205 kN/mm2 may be assumed for wires and bars, and 195 kN/mm2 for strand (clauses 3.3.6(2) and 3.3.6(3)).

Values of the modulus of elasticity are given in clause 3.1.3 and Table 3.1. The elastic modulus of concrete varies with other factors than just the strength (e.g. the aggregate type), and, if an accurate prediction of serviceability conditions is required, it will be necessary to establish the value of $E _ { \mathrm { { c m } } }$ by tests on the type of concrete actually being used.

The creep coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the creep deformation to the instantaneous elastic deformation, depends upon many factors, the most significant of which are the age at loading, the time under load, the relative humidity, the section geometry, the concrete strength and the type of cement. Other factors such as the aggregate type may also be significant. As with the modulus of elasticity, the only way of determining the creep performance of concrete with any real reliability is to obtain data from creep tests on the concrete actually being used. This information is rarely available, and more approximate means have to be adopted. The equations given in EN 1992-1-1 should be viewed in this light. Full equations for the prediction of the creep coefficient are given in Annex B. These have been used to produce design graphs (Fig. 3.1 in clause 3.1.4).

The free shrinkage strain depends upon the same basic variables as creep, and equations are given in Annex B for its prediction. Simplified values are given in clause 3.1.4.

Table 3.1 gives the mean tensile strength and the upper and lower characteristic tensile strengths as a function of the characteristic compressive strength of the concrete. Equations are also given in Table 3.1.

The question of the possible limitation of stresses under serviceability loads was the subject of a great deal of discussion during the drafting of EN 1992-1-1. The basic reasons for differences of opinion arose from the different way in which design methods had developed in different countries and a natural desire in each country that the new and untried Eurocode should not force design too far from existing experience in that country. Limitations on the compressive stress in the concrete were particularly contentious. In many countries, section design for both prestressed and reinforced concrete has been carried out on the basis of ultimate strength methods, and no explicit check has been required on the concrete stresses under service loads. These countries were determined that no such checks should be introduced since these could be shown to have a significant effect on the economy of some types of member, notably columns. Other countries have not so far adopted ultimate load methods, and still base their design on an elastic analysis of sections combined with a stress limit. While these countries were prepared to accept ultimate strength methods for section design, they also wanted to retain elastic design as an additional requirement to ensure that member sizes, particularly columns, did not become much smaller or more lightly reinforced than those arising from their current design methods. The check on the compressive stress in the concrete at the serviceability limit state provided them with this safeguard.

In order to develop a rational draft for this section of the code which would have some hope of general acceptance, an attempt was made to establish what rational basis existed for a limit on stresses under serviceability conditions. Two limits need to be considered: compressive stress limits and tensile stress limits. These will be considered in turn.

Two reasons are usually put forward for limiting compressive stresses in the concrete. These are (1) to avoid the formation of microcracks in the concrete which might reduce durability and (2) to avoid excessive creep. There is some logic in both reasons. It is commonly accepted that microcracking will start to develop in concrete when the compressive stress exceeds about 70% of the compressive strength. However, none of the established publications on durability suggest any relationship betweeen stress level, microcracking and durability problems (e.g. see CEB Bulletin d’Information 1859 ). EN 1992-1-1 suggests that, in aggressive environments (exposure classes XD, XF and XS), it may be reasonable to limit the stress to $0 . 6 f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ if other measures, such as an increase to the cover to any compressive reinforcement or the provision of confinement to the compressed concrete by transverse reinforcement.

The design methods used for checking serviceability assume that creep will be proportional to stress. This assumption is increasingly invalid as the stress increases above about 50% of the compressive strength. It could therefore be logical to impose a limit on compressive stress under the quasi-permanent combination of loads where a higher level of creep than might be predicted could seriously impair performance. This problem has been dealt with in clause 3.1.4, where a correction equation has been introduced which enables the creep to be calculated for levels of compressive stress above $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k ^ { \prime } } }$

It will be seen that there is no case for a blanket limitation to compressive stresses but that, in particular cases, it may be prudent to apply such limits if the effects of non-linear creep are not explicitly calculated. EN 1992-1-1 (clause 7.2) suggests that non-linear creep should be taken into account if the compressive stress exceeds $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ under the quasi-permanent load.

In UK practice, compressive stresses have been checked in the design of prestressed members where high compressive stresses are likely to be present permanently, but no check has been required in the design of reinforced sections over the last 50 years. There has been no evidence of problems with performance that could be related to high compressive stress levels in service. It therefore seems reasonable to assume that there is no general requirement to check the compressive stresses in reinforced-concrete members under service conditions, although there may be special circumstances where this might be prudent.

In general, stress checks may be avoided for reinforced concrete …

All this information is given in Section 3, but is summarized here for convenience.

For ordinary reinforcement this may be taken as 200 kN/mm2 (clause 3.2.7(4)). For prestressing steel, 205 kN/mm2 may be assumed for wires and bars, and 195 kN/mm2 for strand (clauses 3.3.6(2) and 3.3.6(3)).

Values of the modulus of elasticity are given in clause 3.1.3 and Table 3.1. The elastic modulus of concrete varies with other factors than just the strength (e.g. the aggregate type), and, if an accurate prediction of serviceability conditions is required, it will be necessary to establish the value of by tests on the type of concrete actually being used.

The creep coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the creep deformation to the instantaneous elastic deformation, depends upon many factors, the most significant of which are the age at loading, the time under load, the relative humidity, the section geometry, the concrete strength and the type of cement. Other factors such as the aggregate type may also be significant. As with the modulus of elasticity, the only way of determining the creep performance of concrete with any real reliability is to obtain data from creep tests on the concrete actually being used. This information is rarely available, and more approximate means have to be adopted. The equations given in EN 1992-1-1 should be viewed in this light. Full equations for the prediction of the creep coefficient are given in Annex B. These have been used to produce design graphs (Fig. 3.1 in clause 3.1.4).

The free shrinkage strain depends upon the same basic variables as creep, and equations are given in Annex B for its prediction. Simplified values are given in clause 3.1.4.

Table 3.1 gives the mean tensile strength and the upper and lower characteristic tensile strengths as a function of the characteristic compressive strength of the concrete. Equations are also given in Table 3.1.

The question of the possible limitation of stresses under serviceability loads was the subject of a great deal of discussion during the drafting of EN 1992-1-1. The basic reasons for differences of opinion arose from the different way in which design methods had developed in different countries and a natural desire in each country that the new and untried Eurocode should not force design too far from existing experience in that country. Limitations on the compressive stress in the concrete were particularly contentious. In many countries, section design for both prestressed and reinforced concrete has been carried out on the basis of ultimate strength methods, and no explicit check has been required on the concrete stresses under service loads. These countries were determined that no such checks should be introduced since these could be shown to have a significant effect on the economy of some types of member, notably columns. Other countries have not so far adopted ultimate load methods, and still base their design on an elastic analysis of sections combined with a stress limit. While these countries were prepared to accept ultimate strength methods for section design, they also wanted to retain elastic design as an additional requirement to ensure that member sizes, particularly columns, did not become much smaller or more lightly reinforced than those arising from their current design methods. The check on the compressive stress in the concrete at the serviceability limit state provided them with this safeguard.

In order to develop a rational draft for this section of the code which would have some hope of general acceptance, an attempt was made to establish what rational basis existed for a limit on stresses under serviceability conditions. Two limits need to be considered: compressive stress limits and tensile stress limits. These will be considered in turn.

Two reasons are usually put forward for limiting compressive stresses in the concrete. These are (1) to avoid the formation of microcracks in the concrete which might reduce durability and (2) to avoid excessive creep. There is some logic in both reasons. It is commonly accepted that microcracking will start to develop in concrete when the compressive stress exceeds about 70% of the compressive strength. However, none of the established publications on durability suggest any relationship betweeen stress level, microcracking and durability problems (e.g. see CEB Bulletin d’Information 1859 ). EN 1992-1-1 suggests that, in aggressive environments (exposure classes XD, XF and XS), it may be reasonable to limit the stress to if other measures, such as an increase to the cover to any compressive reinforcement or the provision of confinement to the compressed concrete by transverse reinforcement.

The design methods used for checking serviceability assume that creep will be proportional to stress. This assumption is increasingly invalid as the stress increases above about 50% of the compressive strength. It could therefore be logical to impose a limit on compressive stress under the quasi-permanent combination of loads where a higher level of creep than might be predicted could seriously impair performance. This problem has been dealt with in clause 3.1.4, where a correction equation has been introduced which enables the creep to be calculated for levels of compressive stress above 

It will be seen that there is no case for a blanket limitation to compressive stresses but that, in particular cases, it may be prudent to apply such limits if the effects of non-linear creep are not explicitly calculated. EN 1992-1-1 (clause 7.2) suggests that non-linear creep should be taken into account if the compressive stress exceeds under the quasi-permanent load.

In UK practice, compressive stresses have been checked in the design of prestressed members where high compressive stresses are likely to be present permanently, but no check has been required in the design of reinforced sections over the last 50 years. There has been no evidence of problems with performance that could be related to high compressive stress levels in service. It therefore seems reasonable to assume that there is no general requirement to check the compressive stresses in reinforced-concrete members under service conditions, although there may be special circumstances where this might be prudent.

In general, stress checks may be avoided for reinforced concrete …

sources.original_text:
(1)P Minimum concrete cover, $c _ { \mathsf { m i n } } ,$ shall be provided in order to ensure:

\- the safe transmission of bond forces (see also Sections 7 and 8)

\- the protection of the steel against corrosion (durability)

an adequate fire resistance (see EN 1992-1-2)

(2)P The greater value for $c _ { \mathsf { m i n } }$ satisfying the requirements for both bond and environmental conditions shall be used.



where:

$\pmb { C } _ { \mathrm { m i n , b } }$ minimum cover due to bond requirement, see 4.4.1.2 (3)

$c _ { \mathrm { m i n , d u r } }$ minimum cover due to environmental conditions, see 4.4.1.2 (5)

$\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d u r } , \gamma }$ additive safety element, see 4.4.1.2 (6)

$\Delta c _ { \mathsf { d u r } , \mathsf { s t } }$ reduction of minimum cover for use of stainless steel, see 4.4.1.2 (7)

$\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d u r , a d d } }$ reduction of minimum cover for use of additional protection, see 4.4.1.2 (8)

(3) In order to transmit bond forces safely and to ensure adequate compaction of the concrete, the minimum cover should not be less than $\pmb { C } _ { \mathrm { m i n , b } }$ given in table 4.2.



Note: The values of $c _ { \mathsf { m i n } , \mathsf { b } }$ for post-tensioned circular and rectangular ducts for bonded tendons, and pretensioned tendons for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended values for posttensioned ducts are:

circular ducts: diameter

rectangular ducts: greater of the smaller dimension or half the greater dimension There is no requirement for more than 80 mm for either circular or rectangular ducts.

The recommended values for pre-tensioned tendon:

1,5 x diameter of strand or plain wire

2,5 x diameter of indented wire.

(4) For prestressing tendons, the minimum cover of the anchorage should be provided in accordance with the appropriate European Technical Approval.

(5) The minimum cover values for reinforcement and prestressing tendons in normal weight concrete taking account of the exposure classes and the structural classes is given by cmin,dur.

Note: Structural classification and values of $c _ { \mathrm { m i n , d u r } }$ for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended Structural Class (design working life of 50 years) is S4 for the indicative concrete strengths given in Annex E and the recommended modifications to the structural class is given in Table 4.3N. The recommended minimum Structural Class is S1.

The recommended values of $c _ { \mathrm { m i n , d u r } }$ are given in Table 4.4N (reinforcing steel) and Table 4.5N (prestressing steel).

(1)P Exposure conditions are chemical and physical conditions to which the structure is exposed in addition to the mechanical actions.

(2) Environmental conditions are classified according to Table 4.1, based on EN 206-1.

(3) In addition to the conditions in Table 4.1, particular forms of aggressive or indirect action should be considered including:

chemical attack, arising from e.g.

\- the use of the building or the structure (storage of liquids, etc)

\- solutions of acids or sulfate salts (EN 206-1, ISO 9690)

\- chlorides contained in the concrete (EN 206-1)

\- alkali-aggregate reactions (EN 206-1, National Standards)

physical attack, arising from e.g.

\- temperature change

\- abrasion (see 4.4.1.2 (13))

\- water penetration (EN 206-1).



Note: The composition of the concrete affects both the protection of the reinforcement and the resistance of the concrete to attack. Annex E gives indicative strength classes for the particular environmental exposure classes. This may lead to the choice of higher strength classes than required for the structural design. In such cases the value of $\pmb { f } _ { \mathrm { c t m } }$ should be associated with the higher strength in the calculation of minimum reinforcement and crack width control (see 7.3.2 -7.3.4).

chunks.title: DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2
chunks.section: Serviceability limit states > 9.2. Design for durability
chunks.content:
There are two basic steps in designing for durability. These are:

(1) Establish the aggressivity of the environment to which the member is exposed. This is analogous to establishing the design loading where the ultimate or serviceability limit states are being considered.

(2) Select materials and design the structure to be able to resist the environment for a reasonable lifetime.

The aggressivity of the environment should, in principle, be defined separately for each degredation mechanism, since the factors acting to promote one form of degredation are not necessarily the same as those promoting another. EN 1992-1-1 does this in Table 4.1. This classifies environments into six basic classes. These are:

(1) no risk of corrosion or attack

(2) corrosion induced by carbonation

(3) corrosion induced by chlorides

(4) corrosion induced by chlorides from sea water

(5) freeze-thaw attack

(6) chemical attack.

Each of these basic classifications, which cover the common forms of attack, are subdivided into subclasses which define the severity of the risk of attack. For example, Class 3, ‘corrosion induced by chlorides’, is divided into three subclasses of increasing severity: XD1, ‘moderate humidity’; XD2, ‘wet, rarely dry’; and XD3, ‘cyclic wet and dry’. Each of the environment classes are defined by examples.

Durability is, however, difficult to define on a uniform basis for all countries which might use EN 1992-1-1, and therefore the durability provisions are all Nationally Defined Parameters. The Nationally Defined Parameters for durability in the UK are set out in the UK National Annex, and are reproduced here in Tables 9.1 and 9.2 (overleaf) for convenience. Table 9.1 gives provisions for a 50 year design life while Table 9.2 gives values for a 100 year design life.

Measures relating to the selection of materials and design of a suitable concrete mix are most conveniently found in BS 8500, while measures relating to the design of the structure, such as cover to the reinforcement, are included in EN 1992-1-1. The design of a durable structure thus requires attention to the rules in both documents

For the selection of the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, reference should be made to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

chunks.title: DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2
chunks.section: Prestressed concrete
chunks.content:
In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The principles and methods given in EN 1992-1-1 are, in general, applicable to the full range of reinforced concrete construction. This chapter covers the aspects of design and detailing that are particular to prestressed concrete; those that apply equally to reinforced concrete are covered in other chapters of this guide.

EN 1992-1-1 covers the design of prestressed concrete members in which the prestress is applied by tendons; the tendons may be embedded in the concrete and may be pretensioned and bonded or post-tensioned and bonded or unbonded. The tendons may also be external to the structure with points of contact occurring at deviators and anchorages. It should be noted that second-order moments can be induced in prestressed members with external tendons if their points of contact with the concrete are sufficiently far apart.

The main clauses relating to the design of prestressed concrete in EN 1992-1-1 are summarized in Table 11.1.

Steel reinforcement and prestressing tendons are protected against corrosion by complying with EN 1992-1-1 requirements on stress levels, crack widths and concrete cover. EN 1992-1-1 specifies a ‘minimum’ cover, based on the greater of the requirements for bond or durability, to which a construction tolerance of 10 mm must be added.

For post-tensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should not be less than the duct diameter (for circular ducts), or the greater of the smaller dimension or half the larger dimension (for rectangular ducts). In no case does it need to be greater than 80 mm. Although EN 1992-1-1 specifies requirements for the minimum cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature for curved reinforcing bars, it does not specify similar requirements for curved prestressing tendons. This is an unfortunate omission, and the designer is recommended to refer to other codes, e.g. BS 8110, where specific requirements are stated for the prevention of bursting of the cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature. The requirements of BS 8110 are given in Table 11.2.

For pretensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should be not less than 1.5 the tendon diameter, or 2.5 times the diameter when indented wires are used. The minimum cover is not related to the aggregate size, but this will probably not be a problem in practice when the construction tolerance is taken into account.

The minimum cover to prestressing tendons and concrete strengths for durability requirements are given in Tables 4.3N, 4.5N and E.1N. The UK National Annex replaces these tables with two tables specifying minimum covers and concrete strengths, maximum water/cement ratios, minimum cement content, cement/combination types and equivalent designated concrete for different exposure classes and for intended working lives of 50 and

100 years (see Chapter 9). The tables are limited to exposure classes XC, XD and XS for a working life of 50 years and exposure class XC for a working life of 100 years because there is insufficient data to make recommendations for members exposed to other conditions. For selecting the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, the designer is referred to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

The UK tables allow a greater range of concrete strengths and covers and take advantage of the improved durability of blended cements to reduce minimum concrete strengths and increase water/cement ratios for the same cover. As far as the minimum cover to ensure durability is concerned, the UK Annex does not distinguish between normal reinforcement and prestressing tendons. EN 1992-1-1, on the other hand, suggests that greater covers should be provided to prestressing steel. Presumably this is because it is generally believed that the risks posed to prestressing tendons from the breakdown of the protection provided by the concrete are greater. A simplified composite version of the tables in EN 1992-1-1 is presented as Table 11.3.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . parent_chunks.content:
In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The principles and methods given in EN 1992-1-1 are, in general, applicable to the full range of reinforced concrete construction. This chapter covers the aspects of design and detailing that are particular to prestressed concrete; those that apply equally to reinforced concrete are covered in other chapters of this guide.

EN 1992-1-1 covers the design of prestressed concrete members in which the prestress is applied by tendons; the tendons may be embedded in the concrete and may be pretensioned and bonded or post-tensioned and bonded or unbonded. The tendons may also be external to the structure with points of contact occurring at deviators and anchorages. It should be noted that second-order moments can be induced in prestressed members with external tendons if their points of contact with the concrete are sufficiently far apart.

The main clauses relating to the design of prestressed concrete in EN 1992-1-1 are summarized in Table 11.1.

Steel reinforcement and prestressing tendons are protected against corrosion by complying with EN 1992-1-1 requirements on stress levels, crack widths and concrete cover. EN 1992-1-1 specifies a ‘minimum’ cover, based on the greater of the requirements for bond or durability, to which a construction tolerance of 10 mm must be added.

For post-tensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should not be less than the duct diameter (for circular ducts), or the greater of the smaller dimension or half the larger dimension (for rectangular ducts). In no case does it need to be greater than 80 mm. Although EN 1992-1-1 specifies requirements for the minimum cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature for curved reinforcing bars, it does not specify similar requirements for curved prestressing tendons. This is an unfortunate omission, and the designer is recommended to refer to other codes, e.g. BS 8110, where specific requirements are stated for the prevention of bursting of the cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature. The requirements of BS 8110 are given in Table 11.2.

For pretensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should be not less than 1.5 the tendon diameter, or 2.5 times the diameter when indented wires are used. The minimum cover is not related to the aggregate size, but this will probably not be a problem in practice when the construction tolerance is taken into account.

Clause 6.5.4 of EN 1990 states that the partial safety factor applied to material properties should generally be 1.0.

The properties of the materials which are normally significant in serviceability calculations are the modulus of elasticity of the reinforcement, the modulus of elasticity, the creep coefficient, the shrinkage strain and the tensile strength of the concrete. All this information is given in Section 3, but is summarized here for convenience.

For ordinary reinforcement this may be taken as 200 kN/mm2 (clause 3.2.7(4)). For prestressing steel, 205 kN/mm2 may be assumed for wires and bars, and 195 kN/mm2 for strand (clauses 3.3.6(2) and 3.3.6(3)).

Values of the modulus of elasticity are given in clause 3.1.3 and Table 3.1. The elastic modulus of concrete varies with other factors than just the strength (e.g. the aggregate type), and, if an accurate prediction of serviceability conditions is required, it will be necessary to establish the value of $E _ { \mathrm { { c m } } }$ by tests on the type of concrete actually being used.

The creep coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the creep deformation to the instantaneous elastic deformation, depends upon many factors, the most significant of which are the age at loading, the time under load, the relative humidity, the section geometry, the concrete strength and the type of cement. Other factors such as the aggregate type may also be significant. As with the modulus of elasticity, the only way of determining the creep performance of concrete with any real reliability is to obtain data from creep tests on the concrete actually being used. This information is rarely available, and more approximate means have to be adopted. The equations given in EN 1992-1-1 should be viewed in this light. Full equations for the prediction of the creep coefficient are given in Annex B. These have been used to produce design graphs (Fig. 3.1 in clause 3.1.4).

The free shrinkage strain depends upon the same basic variables as creep, and equations are given in Annex B for its prediction. Simplified values are given in clause 3.1.4.

Table 3.1 gives the mean tensile strength and the upper and lower characteristic tensile strengths as a function of the characteristic compressive strength of the concrete. Equations are also given in Table 3.1.

The question of the possible limitation of stresses under serviceability loads was the subject of a great deal of discussion during the drafting of EN 1992-1-1. The basic reasons for differences of opinion arose from the different way in which design methods had developed in different countries and a natural desire in each country that the new and untried Eurocode should not force design too far from existing experience in that country. Limitations on the compressive stress in the concrete were particularly contentious. In many countries, section design for both prestressed and reinforced concrete has been carried out on the basis of ultimate strength methods, and no explicit check has been required on the concrete stresses under service loads. These countries were determined that no such checks should be introduced since these could be shown to have a significant effect on the economy of some types of member, notably columns. Other countries have not so far adopted ultimate load methods, and still base their design on an elastic analysis of sections combined with a stress limit. While these countries were prepared to accept ultimate strength methods for section design, they also wanted to retain elastic design as an additional requirement to ensure that member sizes, particularly columns, did not become much smaller or more lightly reinforced than those arising from their current design methods. The check on the compressive stress in the concrete at the serviceability limit state provided them with this safeguard.

In order to develop a rational draft for this section of the code which would have some hope of general acceptance, an attempt was made to establish what rational basis existed for a limit on stresses under serviceability conditions. Two limits need to be considered: compressive stress limits and tensile stress limits. These will be considered in turn.

Two reasons are usually put forward for limiting compressive stresses in the concrete. These are (1) to avoid the formation of microcracks in the concrete which might reduce durability and (2) to avoid excessive creep. There is some logic in both reasons. It is commonly accepted that microcracking will start to develop in concrete when the compressive stress exceeds about 70% of the compressive strength. However, none of the established publications on durability suggest any relationship betweeen stress level, microcracking and durability problems (e.g. see CEB Bulletin d’Information 1859 ). EN 1992-1-1 suggests that, in aggressive environments (exposure classes XD, XF and XS), it may be reasonable to limit the stress to $0 . 6 f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ if other measures, such as an increase to the cover to any compressive reinforcement or the provision of confinement to the compressed concrete by transverse reinforcement.

The design methods used for checking serviceability assume that creep will be proportional to stress. This assumption is increasingly invalid as the stress increases above about 50% of the compressive strength. It could therefore be logical to impose a limit on compressive stress under the quasi-permanent combination of loads where a higher level of creep than might be predicted could seriously impair performance. This problem has been dealt with in clause 3.1.4, where a correction equation has been introduced which enables the creep to be calculated for levels of compressive stress above $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k ^ { \prime } } }$

It will be seen that there is no case for a blanket limitation to compressive stresses but that, in particular cases, it may be prudent to apply such limits if the effects of non-linear creep are not explicitly calculated. EN 1992-1-1 (clause 7.2) suggests that non-linear creep should be taken into account if the compressive stress exceeds $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ under the quasi-permanent load.

In UK practice, compressive stresses have been checked in the design of prestressed members where high compressive stresses are likely to be present permanently, but no check has been required in the design of reinforced sections over the last 50 years. There has been no evidence of problems with performance that could be related to high compressive stress levels in service. It therefore seems reasonable to assume that there is no general requirement to check the compressive stresses in reinforced-concrete members under service conditions, although there may be special circumstances where this might be prudent.

In general, stress checks may be avoided for reinforced concrete …

guide_chunks.section: Serviceability limit states > 9.2. Design for durability
guide_chunks.content:
There are two basic steps in designing for durability. These are:

(1) Establish the aggressivity of the environment to which the member is exposed. This is analogous to establishing the design loading where the ultimate or serviceability limit states are being considered.

(2) Select materials and design the structure to be able to resist the environment for a reasonable lifetime.

The aggressivity of the environment should, in principle, be defined separately for each degredation mechanism, since the factors acting to promote one form of degredation are not necessarily the same as those promoting another. EN 1992-1-1 does this in Table 4.1. This classifies environments into six basic classes. These are:

(1) no risk of corrosion or attack

(2) corrosion induced by carbonation

(3) corrosion induced by chlorides

(4) corrosion induced by chlorides from sea water

(5) freeze-thaw attack

(6) chemical attack.

Each of these basic classifications, which cover the common forms of attack, are subdivided into subclasses which define the severity of the risk of attack. For example, Class 3, ‘corrosion induced by chlorides’, is divided into three subclasses of increasing severity: XD1, ‘moderate humidity’; XD2, ‘wet, rarely dry’; and XD3, ‘cyclic wet and dry’. Each of the environment classes are defined by examples.

Durability is, however, difficult to define on a uniform basis for all countries which might use EN 1992-1-1, and therefore the durability provisions are all Nationally Defined Parameters. The Nationally Defined Parameters for durability in the UK are set out in the UK National Annex, and are reproduced here in Tables 9.1 and 9.2 (overleaf) for convenience. Table 9.1 gives provisions for a 50 year design life while Table 9.2 gives values for a 100 year design life.

Measures relating to the selection of materials and design of a suitable concrete mix are most conveniently found in BS 8500, while measures relating to the design of the structure, such as cover to the reinforcement, are included in EN 1992-1-1. The design of a durable structure thus requires attention to the rules in both documents

For the selection of the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, reference should be made to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

根据 EN 1992-1-1 规范，环境暴露等级（Exposure classes）根据环境条件（基于 EN 206-1）被划分为 **6个基本大类**，并进一步细分为多个子类，以定义侵蚀风险的严重程度 [Ref-3], [Ref-7]。

### 1. 详细分类及环境描述

**(1) 无钢筋锈蚀或混凝土腐蚀风险 (No risk of corrosion or attack)**
*   **X0**：对于无钢筋或预埋金属的混凝土：除冻融、磨损或化学腐蚀外的所有暴露环境；对于有钢筋或预埋金属的混凝土：非常干燥的环境（如：空气湿度极低的建筑物内部混凝土） [Ref-3]。

**(2) 碳化引起的钢筋锈蚀 (Corrosion induced by carbonation)**
*   **XC1**：干燥或永久湿润（如：空气湿度低的建筑物内部混凝土、永久淹没在水中的混凝土） [Ref-3]。
*   **XC2**：湿润，极少干燥（如：长期接触水的混凝土表面、许多基础） [Ref-3]。
*   **XC3**：中等湿度（如：空气湿度中等或高的建筑物内部混凝土、免受雨淋的外部混凝土） [Ref-3]。
*   **XC4**：干湿交替（如：接触水但不属于 XC2 类的混凝土表面） [Ref-3]。

**(3) 氯离子引起的钢筋锈蚀 (Corrosion induced by chlorides)**
*   **XD1**：中等湿度（如：暴露于空气中氯离子的混凝土表面） [Ref-3]。
*   **XD2**：湿润，极少干燥（如：游泳池、暴露于含氯工业水中的混凝土构件） [Ref-3]。
*   **XD3**：干湿交替（如：暴露于含氯喷雾的桥梁部件、路面、停车场楼板） [Ref-3]。

**(4) 海水中的氯离子引起的钢筋锈蚀 (Corrosion induced by chlorides from sea water)**
*   **XS1**：暴露于含盐空气中，但不直接接触海水（如：靠近海岸或海岸上的结构） [Ref-3]。
*   **XS2**：永久淹没（如：海洋结构物的部件） [Ref-3]。
*   **XS3**：潮汐区、飞溅区和喷雾区（如：海洋结构物的部件） [Ref-3]。

**(5) 冻融破坏 (Freeze/Thaw Attack)**
*   **XF1**：中等水饱和度，无除冰剂（如：暴露于雨水和冰冻的垂直混凝土表面） [Ref-3]。
*   **XF2**：中等水饱和度，有除冰剂（如：暴露于冰冻和空气中除冰剂的道路结构垂直混凝土表面） [Ref-3]。
*   **XF3**：高水饱和度，无除冰剂（如：暴露于雨水和冰冻的水平混凝土表面） [Ref-3]。
*   **XF4**：高水饱和度，有除冰剂或海水（如：暴露于除冰剂的道路和桥面、暴露于含除冰剂直接喷雾和冰冻的混凝土表面、暴露于冰冻的海洋结构物飞溅区） [Ref-3]。

**(6) 化学腐蚀 (Chemical attack)**
*   **XA1**：根据 EN 206-1 表2，轻微侵蚀性化学环境（如：天然土壤和地下水） [Ref-3]。
*   **XA2**：根据 EN 206-1 表2，中等侵蚀性化学环境（如：天然土壤和地下水） [Ref-3]。
*   **XA3**：根据 EN 206-1 表2，高度侵蚀性化学环境（如：天然土壤和地下水） [Ref-3]。

---

### 2. 适用条件与注意事项

*   **国家附录（National Annex）差异**：耐久性规定（如各暴露等级对应的指示性混凝土强度等级、最小保护层厚度等参数）在不同国家可能存在差异。具体设计时，必须查阅项目所在国的国家附录以获取当地法定参数 [Ref-6], [Ref-7]。
*   **轻骨料混凝土的特殊规定**：对于轻骨料混凝土，可使用与普通密度混凝土相同的指示性暴露等级 [Ref-5], [Ref-9]。但是，轻骨料混凝土的最小保护层厚度（$c_{min}$）必须在规范常规规定值的基础上**增加 5 mm** [Ref-13]。
*   **其他侵蚀形式**：除了上述表格中的分类，设计时还应考虑特定的侵蚀或间接作用，例如：化学攻击（酸或硫酸盐溶液、混凝土内含氯离子、碱骨料反应）和物理攻击（温度变化、磨损、水渗透） [Ref-1]。

---

### 3. 依据位置
*   **环境暴露等级分类表**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, Table 4.1 (页码 47-49) [Ref-3]
*   **环境条件基本原则**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 4.2 (1)P - (3) (页码 47-49) [Ref-1]
*   **轻骨料混凝土规定**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 11.4.1 及 11.4.2 (1)P (页码 189) [Ref-5], [Ref-13]
*   **国家附录及指示性强度说明**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, Annex E.1 (页码 210) [Ref-6]；指南说明 [Ref-7]

sources_summary.section: Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures - Part 1-1: General rules and rules for buildings > 4.2 Environmental conditions
sources_summary.title: EN1992-1-1_2004
sources_summary.locator_text: (1)P Exposure conditions are chemical and physical conditions to which the structure is exposed in addition to the mechanical actions. (2) Environmental conditions are classified according to Table 4.1, based on EN 206-1. (3) In addition
sources_summary.highlight_text:
(1)P Exposure conditions are chemical and physical conditions to which the structure is exposed in addition to the mechanical actions.

(2) Environmental conditions are classified according to Table 4.1, based on EN 206-1.

(3) In addition to the conditions in Table 4.1, particular forms of aggressive or indirect action should be considered including:

chemical attack, arising from e.g.

\- the use of the building or the structure (storage of liquids, etc)

\- solutions of acids or sulfate salts (EN 206-1, ISO 9690)

\- chlorides contained in the concrete (EN 206-1)

\- alkali-aggregate reactions (EN 206-1, National Standards)

physical attack, arising from e.g.

\- temperature change

\- abrasion (see 4.4.1.2 (13))

\- water penetration (EN 206-1).

Note: The composition of the concrete affects both the protection of the reinforcement and the resistance of the concrete to attack. Annex E gives indicative strength classes for the particular environmental exposure classes. This may lead to the choice of higher strength classes than required for the structural design. sources_summary.title: DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2
sources_summary.locator_text: There are two basic steps in designing for durability. These are: (1) Establish the aggressivity of the environment to which the member is exposed. This is analogous to establishing the design loading where the ultimate or serviceability
sources_summary.highlight_text:
There are two basic steps in designing for durability. These are:

(1) Establish the aggressivity of the environment to which the member is exposed. This is analogous to establishing the design loading where the ultimate or serviceability limit states are being considered.

(2) Select materials and design the structure to be able to resist the environment for a reasonable lifetime.

The aggressivity of the environment should, in principle, be defined separately for each degredation mechanism, since the factors acting to promote one form of degredation are not necessarily the same as those promoting another. EN 1992-1-1 does this in Table 4.1. This classifies environments into six basic classes. These are:

(1) no risk of corrosion or attack

(2) corrosion induced by carbonation

(3) corrosion induced by chlorides

(4) corrosion induced by chlorides from sea water

(5) freeze-thaw attack

(6) chemical attack.

Each of these basic classifications, which cover the common forms of attack, are subdivided into subclasses which define the severity of the risk of attack. For example, Class 3, ‘corrosion induced by chlorides’, is divided into three subclasses of increasing severity: XD1, ‘moderate humidity’; XD2, ‘wet, rarely dry’; and XD3, ‘cyclic wet and dry’. Each of the environment classes are defined by examples.

Durability is, however, difficult to define on a uniform basis for all countries which might use EN 1992-1-1, and therefore the durability provisions are all Nationally Defined Parameters. The Nationally Defined Parameters for durability in the UK are set out in the UK National Annex, and are reproduced here in Tables 9.1 and 9.2 (overleaf) for convenience. Table 9.1 gives provisions for a 50 year design life while Table 9.2 gives values for a 100 year design life.

Measures relating to the selection of materials and design of a suitable concrete mix are most conveniently found in BS 8500, while measures relating to the design of the structure, such as cover to the reinforcement, are included in EN 1992-1-1. The design of a durable structure thus requires attention to the rules in both documents

For the selection of the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, reference should be made to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

sources_summary.locator_text: In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The
sources_summary.highlight_text:
In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The principles and methods given in EN 1992-1-1 are, in general, applicable to the full range of reinforced concrete construction. This chapter covers the aspects of design and detailing that are particular to prestressed concrete; those that apply equally to reinforced concrete are covered in other chapters of this guide.

EN 1992-1-1 covers the design of prestressed concrete members in which the prestress is applied by tendons; the tendons may be embedded in the concrete and may be pretensioned and bonded or post-tensioned and bonded or unbonded. The tendons may also be external to the structure with points of contact occurring at deviators and anchorages. It should be noted that second-order moments can be induced in prestressed members with external tendons if their points of contact with the concrete are sufficiently far apart.

The main clauses relating to the design of prestressed concrete in EN 1992-1-1 are summarized in Table 11.1.

Steel reinforcement and prestressing tendons are protected against corrosion by complying with EN 1992-1-1 requirements on stress levels, crack widths and concrete cover. EN 1992-1-1 specifies a ‘minimum’ cover, based on the greater of the requirements for bond or durability, to which a construction tolerance of 10 mm must be added.

For post-tensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should not be less than the duct diameter (for circular ducts), or the greater of the smaller dimension or half the larger dimension (for rectangular ducts). In no case does it need to be greater than 80 mm. Although EN 1992-1-1 specifies requirements for the minimum cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature for curved reinforcing bars, it does not specify similar requirements for curved prestressing tendons. This is an unfortunate omission, and the designer is recommended to refer to other codes, e.g. BS 8110, where specific requirements are stated for the prevention of bursting of the cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature. The requirements of BS 8110 are given in Table 11.2.

For pretensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should be not less than 1.5 the tendon diameter, or 2.5 times the diameter when indented wires are used. The minimum cover is not related to the aggregate size, but this will probably not be a problem in practice when the construction tolerance is taken into account.

The minimum cover to prestressing tendons and concrete strengths for durability requirements are given in Tables 4.3N, 4.5N and E.1N. The UK National Annex replaces these tables with two tables specifying minimum covers and concrete strengths, maximum water/cement ratios, minimum cement content, cement/combination types and equivalent designated concrete for different exposure classes and for intended working lives of 50 and

sources_summary.highlight_text:
Steel reinforcement and prestressing tendons are protected against corrosion by complying with EN 1992-1-1 requirements on stress levels, crack widths and concrete cover. EN 1992-1-1 specifies a ‘minimum’ cover, based on the greater of the requirements for bond or durability, to which a construction tolerance of 10 mm must be added.

For post-tensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should not be less than the duct diameter (for circular ducts), or the greater of the smaller dimension or half the larger dimension (for rectangular ducts). In no case does it need to be greater than 80 mm. Although EN 1992-1-1 specifies requirements for the minimum cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature for curved reinforcing bars, it does not specify similar requirements for curved prestressing tendons. This is an unfortunate omission, and the designer is recommended to refer to other codes, e.g. BS 8110, where specific requirements are stated for the prevention of bursting of the cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature. The requirements of BS 8110 are given in Table 11.2.

For pretensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should be not less than 1.5 the tendon diameter, or 2.5 times the diameter when indented wires are used. The minimum cover is not related to the aggregate size, but this will probably not be a problem in practice when the construction tolerance is taken into account.

The minimum cover to prestressing tendons and concrete strengths for durability requirements are given in Tables 4.3N, 4.5N and E.1N. The UK National Annex replaces these tables with two tables specifying minimum covers and concrete strengths, maximum water/cement ratios, minimum cement content, cement/combination types and equivalent designated concrete for different exposure classes and for intended working lives of 50 and

The tables are limited to exposure classes XC, XD and XS for a working life of 50 years and exposure class XC for a working life of 100 years because there is insufficient data to make recommendations for members exposed to other conditions. For selecting the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, the designer is referred to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

The UK tables allow a greater range of concrete strengths and covers and take advantage of the improved durability of blended cements to reduce minimum concrete strengths and increase water/cement ratios for the same cover. As far as the minimum cover to ensure durability is concerned, the UK Annex does not distinguish between normal reinforcement and prestressing tendons. EN 1992-1-1, on the other hand, suggests that greater covers should be provided to prestressing steel. Presumably this is because it is generally believed that the risks posed to prestressing tendons from the breakdown of the protection provided by the concrete are greater. This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Analysis may be elastic (without redistribution). This analysis may normally be based on the stiffness of the uncracked section; however, if it is suspected that cracking may have a significant unfavourable effect on the performance, then a more realistic analysis taking account of the cracking should be used. This possibility may be ignored for normal building structures.

The determination of the effects of prestress is covered in clause 5.10.9.

Clause 6.5.4 of EN 1990 states that the partial safety factor applied to material properties should generally be 1.0.

The properties of the materials which are normally significant in serviceability calculations are the modulus of elasticity of the reinforcement, the modulus of elasticity, the creep coefficient, the shrinkage strain and the tensile strength of the concrete. All this information is given in Section 3, but is summarized here for convenience.

For ordinary reinforcement this may be taken as 200 kN/mm2 (clause 3.2.7(4)). For prestressing steel, 205 kN/mm2 may be assumed for wires and bars, and 195 kN/mm2 for strand (clauses 3.3.6(2) and 3.3.6(3)).

Values of the modulus of elasticity are given in clause 3.1.3 and Table 3.1. The elastic modulus of concrete varies with other factors than just the strength (e.g. the aggregate type), and, if an accurate prediction of serviceability conditions is required, it will be necessary to establish the value of by tests on the type of concrete actually being used.

The creep coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the creep deformation to the instantaneous elastic deformation, depends upon many factors, the most significant of which are the age at loading, the time under load, the relative humidity, the section geometry, the concrete strength and the type of cement. Other factors such as the aggregate type may also be significant. As with the modulus of elasticity, the only way of determining the creep performance of concrete with any real reliability is to obtain data from creep tests on the concrete actually being used. This information is rarely available, and more approximate means have to be adopted. The equations given in EN 1992-1-1 should be viewed in this light. Full equations for the prediction of the creep coefficient are given in Annex B. These have been used to produce design graphs (Fig. 3.1 in clause 3.1.4).

The free shrinkage strain depends upon the same basic variables as creep, and equations are given in Annex B for its prediction. Simplified values are given in clause 3.1.4.

Table 3.1 gives the mean tensile strength and the upper and lower characteristic tensile strengths as a function of the characteristic compressive strength of the concrete. Equations are also given in Table 3.1.

The question of the possible limitation of stresses under serviceability loads was the subject of a great deal of discussion during the drafting of EN 1992-1-1. The basic reasons for differences of opinion arose from the different way in which design methods had developed in different countries and a natural desire in each country that the new and untried Eurocode should not force design too far from existing experience in that country. Limitations on the compressive stress in the concrete were particularly contentious. In many countries, section design for both prestressed and reinforced concrete has been carried out on the basis of ultimate strength methods, and no explicit check has been required on the concrete stresses under service loads. These countries were determined that no such checks should be introduced since these could be shown to have a significant effect on the economy of some types of member, notably columns. Other countries have not so far adopted ultimate load methods, and still base their design on an elastic analysis of sections combined with a stress limit. While these countries were prepared to accept ultimate strength methods for section design, they also wanted to retain elastic design as an additional requirement to ensure that member sizes, particularly columns, did not become much smaller or more lightly reinforced than those arising from their current design methods. The check on the compressive stress in the concrete at the serviceability limit state provided them with this safeguard.

In order to develop a rational draft for this section of the code which would have some hope of general acceptance, an attempt was made to establish what rational basis existed for a limit on stresses under serviceability conditions. Two limits need to be considered: compressive stress limits and tensile stress limits. These will be considered in turn.

Two reasons are usually put forward for limiting compressive stresses in the concrete. These are (1) to avoid the formation of microcracks in the concrete which might reduce durability and (2) to avoid excessive creep. There is some logic in both reasons. It is commonly accepted that microcracking will start to develop in concrete when the compressive stress exceeds about 70% of the compressive strength. However, none of the established publications on durability suggest any relationship betweeen stress level, microcracking and durability problems (e.g. see CEB Bulletin d’Information 1859 ). EN 1992-1-1 suggests that, in aggressive environments (exposure classes XD, XF and XS), it may be reasonable to limit the stress to if other measures, such as an increase to the cover to any compressive reinforcement or the provision of confinement to the compressed concrete by transverse reinforcement.

The design methods used for checking serviceability assume that creep will be proportional to stress. This assumption is increasingly invalid as the stress increases above about 50% of the compressive strength. It could therefore be logical to impose a limit on compressive stress under the quasi-permanent combination of loads where a higher level of creep than might be predicted could seriously impair performance. It will be seen that there is no case for a blanket limitation to compressive stresses but that, in particular cases, it may be prudent to apply such limits if the effects of non-linear creep are not explicitly calculated. In UK practice, compressive stresses have been checked in the design of prestressed members where high compressive stresses are likely to be present permanently, but no check has been required in the design of reinforced sections over the last 50 years. There has been no evidence of problems with performance that could be related to high compressive stress levels in service. It therefore seems reasonable to assume that there is no general requirement to check the compressive stresses in reinforced-concrete members under service conditions, although there may be special circumstances where this might be prudent.

In general, stress checks may be avoided for reinforced concrete …

items.question: 保护层都与什么因素相关，该怎么计算?
items.category: 复杂场景与多参数耦合层
items.answer:
根据欧洲规范 EN 1992-1-1，混凝土保护层的设计需要综合考虑粘结力传递、耐久性（防腐蚀）以及耐火性等因素。以下是保护层的相关因素及计算方法的详细说明：

### 1. 核心计算公式与定义
**混凝土保护层**是指最靠近混凝土表面的钢筋（包括箍筋和表面构造钢筋）表面与最近的混凝土表面之间的距离 [Ref-2, Ref-11]。
在图纸上必须标注的是**名义保护层（Nominal cover, $c_{nom}$）**，其计算公式为 [Ref-2, Ref-8, Ref-11]：
$$c_{nom} = c_{min} + \Delta c_{dev}$$
- **$c_{min}$**：最小保护层（Minimum cover）
- **$\Delta c_{dev}$**：设计时考虑的施工允许偏差（Allowance in design for deviation）

---

### 2. 最小保护层 ($c_{min}$) 的相关因素与计算
最小保护层 $c_{min}$ 必须同时满足**安全传递粘结力**、**保护钢筋免受腐蚀（耐久性）**以及**足够的耐火性**（依据 EN 1992-1-2）的要求 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
计算时，应取满足“粘结要求”和“环境条件（耐久性）要求”两者中的**较大值** [Ref-9, Ref-11]：

#### (1) 基于粘结要求的最小保护层 ($c_{min,b}$)
为了保证粘结力的安全传递和混凝土的充分振捣，保护层不得小于 $c_{min,b}$ [Ref-9, Ref-11]：
- **普通钢筋**：通常与钢筋直径相关（具体查表 4.2）。
- **后张法预应力管道**：圆形管道为管道直径；矩形管道为较小尺寸或较大尺寸一半的较大值，且最大不超过 80 mm [Ref-6, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
- **先张法预应力筋**：钢绞线或光面钢丝为 1.5 倍直径；刻痕钢丝；刻痕钢丝为 2.5 倍直径 [Ref-6, Ref-9, Ref-11]。

#### (2) 基于环境条件（耐久性）的最小保护层 ($c_{min,dur}$)
该值主要取决于结构所处的**暴露等级（Exposure classes）**和**结构分类（Structural classes）** [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
环境条件计算中还需考虑以下修正参数 [Ref-9, Ref-11]：
- **$\Delta c_{dur,\gamma}$**：附加安全元素。
- **$\Delta c_{dur,st}$**：使用不锈钢时的保护层折减值。
- **$\Delta c_{dur,add}$**：使用附加保护措施时的保护层折减值。
*(注：普通钢筋和预应力钢的 $c_{min,dur}$ 推荐值分别见规范表 4.4N 和表 4.5N，但规范建议为预应力钢提供更大的保护层以降低腐蚀风险 [Ref-6, Ref-9, Ref-11]。)*

---

### 3. 施工允许偏差 ($\Delta c_{dev}$) 的相关因素与取值
$\Delta c_{dev}$ 是为了弥补施工过程中的负偏差而增加的余量 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
- **常规推荐值**：10 mm [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
- **可折减的情况**（需查阅国家附录确认是否适用） [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]：
  - 若制造受质量保证体系控制，且监测包含保护层测量：可折减至 **5 mm ~ 10 mm**。
  - 若使用高精度测量设备监测并拒收不合格构件（如预制构件）：可折减至 **0 mm ~ 10 mm**。

---

### 4. 特殊工况下的保护层调整
当混凝土浇筑在**不平整表面**上时，必须增加最小保护层以允许更大的设计偏差 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]：
- **在准备好的地基（含垫层）上浇筑**：最小保护层至少为 $k_1$（推荐值 **40 mm**） [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
- **直接在土壤上浇筑**：最小保护层至少为 $k_2$（推荐值 **75 mm**） [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
- **表面具有特殊特征**（如肋状饰面或裸露骨料）：也必须增加保护层以考虑表面的不平整度 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。

---

### ⚠️ 工程师应用提醒（国家附录与前提条件）
1. **国家附录（National Annex）优先**：上述提到的 $c_{min,dur}$ 具体数值、结构分类（推荐 S4）、偏差折减范围（$\Delta c_{dev}$）以及不平整表面系数（$k_1, k_2$）的**最终取值必须以项目所在国的国家附录为准** [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
2. **耐火设计**：若项目有严格的防火要求，保护层厚度还需满足 EN 1992-1-2 的耐火验算要求，此时 $c_{min}$ 可能需要进一步放大 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
3. **图纸标注**：计算得出的名义保护层 $c_{nom}$ 必须直接用于结构计算，并明确标注在施工图纸上 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。

### 依据位置
- 保护层定义与名义保护层公式：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 4.4.1.1 (1)P, (2)P, 公式 4.1 [Ref-2, Ref-3, Ref-8, Ref-11]
- 最小保护层 $c_{min}$ 影响因素及参数：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 4.4.1.2 (1)P~(5) [Ref-9, Ref-11]
- 施工偏差 $\Delta c_{dev}$ 及不平整表面调整：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 4.4.1.3 (1)P~(4) [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]
- 预应力构件保护层特殊指南说明：DG_EN1992-1-1, Chapter 11 (Prestressed concrete) [Ref-6]
items.reasoning:
用户问的是“保护层都与什么因素相关，该怎么计算?”
根据提供的证据，我需要整理出关于混凝土保护层（concrete cover）的相关因素和计算方法。

首先，明确保护层的定义：
混凝土保护层是指最靠近混凝土表面的钢筋（包括箍筋、构造钢筋等）表面与最近的混凝土表面之间的距离 [Ref-2, Ref-3, Ref-11]。

其次，保护层计算的目标是确定“名义保护层”（nominal cover, $c_{nom}$），并在图纸上注明 [Ref-2, Ref-3, Ref-11]。

计算公式：
$c_{nom} = c_{min} + \Delta c_{dev}$ [Ref-8]Ref-8]
其中：
- $c_{min}$ 是最小保护层（minimum cover） [Ref-2, Ref-11]
- $\Delta c_{dev}$ 是设计时考虑的允许偏差（allowance in design for deviation） [Ref-2, Ref-11]

接下来，分析 $c_{min}$ 的相关因素和计算方法：
最小保护层 $c_{min}$ 必须满足以下要求 [Ref-9, Ref-11]：
1. 安全传递粘结力（bond forces）
2. 保护钢筋免受腐蚀（耐久性，durability）
3. 足够的耐火性（fire resistance，见 EN 1992-1-2）

$c_{min}$ 的计算公式为 [Ref-9, Ref-11]：
$c_{min} = \max \{ c_{min,b}; c_{min,dur} + \Delta c_{dur,\gamma} - \Delta c_{dur,st} - \Delta c_{dur,add} \}$ （根据公式推断，虽然证据里没直接给出完整公式，但列出了参数：$c_{min,b}$, $c_{min,dur}$, $\Delta c_{dur,\gamma}$, $\Delta c_{dur,st}$, $\Delta c_{dur,add}$，并说明取满足粘结和环境条件的较大值 [Ref-9, Ref-11]）。
具体参数含义：
- $c_{min,b}$：由于粘结要求的最小保护层 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
  - 对于后张法圆形和矩形管道，推荐值为：圆形管道为直径；矩形管道为较小尺寸或较大尺寸的一半的较大值，且不超过80mm [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
  - 对于先张法预应力筋：钢绞线或光面钢丝为1.5倍直径，刻痕钢丝为2.5倍直径 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
- $c_{min,dur}$：由于环境条件（耐久性）要求的最小保护层 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。取决于暴露等级（exposure classes）和结构分类（structural classes） [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
- $\Delta c_{dur,\gamma}$：附加安全元素 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
- $\Delta c_{dur,st}$：使用不锈钢时的最小保护层折减 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
- $\Delta c_{dur,add}$：使用附加保护时的最小保护层折减 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。

然后，分析 $\Delta c_{dev}$ 的相关因素和计算方法：
$\Delta c_{dev}$ 是设计时考虑的允许偏差（施工偏差） [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
- 推荐值为 10 mm [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
- 在某些情况下可以折减（需查阅国家附录） [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]：
  - 如果制造受质量保证体系控制，且监测包括混凝土保护层测量，可折减至 $5 \text{ mm} \le \Delta c_{dev} \le 10 \text{ mm}$ [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
  - 如果使用非常精确的测量设备进行监测并拒收不合格构件（如预制构件），可折减至 $0 \text{ mm} \le \Delta c_{dev} \le 10 \text{ mm}$ [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
- 对于在不平整表面浇筑的混凝土，最小保护层通常应增加以允许更大的设计偏差 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]：
  - 在准备好的地基（包括垫层）上浇筑，至少为 $k_1$ mm（推荐 40 mm） [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
  - 直接在土壤上浇筑，至少为 $k_2$ mm（推荐 75 mm） [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。
  - 对于表面特征（如肋状饰面或裸露骨料），也应增加保护层以考虑不平整表面 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7]。

另外，关于预应力混凝土的特殊说明（来自指南 DG_EN1992-1-1）：
- 后张法构件：粘结要求的最小保护层不应小于管道直径（圆形）或较小尺寸/一半较大尺寸（矩形），且不需要大于80mm [Ref-6]。
- 。
- 先张法构件：粘结要求的最小保护层不应小于1.5倍预应力筋直径，刻痕钢丝为2.5倍直径 [Ref-6]。
- 英国国家附录（UK NA）对耐久性保护层不区分普通钢筋和预应力筋，但 EN 1992-1-1 建议为预应力钢提供更大的保护层 [Ref-6]。

结构组织：
1. 直接结论（保护层定义及核心计算公式）
2. 最小保护层 $c_{min}$ 的影响因素与计算
3. 施工允许偏差 $\Delta c_{dev}$ 的影响因素与取值
4. 特殊工况下的保护层调整（不平整表面、预应力构件）
5. 依据位置

检查是否有遗漏：
- 耐火性（fire resistance）：由 EN 1992-1-2 规定，也是决定保护层的一个因素 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。
- 国家附录（National Annex）：很多参数（如 $\Delta c_{dev}$ 的折减、$c_{min,dur}$ 的具体数值、结构分类等）都需要查阅具体国家的国家附录 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-7, Ref-9, Ref-11]。必须提醒用户。

开始撰写回复。保持专业、清晰，严格使用 [Ref-N] 标注。
公式部分：
$c_{nom} = c_{min} + \Delta c_{dev}$ [Ref-8]
$c_{min} = \max(c_{min,b}; c_{min,dur} + \Delta c_{dur,\gamma} - \Delta c_{dur,st} - \Delta c_{dur,add})$ （根据参数列表推导，或者直接列出参数说明取较大值）。证据中写的是 "The greater value for $c_{min}$ satisfying the requirements for both bond and environmental conditions shall be used." 并给出了参数 [Ref-9, Ref-11]。我可以写明取粘结要求和环境条件要求两者的较大值。

细节打磨：
- 定义：最靠近混凝土表面的钢筋（包括箍筋、构造钢筋等）表面与最近的混凝土表面之间的距离 [Ref-2, Ref-11]。
- 名义保护层 $c_{nom}$ 必须在图纸上注明 [Ref-2, Ref-11]。
- 参数解释要准确对应证据。
- 提醒用户：具体数值（如环境条件对应的 $c_{min,dur}$、偏差折减值等）需查阅项目所在国的**国家附录（National Annex）**。

sources.original_text:
(1)P To calculate the nominal cover, $c _ { \mathsf { n o m } } ,$ , an addition to the minimum cover shall be made in design to allow for the deviation $( \Delta c _ { \mathsf { d e v } } )$ . The required minimum cover shall be increased by the absolute value of the accepted negative deviation.

Note: The value of $\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d e v } }$ for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended value is 10 mm.

(2) For Buildings, ENV 13670-1 gives the acceptable deviation. This is normally also sufficient for other types of structures. It should be considered when choosing the value of nominal cover for design. The nominal value of cover for design should be used in the calculations and stated on the drawings, unless a value other than the nominal cover is specified (e.g. minimum value).

(3) In certain situations, the accepted deviation and hence allowance, $\Delta c _ { \mathsf { d e v } }$ , may be reduced.

Note: The reduction in $\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d e v } }$ in such circumstances for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended values are:

\- where fabrication is subjected to a quality assurance system, in which the monitoring includes

measurements of the concrete cover, the allowance in design for deviation $\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d e v } }$ may be reduced: $1 0 \mathrm { m m } \geq \Delta c _ { \mathrm { d e v } } \geq 5$ mm

(4.3N)

\- where it can be assured that a very accurate measurement device is used for monitoring and non conforming members are rejected (e.g. precast elements), the allowance in design for deviation $\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d e v } }$ may be reduced:

10 mm ≥ $\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d e v } } \geq 0$ mm

(4.4N)

(4) For concrete cast against uneven surfaces, the minimum cover should generally be increased by allowing larger deviations in design. The increase should comply with the difference caused by the unevenness, but the minimum cover should be at least $k _ { 1 }$ mm for concrete cast against prepared ground (including blinding) and $k _ { 2 }$ mm for concrete cast directly against soil. The cover to the reinforcement for any surface feature, such as ribbed finishes or exposed aggregate, should also be increased to take account of the uneven surface (see 4.4.1.2 (11)).

Note: The values of $k _ { 1 }$ and $k _ { 2 }$ for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended values are 40 mm and 75 mm.

sources.section: Detailing > 10.1. General
sources.original_text:
The main guidance on detailing is contained in Sections 8 and 9 of EN 1992-1-1. Cover requirements are in Section 4, under durability.

The main aspects of detailing are concerned with anchoring bars carrying stress and lapping of reinforcement. Most of the provisions regarding anchorage and laps were reputedly deduced from tests carried out in many countries, principally in Austria, France, Germany, Sweden and the USA. It is understood that the global safety factor $\gamma _ { \mathrm { m } } \gamma _ { f }$ against the 5% fractile of test results is 2.1. $\mathbf { A s } \gamma _ { \mathrm { m } } = 1 .$ .5 for concrete, this gives a value of $\dot { \gamma } _ { f } = 1 . 4$ for loads, which is clearly considered acceptable in EN 1992-1-1.

Anchorage and lap requirements are checked at the ultimate limit stage. The general detailing provisions are deemed to ensure satisfactory behaviour of the structure at serviceability conditions.

The code covers (1) high-bond bars, (2) welded mesh and (3) different types of structural members. Bars may be used in bundles with certain limitations.

In the main, the detailing requirements are governed by bond-related phenomena, which are significantly influenced by:

the surface characteristics of the bars (plain, ribbed)

the shape of the bars (straight, with hooks or bends)

the presence of welded transverse bars

the confinement offered by concrete (mainly controlled by the size of the concrete cover in relation to the bar diameter)

the confinement offered by non-welded transverse reinforcement (such as links)

• the confinement offered by transverse pressure.

The rules governing detailing make allowance for the above. Particular emphasis is placed on the need for adequate concrete cover and transverse reinforcement to cater for tensile stresses in concrete in regions of high bond stresses.

Bond stresses for high-bond bars are a function of the tensile strength of concrete $( f _ { \mathrm { c t k } } )$

The guidance for detailing different types of members includes requirements for minimum areas of reinforcement. This is stipulated in order to (1) prevent a brittle failure, (2) prevent wide cracks and (3) resist stresses arising from temperature effects, shrinkage and other restrained actions.

The main guidance on detailing is contained in Sections 8 and 9 of EN 1992-1-1. Cover requirements are in Section 4, under durability.

The main aspects of detailing are concerned with anchoring bars carrying stress and lapping of reinforcement. Most of the provisions regarding anchorage and laps were reputedly deduced from tests carried out in many countries, principally in Austria, France, Germany, Sweden and the USA. It is understood that the global safety factor against the 5% fractile of test results is 2.1. .5 for concrete, this gives a value of for loads, which is clearly considered acceptable in EN 1992-1-1.

Anchorage and lap requirements are checked at the ultimate limit stage. The general detailing provisions are deemed to ensure satisfactory behaviour of the structure at serviceability conditions.

The code covers (1) high-bond bars, (2) welded mesh and (3) different types of structural members. Bars may be used in bundles with certain limitations.

In the main, the detailing requirements are governed by bond-related phenomena, which are significantly influenced by:

the surface characteristics of the bars (plain, ribbed)

the shape of the bars (straight, with hooks or bends)

the presence of welded transverse bars

the confinement offered by concrete (mainly controlled by the size of the concrete cover in relation to the bar diameter)

the confinement offered by non-welded transverse reinforcement (such as links)

• the confinement offered by transverse pressure.

The rules governing detailing make allowance for the above. Particular emphasis is placed on the need for adequate concrete cover and transverse reinforcement to cater for tensile stresses in concrete in regions of high bond stresses.

Bond stresses for high-bond bars are a function of the tensile strength of concrete 

The guidance for detailing different types of members includes requirements for minimum areas of reinforcement. This is stipulated in order to (1) prevent a brittle failure, (2) prevent wide cracks and (3) resist stresses arising from temperature effects, shrinkage and other restrained actions.

Note: The value of $\Delta c _ { \mathrm { d e v } }$ for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended value is $1 0 \mathsf { m m }$ .

(2) For Buildings, ENV 13670-1 gives the acceptable deviation. This is normally also sufficient for other types of structures. It should be considered when choosing the value of nominal cover for design. The nominal value of cover for design should be used in the calculations and stated on the drawings, unless a value other than the nominal cover is specified (e.g. minimum value).
