In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

sources_summary.locator_text: Limit states are defined as states beyond which the structure infringes an agreed performance criterion. Two basic groups of limit states to be considered are (1) ultimate limit states and (2) serviceability limit states. Ultimate limit
sources_summary.highlight_text:
Limit states are defined as states beyond which the structure infringes an agreed performance criterion. Two basic groups of limit states to be considered are (1) ultimate limit states and (2) serviceability limit states.

Ultimate limit states are those associated with collapse or failure, and generally govern the strength of the structure or components. They also include loss of equilibrium or stability of the structure as a whole. As the structure will undergo severe deformation prior to reaching collapse conditions (e.g. beams becoming catenaries), for simplicity these states are also regarded as ultimate limit states, although this condition is between serviceability and ultimate limit states; these states are equivalent to collapse, as they will necessitate replacement of the structure or element.

Serviceability limit states generally correspond to conditions of the structure in use. They include deformation, cracking and vibration which:

(1) damage the structure or non-structural elements (finishes, partitions, etc.) or the contents of buildings (such as machinery)

(2) cause discomfort to the occupants of buildings

(3) affect adversely appearance, durability or water and weather tightness.

They will generally govern the stiffness of the structure and the detailing of reinforcement within it.

Figure 2.1 illustrates a typical load-deformation relationship of reinforced-concrete structures and the limit states.

sources_summary.highlight_text:
(1)P The design of concrete structures shall be in accordance with the general rules given in EN 1990.

(2)P The supplementary provisions for concrete structures given in this section shall also be applied.

(3) The basic requirements of EN 1990 Section 2 are deemed to be satisfied for concrete structures when the following are applied together:

\- limit state design in conjunction with the partial factor method in accordance with EN 1990,

\- actions in accordance with EN 1991,

\- combination of actions in accordance with EN 1990 and

\- resistances, durability and serviceability in accordance with this Standard.

Note: Requirements for fire resistance (see EN 1990 Section 5 and EN 1992-1-2) may dictate a greater size of member than that required for structural resistance at normal temperature.

What has been done here is to provide a further complete set of charts for 90 N/mm2 concrete (Figs 5.9a-l). Interpolation may be used between the charts for 50 and 90 N/mm2 concrete for intermediate strengths.

items.question: 混凝土抗压强度标准值、设计值与平均强度之间是什么关系？
items.category: 基础概念与符号体系层
items.answer:
### 核心结论
在欧洲规范（Eurocode）中，混凝土抗压强度的平均强度（$f_{cm}$）、标准值（$f_{ck}$）与设计值（$f_{cd}$）之间存在明确的数学换算关系：
1. **平均强度与标准值**：$f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8 \text{ MPa}$ （针对28天龄期圆柱体强度）。
2. **标准值与设计值**：$f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc} \frac{f_{ck}}{\gamma_c}$。

---

### 详细关系说明

#### 1. 平均强度 ($f_{cm}$) 与 标准值 ($f_{ck}$) 的关系
* **标准值的定义**：混凝土抗压强度标准值 $f_{ck}$ 是指28天圆柱体抗压强度的5%分位值，即在所有测试结果中，仅有不超过5%的概率会低于该强度值 [Ref-5, Ref-7]。
* **数值换算**：在28天龄期时，混凝土圆柱体平均抗压强度 $f_{cm}$ 与标准值 $f_{ck}$ 的差值恒为 8 MPa，即 $f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8 \text{ MPa}$ [Ref-8, Ref-16, Ref-18]。
* **早龄期关系**：对于 $3 < t < 28$ 天的早龄期混凝土，其标准值与平均强度的关系同样为 $f_{ck}(t) = f_{cm}(t) - 8 \text{ MPa}$ [Ref-8, Ref-16]。

#### 2. 标准值 ($f_{ck}$) 与 设计值 ($f_{cd}$) 的关系
* **设计值的计算**：抗压强度设计值 $f_{cd}$ 是通过将标准值 $f_{ck}$ 除以混凝土材料分项安全系数 $\gamma_c$，并乘以转换系数 $\alpha_{cc}$ 来确定的 [Ref-6, Ref-11]。
* **计算公式**：$f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc} \frac{f_{ck}}{\gamma_c}$ [Ref-6, Ref-11]。

---

### 关键参数与适用条件提醒
* **系数 $\alpha_{cc}$**：该系数用于考虑长期荷载效应对抗压强度的影响以及加载方式带来的不利影响 [Ref-11, Ref-13]。规范推荐值为 **1.0**，但具体取值（通常在 0.8 到 1.0 之间）**必须查阅项目所在国的国家附录（National Annex）** [Ref-11]。例如，英国国家附录（UK NA）推荐取值为 0.85 [Ref-13]。
* **材料分项系数 $\gamma_c$**：用于覆盖材料性能可能出现的不利偏差，其具体数值需根据设计状况（如持久、短暂或偶然状况）及国家附录确定 [Ref-2, Ref-11]。
* **试件形状差异**：上述 $f_{cm}$ 与 $f_{ck}$ 的直接加减关系基于**圆柱体试件（cylinder）**。若使用立方体试件（cube），其标准值记为 $f_{ck,cube}$，圆柱体与立方体标准值之间存在特定的换算关系，需查阅规范中的强度等级对照表（如 EN 1992-1-1 的 Table 3.1） [Ref-5, Ref-18]。

---

### 依据位置
* **符号定义**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 1.6 [Ref-1]
* **标准值定义及与平均强度关系**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 3.1.2 [Ref-5, Ref-8, Ref-16]
* **设计值计算公式**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 3.1.6(1)P [Ref-11]；DG EN 1990, 6.3.3 [Ref-6]
* **强度等级与参数对照表**：DG EN 19921992-1-1, Table 4.1 [Ref-18]
* **$\alpha_{cc}$ 系数说明及国家附录差异**：DG EN 1992-1-1, 4.1 [Ref-13]

需要提取的证据：

2. 混凝土抗压强度设计值（$f_{cd}$）与标准值（$f_{ck}$）的关系。
3. 这些参数的定义和符号。

分析证据：
- [Ref-1] 符号定义：
  - $f_c$: Compressive strength of concrete
  - $f_{cd}$: Design value of concrete compressive strength
  - $f_{ck}$: Characteristic compressive cylinder strength of concrete at 28 days
  - $f_{cm}$: Mean value of concrete cylinder compressive strength
- [Ref-5], [Ref-8], [Ref-11] 3.1.2 (1)P: 混凝土抗压强度由强度等级表示，与28天特征圆柱体强度 $f_{ck}$（5%分位值）或立方体强度相关。
- [Ref-7], [Ref-13]: 特征强度（characteristic strength）定义为不超过5%的测试结果可能低于该值的强度。
- [Ref-8], [Ref-16] 16] 3.1.2 (5): $f_{ck}(t) = f_{cm}(t) - 8$ (MPa) 对于 $3 < t < 28$ 天。对于 $t \ge 28$ 天，$f_{ck}(t) = f_{ck}$。
  注意：这里 $f_{cm}(t)$ 是 t 天的平均强度。28天的平均强度是 $f_{cm}$。所以 $f_{ck} = f_{cm} - 8$ MPa （在28天时）。
- [Ref-18] Table 4.1 给出了 $f_{ck}$ 和 $f_{cm}$ 的对应数值关系，例如 $f_{ck}=20$ 时 $f_{cm}=28$ (差8)；$f_{ck}=30$ 时 $f_{cm}=38$ (差8)；$f_{ck}=90$ 时 $f_{cm}=98$ (差8)。这证实了 $f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8$ MPa。
- [Ref-6], [Ref-11] 3.1.6 (1)P: 设计抗压强度 $f_{cd}$ 的定义：
  $f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc} \frac{f_{ck}}{\gamma_c}$
  其中 $\gamma_c$ 是混凝土的分项安全系数，$\alpha_{cc}$ 是考虑长期效应和加载方式不利影响的系数（推荐值为1.0，但国家附录可能规定0.8到1.0之间，如英国NA规定0.85）。

整理逻辑：
1. **直接结论**：
   - 平均强度（$f_{cm}$）与标准值（$f_{ck}$）的关系：$f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8 \text{ MPa}$（针对28天圆柱体强度）。
   - 设计值（$f_{cd}$）与标准值（$f_{ck}$）的关系：$f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc} \frac{f_{ck}}{\gamma_c}$。
2. **依据与说明**：
   - **标准值与平均强度的关系**：标准值 $f_{ck}$ 定义为28天圆柱体抗压强度的5%分位值（即仅有5%的测试结果可能低于此值）[Ref-5, Ref-7]。在28天时，平均抗压强度 $f_{cm}$ 与标准值 $f_{ck}$ 的数值关系为 $f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8 \text{ MPa}$ [Ref-8, Ref-16, Ref-18]。对于早龄期（$3 < t < 28$ 天），$f_{ck}(t) = f_{cm}(t) - 8 \text{ MPa}$ [Ref-8, Ref-16]。
   - **设计值与标准值的关系**：设计值 $f_{cd}$ 是通过将标准值 $f_{ck}$ 除以混凝土材料分项系数 $\gamma_c$，并乘以考虑长期效应及加载方式不利影响的系数 $\alpha_{cc}$ 得到的 [Ref-6, Ref-11]。公式为 $f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc} \frac{f_{ck}}{\gamma_c}$ [Ref-6, Ref-11]。

   - $\gamma_c$：混凝土的材料分项安全系数，具体数值需根据设计状况（如持久、短暂或偶然）及国家附录确定 [Ref-11]。

sources.original_text:
In EN 1992-1-1 the compressive strength of concrete is denoted by concrete strength classes, which relate to the characteristic cylinder strength $f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ or the cube strength $\bar { f } _ { \mathrm { c k , c u b e } } .$ The characteristic strength is defined as that strength below which not more than 5% of all test results are likely to fall. The relationship between the cylinder and cube strengths is given in the code, and is reproduced in Table 4.1.

The code provides models for strength development with time, and these should be used when concrete strength need to be calculated.

Table 4.1 also gives the mean tensile strength of concrete.

(1) The elastic deformations of concrete largely depend on its composition (especially the aggregates). The values given in this Standard should be regarded as indicative for general applications. However, they should be specifically assessed if the structure is likely to be sensitive to deviations from these general values.

(2) The modulus of elasticity of a concrete is controlled by the moduli of elasticity of its components. Where there is only one variable action:



• Where there are two or more variable actions:



Analysis may be elastic (without redistribution). This analysis may normally be based on the stiffness of the uncracked section; however, if it is suspected that cracking may have a significant unfavourable effect on the performance, then a more realistic analysis taking account of the cracking should be used. This possibility may be ignored for normal building structures.

The determination of the effects of prestress is covered in clause 5.10.9.
[-> Formula]
[-> Formula]
[-> Formula]
[-> Formula]
[-> Formula]

Clause 6.5.4 of EN 1990 states that the partial safety factor applied to material properties should generally be 1.0.

The properties of the materials which are normally significant in serviceability calculations are the modulus of elasticity of the reinforcement, the modulus of elasticity, the creep coefficient, the shrinkage strain and the tensile strength of the concrete. All this information is given in Section 3, but is summarized here for convenience.

For ordinary reinforcement this may be taken as 200 kN/mm2 (clause 3.2.7(4)). For prestressing steel, 205 kN/mm2 may be assumed for wires and bars, and 195 kN/mm2 for strand (clauses 3.3.6(2) and 3.3.6(3)).

Values of the modulus of elasticity are given in clause 3.1.3 and Table 3.1. The elastic modulus of concrete varies with other factors than just the strength (e.g. the aggregate type), and, if an accurate prediction of serviceability conditions is required, it will be necessary to establish the value of $E _ { \mathrm { { c m } } }$ by tests on the type of concrete actually being used.

The creep coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the creep deformation to the instantaneous elastic deformation, depends upon many factors, the most significant of which are the age at loading, the time under load, the relative humidity, the section geometry, the concrete strength and the type of cement. Other factors such as the aggregate type may also be significant. As with the modulus of elasticity, the only way of determining the creep performance of concrete with any real reliability is to obtain data from creep tests on the concrete actually being used. This information is rarely available, and more approximate means have to be adopted. The equations given in EN 1992-1-1 should be viewed in this light. Full equations for the prediction of the creep coefficient are given in Annex B. These have been used to produce design graphs (Fig. 3.1 in clause 3.1.4).

The free shrinkage strain depends upon the same basic variables as creep, and equations are given in Annex B for its prediction. Simplified values are given in clause 3.1.4.

Table 3.1 gives the mean tensile strength and the upper and lower characteristic tensile strengths as a function of the characteristic compressive strength of the concrete. Equations are also given in Table 3.1.

The question of the possible limitation of stresses under serviceability loads was the subject of a great deal of discussion during the drafting of EN 1992-1-1. The basic reasons for differences of opinion arose from the different way in which design methods had developed in different countries and a natural desire in each country that the new and untried Eurocode should not force design too far from existing experience in that country. Limitations on the compressive stress in the concrete were particularly contentious. In many countries, section design for both prestressed and reinforced concrete has been carried out on the basis of ultimate strength methods, and no explicit check has been required on the concrete stresses under service loads. These countries were determined that no such checks should be introduced since these could be shown to have a significant effect on the economy of some types of member, notably columns. Other countries have not so far adopted ultimate load methods, and still base their design on an elastic analysis of sections combined with a stress limit. While these countries were prepared to accept ultimate strength methods for section design, they also wanted to retain elastic design as an additional requirement to ensure that member sizes, particularly columns, did not become much smaller or more lightly reinforced than those arising from their current design methods. The check on the compressive stress in the concrete at the serviceability limit state provided them with this safeguard.

In order to develop a rational draft for this section of the code which would have some hope of general acceptance, an attempt was made to establish what rational basis existed for a limit on stresses under serviceability conditions. Two limits need to be considered: compressive stress limits and tensile stress limits. These will be considered in turn.

Two reasons are usually put forward for limiting compressive stresses in the concrete. These are (1) to avoid the formation of microcracks in the concrete which might reduce durability and (2) to avoid excessive creep. There is some logic in both reasons. It is commonly accepted that microcracking will start to develop in concrete when the compressive stress exceeds about 70% of the compressive strength. However, none of the established publications on durability suggest any relationship betweeen stress level, microcracking and durability problems (e.g. see CEB Bulletin d’Information 1859 ). EN 1992-1-1 suggests that, in aggressive environments (exposure classes XD, XF and XS), it may be reasonable to limit the stress to $0 . 6 f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ if other measures, such as an increase to the cover to any compressive reinforcement or the provision of confinement to the compressed concrete by transverse reinforcement.

The design methods used for checking serviceability assume that creep will be proportional to stress. This assumption is increasingly invalid as the stress increases above about 50% of the compressive strength. It could therefore be logical to impose a limit on compressive stress under the quasi-permanent combination of loads where a higher level of creep than might be predicted could seriously impair performance. This problem has been dealt with in clause 3.1.4, where a correction equation has been introduced which enables the creep to be calculated for levels of compressive stress above $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k ^ { \prime } } }$

EN 1992-1-1 covers concrete of strength up to 90 MPa in normal-weight concrete and 80 MPa in lightweight concrete. It relies on EN 206-1 for the specification and production of concrete.

In EN 1992-1-1 the compressive strength of concrete is denoted by concrete strength classes, which relate to the characteristic cylinder strength $f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ or the cube strength $\bar { f } _ { \mathrm { c k , c u b e } } .$ The characteristic strength is defined as that strength below which not more than 5% of all test results are likely to fall. The relationship between the cylinder and cube strengths is given in the code, and is reproduced in Table 4.1.

The code provides models for strength development with time, and these should be used when concrete strength need to be calculated.

Table 4.1 also gives the mean tensile strength of concrete.

EN 1992-1-1 recognizes that deformation properties are crucially dependent on the composition of concrete, and in particular on the aggregates. Therefore, it provides only indicative information, which should be sufficient for most normal structures. However, in structures that are likely to be sensitive to deformation, it is advisable to determine the properties by controlled testing and appropriate specification.

Table 4.1 reproduces the mean values for the modulus of elasticity given in the code. The values given apply to concretes with quartzite aggregates. The reduction factors for other aggregates are as follows: limestone aggregates, 10%; basalt aggregates, 20%; and sandstone aggregates, 30%.



Poisson’s ratio may be taken as 0.2 for uncracked concrete, and 0 for cracked concrete. The coefficient of linear thermal expansion may be taken as $1 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 } / \mathrm { K }$
[-> Table]

The creep and shrinkage of concrete depend on a number of factors, including the ambient humidity, the dimensions of the element, the composition of the concrete and the age of concrete at the time of loading. The long-term values of the creep coefficient $\varphi ( \infty , t _ { 0 } )$ are shown in Figs 4.1 and 4.2 for inside and outside conditions, respectively. The resulting strain in the member will be $\varphi ( \infty , t _ { 0 } ) ( \sigma _ { \mathrm { c } } / E _ { \mathrm { c } } )$ . When the compressive stress at time $t _ { 0 }$ exceeds $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k } } ( t _ { 0 } )$ , the creep coefficient should be multiplied by a factor shown in Table 4.2, depending on the ratio



to allow for the non-linearity of creep development.

Shrinkage has two components, namely drying shrinkage $( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c d } } )$ and autogenous shrinkage $( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c a } } )$ . Drying shrinkage is the result of expiration of moisture from the concrete to the surrounding air. On the other hand, the background document to EN 1992-1-1 defines autogenous shrinkage as ‘the macroscopic volume reduction of cementitious materials when cement hydrates, after initial setting. It does not include the volume change due to loss or ingress of substances, temperature variation or the application of external force and restraint’. Autogenous shrinkage is related inversely to the water/cement ratio, and will be significant for concretes of high strength.

The drying shrinkage strain at age t is $\beta _ { \mathrm { d s } } ( t , t _ { \mathrm { s } } ) k _ { \mathrm { h } } \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c d , 0 } } .$ . Tables 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 give the data for calculating shrinkage at 30, 100 and 1000 days, respectively.

Autogenous shrinkage strain at age t is given by $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c a } } ( t ) = \beta _ { \mathrm { a s } } \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c a } } ( \infty )$ . Values at 30, 100 and 1000 days are given in Table 4.6.

A distinction should be made between the stress-strain curve used for analysis and that used for the design of cross-sections. Figure 4.3 defines the parameters for the curve used for analysis. For numerical values, see EN 1992-1-1.

EN 1992-1-1 offers two alternatives for the design of cross-sections. These are parabolarectangle (Fig. 4.4) and bi-linear (Fig. 4.5) diagrams. For numerical values of the parameters, see EN 1992-1-1.

The basic compressive stress is $f _ { \mathrm { c d } } = \alpha _ { \mathrm { c c } } f _ { \mathrm { c k } } / \gamma _ { \mathrm { c } } .$ The coefficient $\alpha _ { \mathrm { c c } }$ is said to take account of long-term effects on the compressive strength and of the unfavourable effects resulting from the way the load is applied. EN 1992-1-1 recommends a value of 1.0 for this coefficient, but the UK in its National Annex proposes 0.85. This reduced value, which was used in the ENV version of EN 1992-1-1, is considered necessary as a calibration factor between the predicted strength and that obtained in experiments. This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these te…

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these te…

The variability in geometrical quantities is usually less significant than the variability in actions and material or product properties, and in many cases is negligible. Consequently, design values of geometrical data are generally represented by the nominal value (clause 6.3.4(1)):

Clause 6.3.4(1)



The nominal (reference) dimension $a _ { \mathrm { n o m } }$ is the basic dimension which is used in design drawings and documentation. All deviations of the geometric quantities are related to it. The geometrical value $a _ { \mathrm { n o m } }$ comprises not only the geometrical data as lengths and widths of a frame but also represents the so-called ‘perfect geometry’, in that sway imperfections of the frame or curvature imperfections of the members or inaccuracy of the excavation depth in front of sheet pilings are not considered. Such imperfections are reflected in the ‘additive reliability elements’ $\Delta a .$ , as explained below. The design Eurocodes 1 to 9 give appropriate specifications.

Where deviations in the geometrical data have a significant effect on the reliability of a structure (e.g. slender columns or thin silo walls), the geometrical design values are defined by (clause 6.3.4(2)P)

Clause 6.3.4(2)P



where $\Delta a$ takes account of the possibility of unfavourable deviations from the characteristic or nominal values and the cumulative effect of a simultaneous occurrence of several geometrical deviations. It should be noted that $\Delta a$ is introduced only where the influence of deviations is critical (e.g. imperfections in buckling analysis). Values of $\Delta a$ are given in Eurocodes 2 to 9.

where $\gamma _ { \mathrm { R d } }$ is a partial factor covering uncertainty in the resistance model, plus geometric deviations if these are not modelled explicitly (see clause 6.3.4(2)), and $X _ { \mathrm { d } , i }$ is the design value of material property i.

Clause 6.3.4(2)

Variations of expression (6.6) are given in the design Eurocodes 1 to 9, because the characteristic value of the resistance $R _ { \mathrm { k } }$ for a given material, or way of construction, may be expressed in various ways, for example:

as the resistance of a member (e.g. the beam–column resistance), where $R _ { \mathrm { k } }$ may be a linear or a non-linear function of many geometrical parameters, material parameters and parameters for structural and geometrical imperfections

as the resistance of a cross-section, generally expressed in terms of a linear or non-linear interaction formula comprising geometrical data and material data compatible with the action effects

as a local resistance in terms of stresses, strains, stress intensity factors (or rotation capacity), etc.

In a general manner, the characteristic value $R _ { \mathrm { k } }$ of the resistance of a structural member is a function of one or more parameters which may be expressed in terms of individual characteristic values $X _ { \mathbf { k } , i } ,$ or individual nominal values $X _ { \mathrm { n o m } , j } ,$ so that



Depending on the case, $X _ { \mathrm { k } } , X _ { \mathrm { n o m } } , a _ { \mathrm { n o m } }$ or $R _ { \mathrm { k } }$ may be described as a property of a product in a material or product standard. The particular property may therefore be controlled by testing (see Chapter 10) in order to verify that the definition of $R _ { \mathrm { k } }$ as a characteristic value (a given fractile of the distribution of R) is fulfilled.

Analysis may be elastic (without redistribution). This analysis may normally be based on the stiffness of the uncracked section; however, if it is suspected that cracking may have a significant unfavourable effect on the performance, then a more realistic analysis taking account of the cracking should be used. This possibility may be ignored for normal building structures.

The determination of the effects of prestress is covered in clause 5.10.9.

Clause 6.5.4 of EN 1990 states that the partial safety factor applied to material properties should generally be 1.0.

The properties of the materials which are normally significant in serviceability calculations are the modulus of elasticity of the reinforcement, the modulus of elasticity, the creep coefficient, the shrinkage strain and the tensile strength of the concrete. All this information is given in Section 3, but is summarized here for convenience.

For ordinary reinforcement this may be taken as 200 kN/mm2 (clause 3.2.7(4)). For prestressing steel, 205 kN/mm2 may be assumed for wires and bars, and 195 kN/mm2 for strand (clauses 3.3.6(2) and 3.3.6(3)).

Values of the modulus of elasticity are given in clause 3.1.3 and Table 3.1. The elastic modulus of concrete varies with other factors than just the strength (e.g. the aggregate type), and, if an accurate prediction of serviceability conditions is required, it will be necessary to establish the value of $E _ { \mathrm { { c m } } }$ by tests on the type of concrete actually being used.

The creep coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the creep deformation to the instantaneous elastic deformation, depends upon many factors, the most significant of which are the age at loading, the time under load, the relative humidity, the section geometry, the concrete strength and the type of cement. Other factors such as the aggregate type may also be significant. As with the modulus of elasticity, the only way of determining the creep performance of concrete with any real reliability is to obtain data from creep tests on the concrete actually being used. This information is rarely available, and more approximate means have to be adopted. The equations given in EN 1992-1-1 should be viewed in this light. Full equations for the prediction of the creep coefficient are given in Annex B. These have been used to produce design graphs (Fig. 3.1 in clause 3.1.4).

The free shrinkage strain depends upon the same basic variables as creep, and equations are given in Annex B for its prediction. Simplified values are given in clause 3.1.4.

Table 3.1 gives the mean tensile strength and the upper and lower characteristic tensile strengths as a function of the characteristic compressive strength of the concrete. Equations are also given in Table 3.1.

The question of the possible limitation of stresses under serviceability loads was the subject of a great deal of discussion during the drafting of EN 1992-1-1. The basic reasons for differences of opinion arose from the different way in which design methods had developed in different countries and a natural desire in each country that the new and untried Eurocode should not force design too far from existing experience in that country. Limitations on the compressive stress in the concrete were particularly contentious. In many countries, section design for both prestressed and reinforced concrete has been carried out on the basis of ultimate strength methods, and no explicit check has been required on the concrete stresses under service loads. These countries were determined that no such checks should be introduced since these could be shown to have a significant effect on the economy of some types of member, notably columns. Other countries have not so far adopted ultimate load methods, and still base their design on an elastic analysis of sections combined with a stress limit. While these countries were prepared to accept ultimate strength methods for section design, they also wanted to retain elastic design as an additional requirement to ensure that member sizes, particularly columns, did not become much smaller or more lightly reinforced than those arising from their current design methods. The check on the compressive stress in the concrete at the serviceability limit state provided them with this safeguard.

In order to develop a rational draft for this section of the code which would have some hope of general acceptance, an attempt was made to establish what rational basis existed for a limit on stresses under serviceability conditions. Two limits need to be considered: compressive stress limits and tensile stress limits. These will be considered in turn.

Two reasons are usually put forward for limiting compressive stresses in the concrete. These are (1) to avoid the formation of microcracks in the concrete which might reduce durability and (2) to avoid excessive creep. There is some logic in both reasons. It is commonly accepted that microcracking will start to develop in concrete when the compressive stress exceeds about 70% of the compressive strength. However, none of the established publications on durability suggest any relationship betweeen stress level, microcracking and durability problems (e.g. see CEB Bulletin d’Information 1859 ). EN 1992-1-1 suggests that, in aggressive environments (exposure classes XD, XF and XS), it may be reasonable to limit the stress to $0 . 6 f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ if other measures, such as an increase to the cover to any compressive reinforcement or the provision of confinement to the compressed concrete by transverse reinforcement.

The design methods used for checking serviceability assume that creep will be proportional to stress. This assumption is increasingly invalid as the stress increases above about 50% of the compressive strength. It could therefore be logical to impose a limit on compressive stress under the quasi-permanent combination of loads where a higher level of creep than might be predicted could seriously impair performance. This problem has been dealt with in clause 3.1.4, where a correction equation has been introduced which enables the creep to be calculated for levels of compressive stress above $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k ^ { \prime } } }$

It will be seen that there is no case for a blanket limitation to compressive stresses but that, in particular cases, it may be prudent to apply such limits if the effects of non-linear creep are not explicitly calculated. EN 1992-1-1 (clause 7.2) suggests that non-linear creep should be taken into account if the compressive stress exceeds $0 . 4 5 f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ under the quasi-permanent load.

In UK practice, compressive stresses have been checked in the design of prestressed members where high compressive stresses are likely to be present permanently, but no check has been required in the design of reinforced sections over the last 50 years. There has been no evidence of problems with performance that could be related to high compressive stress levels in service. It therefore seems reasonable to assume that there is no general requirement to check the compressive stresses in reinforced-concrete members under service conditions, although there may be special circumstances where this might be prudent.

In general, stress checks may be avoided for reinforced concrete …

EN 1992-1-1 covers concrete of strength up to 90 MPa in normal-weight concrete and 80 MPa in lightweight concrete. It relies on EN 206-1 for the specification and production of concrete.

In EN 1992-1-1 the compressive strength of concrete is denoted by concrete strength classes, which relate to the characteristic cylinder strength $f _ { \mathrm { c k } }$ or the cube strength $\bar { f } _ { \mathrm { c k , c u b e } } .$ The characteristic strength is defined as that strength below which not more than 5% of all test results are likely to fall. The relationship between the cylinder and cube strengths is given in the code, and is reproduced in Table 4.1.

The code provides models for strength development with time, and these should be used when concrete strength need to be calculated.

Table 4.1 also gives the mean tensile strength of concrete.

EN 1992-1-1 recognizes that deformation properties are crucially dependent on the composition of concrete, and in particular on the aggregates. Therefore, it provides only indicative information, which should be sufficient for most normal structures. However, in structures that are likely to be sensitive to deformation, it is advisable to determine the properties by controlled testing and appropriate specification.

Table 4.1 reproduces the mean values for the modulus of elasticity given in the code. The values given apply to concretes with quartzite aggregates. The reduction factors for other aggregates are as follows: limestone aggregates, 10%; basalt aggregates, 20%; and sandstone aggregates, 30%.



Poisson’s ratio may be taken as 0.2 for uncracked concrete, and 0 for cracked concrete. The coefficient of linear thermal expansion may be taken as $1 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 } / \mathrm { K }$

The creep and shrinkage of concrete depend on a number of factors, including the ambient humidity, the dimensions of the element, the composition of the concrete and the age of concrete at the time of loading. The long-term values of the creep coefficient $\varphi ( \infty , t _ { 0 } )$ are shown in Figs 4.1 and 4.2 for inside and outside conditions, respectively. The resulting strain in the member will be $\varphi ( \infty , t _ { 0 } ) ( \sigma _ { \mathrm { c } } / E _ { \mathrm { c } } )$ . to allow for the non-linearity of creep development.

Shrinkage has two components, namely drying shrinkage $( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c d } } )$ and autogenous shrinkage $( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c a } } )$ . Drying shrinkage is the result of expiration of moisture from the concrete to the surrounding air. On the other hand, the background document to EN 1992-1-1 defines autogenous shrinkage as ‘the macroscopic volume reduction of cementitious materials when cement hydrates, after initial setting. It does not include the volume change due to loss or ingress of substances, temperature variation or the application of external force and restraint’. Autogenous shrinkage is related inversely to the water/cement ratio, and will be significant for concretes of high strength.

The drying shrinkage strain at age t is $\beta _ { \mathrm { d s } } ( t , t _ { \mathrm { s } } ) k _ { \mathrm { h } } \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c d , 0 } } .$ . Tables 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 give the data for calculating shrinkage at 30, 100 and 1000 days, respectively.

Autogenous shrinkage strain at age t is given by $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c a } } ( t ) = \beta _ { \mathrm { a s } } \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { c a } } ( \infty )$ . Values at 30, 100 and 1000 days are given in Table 4.6.

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these te…

### 核心结论
在欧洲规范（Eurocode）中，混凝土抗压强度的平均强度（$f_{cm}$）、标准值（$f_{ck}$）与设计值（$f_{cd}$）之间存在明确的数学换算关系：
1. **平均强度与标准值**：$f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8 \text{ MPa}$ （针对28天龄期圆柱体强度）。
2. **标准值与设计值**：$f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc} \frac{f_{ck}}{\gamma_c}$。

---

### 详细关系说明

#### 1. 平均强度 ($f_{cm}$) 与 标准值 ($f_{ck}$) 的关系
* **标准值的定义**：混凝土抗压强度标准值 $f_{ck}$ 是指28天圆柱体抗压强度的5%分位值，即在所有测试结果中，仅有不超过5%的概率会低于该强度值 [Ref-5, Ref-7]。
* **数值换算**：在28天龄期时，混凝土圆柱体平均抗压强度 $f_{cm}$ 与标准值 $f_{ck}$ 的差值恒为 8 MPa，即 $f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8 \text{ MPa}$ [Ref-8, Ref-16, Ref-18]。
* **早龄期关系**：对于 $3 < t < 28$ 天的早龄期混凝土，其标准值与平均强度的关系同样为 $f_{ck}(t) = f_{cm}(t) - 8 \text{ MPa}$ [Ref-8, Ref-16]。

#### 2. 标准值 ($f_{ck}$) 与 设计值 ($f_{cd}$) 的关系
* **设计值的计算**：抗压强度设计值 $f_{cd}$ 是通过将标准值 $f_{ck}$ 除以混凝土材料分项安全系数 $\gamma_c$，并乘以转换系数 $\alpha_{cc}$ 来确定的 [Ref-6, Ref-11]。
* **计算公式**：$f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc} \frac{f_{ck}}{\gamma_c}$ [Ref-6, Ref-11]。

---

### 关键参数与适用条件提醒
* **系数 $\alpha_{cc}$**：该系数用于考虑长期荷载效应对抗压强度的影响以及加载方式带来的不利影响 [Ref-11, Ref-13]。规范推荐值为 **1.0**，但具体取值（通常在 0.8 到 1.0 之间）**必须查阅项目所在国的国家附录（National Annex）** [Ref-11]。例如，英国国家附录（UK NA）推荐取值为 0.85 [Ref-13]。
* **材料分项系数 $\gamma_c$**：用于覆盖材料性能可能出现的不利偏差，其具体数值需根据设计状况（如持久、短暂或偶然状况）及国家附录确定 [Ref-2, Ref-11]。
* **试件形状差异**：上述 $f_{cm}$ 与 $f_{ck}$ 的直接加减关系基于**圆柱体试件（cylinder）**。若使用立方体试件（cube），其标准值记为 $f_{ck,cube}$，圆柱体与立方体标准值之间存在特定的换算关系，需查阅规范中的强度等级对照表（如 EN 1992-1-1 的 Table 3.1） [Ref-5, Ref-18]。

---

### 依据位置
* **符号定义**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 1.6 [Ref-1]
* **标准值定义及与平均强度关系**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 3.1.2 [Ref-5, Ref-8, Ref-16]
* **设计值计算公式**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 3.1.6(1)P [Ref-11]；DG EN 1990, 6.3.3 [Ref-6]
* **强度等级与参数对照表**：DG EN 1992-1-1, Table 4.1 [Ref-18]
* **$\alpha_{cc}$ 系数说明及国家附录差异**：DG EN 1992-1-1, 4.1 [Ref-13]

The relationship between the cylinder and cube strengths is given in the code, and is reproduced in Table 4.1.

The code provides models for strength development with time, and these should be used when concrete strength need to be calculated.

Table 4.1 also gives the mean tensile strength of concrete.

sources_summary.highlight_text:
(1) The choice of adequately durable concrete for corrosion protection of reinforcement and protection of concrete attack, requires consideration of the composition of concrete. This may result in a higher compressive strength of the concrete than is required for structural design. Analysis may be elastic (without redistribution). This analysis may normally be based on the stiffness of the uncracked section; however, if it is suspected that cracking may have a significant unfavourable effect on the performance, then a more realistic analysis taking account of the cracking should be used. This possibility may be ignored for normal building structures.

The determination of the effects of prestress is covered in clause 5.10.9.

Clause 6.5.4 of EN 1990 states that the partial safety factor applied to material properties should generally be 1.0.

The properties of the materials which are normally significant in serviceability calculations are the modulus of elasticity of the reinforcement, the modulus of elasticity, the creep coefficient, the shrinkage strain and the tensile strength of the concrete. All this information is given in Section 3, but is summarized here for convenience.

For ordinary reinforcement this may be taken as 200 kN/mm2 (clause 3.2.7(4)). For prestressing steel, 205 kN/mm2 may be assumed for wires and bars, and 195 kN/mm2 for strand (clauses 3.3.6(2) and 3.3.6(3)).

Values of the modulus of elasticity are given in clause 3.1.3 and Table 3.1. The elastic modulus of concrete varies with other factors than just the strength (e.g. the aggregate type), and, if an accurate prediction of serviceability conditions is required, it will be necessary to establish the value of by tests on the type of concrete actually being used.

The creep coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the creep deformation to the instantaneous elastic deformation, depends upon many factors, the most significant of which are the age at loading, the time under load, the relative humidity, the section geometry, the concrete strength and the type of cement. Other factors such as the aggregate type may also be significant. As with the modulus of elasticity, the only way of determining the creep performance of concrete with any real reliability is to obtain data from creep tests on the concrete actually being used. This information is rarely available, and more approximate means have to be adopted. The equations given in EN 1992-1-1 should be viewed in this light. Full equations for the prediction of the creep coefficient are given in Annex B. These have been used to produce design graphs (Fig. 3.1 in clause 3.1.4).

The free shrinkage strain depends upon the same basic variables as creep, and equations are given in Annex B for its prediction. Simplified values are given in clause 3.1.4.

Table 3.1 gives the mean tensile strength and the upper and lower characteristic tensile strengths as a function of the characteristic compressive strength of the concrete. Equations are also given in Table 3.1.

The question of the possible limitation of stresses under serviceability loads was the subject of a great deal of discussion during the drafting of EN 1992-1-1. The basic reasons for differences of opinion arose from the different way in which design methods had developed in different countries and a natural desire in each country that the new and untried Eurocode should not force design too far from existing experience in that country. Limitations on the compressive stress in the concrete were particularly contentious. In many countries, section design for both prestressed and reinforced concrete has been carried out on the basis of ultimate strength methods, and no explicit check has been required on the concrete stresses under service loads. These countries were determined that no such checks should be introduced since these could be shown to have a significant effect on the economy of some types of member, notably columns. Other countries have not so far adopted ultimate load methods, and still base their design on an elastic analysis of sections combined with a stress limit. While these countries were prepared to accept ultimate strength methods for section design, they also wanted to retain elastic design as an additional requirement to ensure that member sizes, particularly columns, did not become much smaller or more lightly reinforced than those arising from their current design methods. The check on the compressive stress in the concrete at the serviceability limit state provided them with this safeguard.

In order to develop a rational draft for this section of the code which would have some hope of general acceptance, an attempt was made to establish what rational basis existed for a limit on stresses under serviceability conditions. Two limits need to be considered: compressive stress limits and tensile stress limits. These will be considered in turn.

Two reasons are usually put forward for limiting compressive stresses in the concrete. These are (1) to avoid the formation of microcracks in the concrete which might reduce durability and (2) to avoid excessive creep. There is some logic in both reasons. It is commonly accepted that microcracking will start to develop in concrete when the compressive stress exceeds about 70% of the compressive strength. However, none of the established publications on durability suggest any relationship betweeen stress level, microcracking and durability problems (e.g. see CEB Bulletin d’Information 1859 ). EN 1992-1-1 suggests that, in aggressive environments (exposure classes XD, XF and XS), it may be reasonable to limit the stress to if other measures, such as an increase to the cover to any compressive reinforcement or the provision of confinement to the compressed concrete by transverse reinforcement.

The design methods used for checking serviceability assume that creep will be proportional to stress. This assumption is increasingly invalid as the stress increases above about 50% of the compressive strength. It could therefore be logical to impose a limit on compressive stress under the quasi-permanent combination of loads where a higher level of creep than might be predicted could seriously impair performance. This problem has been dealt with in clause 3.1.4, where a correction equation has been introduced which enables the creep to be calculated for levels of compressive stress above 

It will be seen that there is no case for a blanket limitation to compressive stresses but that, in particular cases, it may be prudent to apply such limits if the effects of non-linear creep are not explicitly calculated. EN 1992-1-1 (clause 7.2) suggests that non-linear creep should be taken into account if the compressive stress exceeds under the quasi-permanent load.

In UK practice, compressive stresses have been checked in the design of prestressed members where high compressive stresses are likely to be present permanently, but no check has been required in the design of reinforced sections over the last 50 years. There has been no evidence of problems with performance that could be related to high compressive stress levels in service. It therefore seems reasonable to assume that there is no general requirement to check the compressive stresses in reinforced-concrete members under service conditions, although there may be special circumstances where this might be prudent.

In general, stress checks may be avoided for reinforced concrete …

EN 1992-1-1 covers concrete of strength up to 90 MPa in normal-weight concrete and 80 MPa in lightweight concrete. It relies on EN 206-1 for the specification and production of concrete.

In EN 1992-1-1 the compressive strength of concrete is denoted by concrete strength classes, which relate to the characteristic cylinder strength or the cube strength The characteristic strength is defined as that strength below which not more than 5% of all test results are likely to fall. The relationship between the cylinder and cube strengths is given in the code, and is reproduced in Table 4.1.

The code provides models for strength development with time, and these should be used when concrete strength need to be calculated.

Table 4.1 also gives the mean tensile strength of concrete.

EN 1992-1-1 recognizes that deformation properties are crucially dependent on the composition of concrete, and in particular on the aggregates. Therefore, it provides only indicative information, which should be sufficient for most normal structures. However, in structures that are likely to be sensitive to deformation, it is advisable to determine the properties by controlled testing and appropriate specification.

Table 4.1 reproduces the mean values for the modulus of elasticity given in the code. The values given apply to concretes with quartzite aggregates. The reduction factors for other aggregates are as follows: limestone aggregates, 10%; basalt aggregates, 20%; and sandstone aggregates, 30%.

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these te…

The partial factor is intended to cover the possibility of unfavourable deviations of the material or product property from its characteristic value and the random part of the conversion factor. Indeed, the conversion factor may be considered as a random variable: its scatter around the mean value is assumed to be taken into account in the factor.

The variability in geometrical quantities is usually less significant than the variability in actions and material or product properties, and in many cases is negligible. Consequently, design values of geometrical data are generally represented by the nominal value (clause 6.3.4(1)):

Clause 6.3.4(1)

The nominal (reference) dimension is the basic dimension which is used in design drawings and documentation. All deviations of the geometric quantities are related to it. The geometrical value comprises not only the geometrical data as lengths and widths of a frame but also represents the so-called ‘perfect geometry’, in that sway imperfections of the frame or curvature imperfections of the members or inaccuracy of the excavation depth in front of sheet pilings are not considered. Such imperfections are reflected in the ‘additive reliability elements’ , as explained below. The design Eurocodes 1 to 9 give appropriate specifications.

Where deviations in the geometrical data have a significant effect on the reliability of a structure (e.g. slender columns or thin silo walls), the geometrical design values are defined by (clause 6.3.4(2)P)

Clause 6.3.4(2)P

where takes account of the possibility of unfavourable deviations from the characteristic or nominal values and the cumulative effect of a simultaneous occurrence of several geometrical deviations. It should be noted that is introduced only where the influence of deviations is critical (e.g. imperfections in buckling analysis). Values of are given in Eurocodes 2 to 9.

The general expression of the design resistance of a structural member is (clause 6.3.5(1))

where is a partial factor covering uncertainty in the resistance model, plus geometric deviations if these are not modelled explicitly (see clause 6.3.4(2)), and is the design value of material property i.

Clause 6.3.4(2)

Variations of expression (6.6) are given in the design Eurocodes 1 to 9, because the characteristic value of the resistance for a given material, or way of construction, may be expressed in various ways, for example:

as the resistance of a member (e.g. the beam–column resistance), where may be a linear or a non-linear function of many geometrical parameters, material parameters and parameters for structural and geometrical imperfections

items.question: 钢筋的锚固长度与搭接长度受哪些因素影响？
items.category: 构造规定与抗震补充层
items.answer:
根据欧洲规范 EN 1992-1-1 及其相关设计指南，钢筋的锚固长度与搭接长度受钢筋自身属性、混凝土性能、构造细节及受力状态等多方面因素的综合影响。具体影响因素可划分为以下三个层次：

### 一、 影响基本锚固长度（$l_{b,rqd}$）的核心因素
基本锚固长度是计算设计锚固长度和搭接长度的基础，主要受以下因素影响：
1. **钢筋特性**：包括钢筋直径（$\phi$）、钢筋在设计截面处的设计应力（$\sigma_{sd}$）以及钢筋的表面特征（如光圆或带肋）[Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-11, Ref-14]。对于大直径钢筋，其极限粘结应力会有所降低 [Ref-2, Ref-4]。
2. **混凝土性能**：极限粘结应力主要取决于混凝土的抗拉强度设计值（$f_{ctd}$ 或 $f_{ctk}$）[Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-11]。
3. **粘结条件（Bond condition）**：与钢筋在混凝土中的位置及浇筑方向有关。规范将其分为“良好（good）”和“较差（poor）”两种粘结条件，较差的粘结条件会显著降低粘结应力（折减系数 $\eta_1 = 0.7$）[Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-11]。

### 二、 影响设计锚固长度（$l_{bd}$）的构造与修正因素
设计锚固长度是在基本锚固长度的基础上，通过乘以一系列修正系数（$\alpha_1 \sim \alpha_5$）来确定的，主要受以下构造和受力因素影响：
1. **钢筋形状（$\alpha_1$）**：直筋、标准弯钩、弯折或环形等不同锚固形状的影响 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
2. **混凝土保护层厚度（$\alpha_2$）**：最小混凝土保护层厚度或钢筋净距对劈裂裂缝的约束影响 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
3. **横向钢筋约束（$\alpha_3$）**：非焊接横向钢筋（如箍筋）提供的约束作用 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
4. **焊接横向钢筋（$\alpha_4$）**：沿设计锚固长度内存在的焊接横向钢筋（直径 $>0.6\phi$）的影响 [Ref-4]。
5. **横向压力（$\alpha_5$）**：垂直于潜在劈裂面的横向压力影响 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
*注：设计锚固长度还必须满足规范规定的最小锚固长度（$l_{b,min}$）限值要求 [Ref-4]。*

### 三、 影响搭接长度（$l_0$）的特有因素
搭接长度基于基本锚固长度计算，因此受上述所有基本因素的影响 [Ref-3, Ref-7]。此外，还受以下搭接特有因素影响：
1. **同一截面搭接钢筋比例（$\alpha_6$）**：同一截面（包含该截面两侧 $0.65l_0$ 范围内）搭接钢筋面积占总钢筋面积的比例（$\rho_1$）。当搭接比例大于 50% 时，搭接长度需乘以 1.0 至 1.5 的放大系数 [Ref-3, Ref-7]。
2. **搭接钢筋的净距**：当搭接钢筋之间的净距大于 4 倍钢筋直径（$4\phi$）时，搭接长度需要增加，增加量等于净距超出 $4\phi$ 的部分 [Ref-9]。

### 四、 国家附录与适用条件提示
- **大直径钢筋折减差异**：欧洲规范 EN 1992-1-1 规定当钢筋直径 $\phi > 32\text{ mm}$ 时需对粘结应力进行折减（系数 $\eta_2$）[Ref-4]。但在**英国国家附录（UK National Annex）** 中，大直径钢筋被定义为 $\phi > 40\text{ mm}$，且其折减计算公式与欧洲规范原版存在差异 [Ref-2, Ref-11]。工程师在实际项目中需确认所适用国家附录的具体规定。
- **高强混凝土限制**：由于高强混凝土的脆性增加，在计算粘结粘结应力时，混凝土抗拉强度特征值（$f_{ctk,0.05}$）的上限被限制为 C60/75 强度等级的值，除非能证明平均粘结强度在此限值之上仍有提高 [Ref-4]。

### 依据位置
- **基本锚固长度与粘结应力**：[Ref-1] (6.6节), [Ref-2] (10.2.4节), [Ref-4] (8.4.2节, 8.4.3节), [Ref-5] (8.4.3节), [Ref-8] (6.6节), [Ref-10] (8.4.3节), [Ref-11] (Detailing章节), [Ref-13] (10.2节), [Ref-14] (公式8.3)
- **设计锚固长度修正系数**：[Ref-4] (8.4.4节及Table 8.2相关说明), [Ref-9] (10.3节), [Ref-11] (Detailing章节)
- **搭接长度及特有修正系数**：[Ref-3] (10.5节), [Ref-7] (10.5.2节), [Ref-9] (图10.6说明)

我需要根据提供的证据片段，整理出影响钢筋锚固长度和搭接长度的因素，并给出依据。

首先，分析锚固长度（Anchorage length）的影响因素：
1. 基本锚固长度（Basic anchorage length, $l_{b,rqd}$）：
   - 钢筋直径（$\phi$） [Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-5, Ref-10, Ref-11, Ref-13, Ref-14]
   - 钢筋设计应力（$\sigma_{sd}$） [Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-5, Ref-10, Ref-11, Ref-13, Ref-14]
   - 极限粘结应力设计值（$f_{bd}$） [Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-5, Ref-10, Ref-11, Ref-13, Ref-14]
     - 混凝土抗拉强度（$f_{ctd}$ 或 $f_{ctk}$） [Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-11, Ref-13]
     - 粘结条件（Bond condition，'good' 或 'poor'，与钢筋在混凝土中的位置/浇筑方向有关，系数 $\eta_1$） [Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-11, Ref-13]
     - 钢筋直径大小（大直径钢筋如 >32mm 会降低粘结应力，系数 $\eta_2$） [Ref-2, Ref-4, Ref-11, Ref-13]
     - 钢筋表面特征（如带肋钢筋） [Ref-1, Ref-4, Ref-8, Ref-11]
2. 设计锚固长度（Design anchorage length, $l_{bd}$）：
   - 在基本锚固长度基础上乘以修正系数（$\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3, \alpha_4, \alpha_5$） [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]
   - $\alpha_1$：钢筋形状（直筋、弯钩、弯折等）的影响 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-9, Ref-11]
   - $\alpha_2$：混凝土最小保护层厚度的影响 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]
   - $\alpha_3$：横向钢筋（非焊接）提供的约束作用 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]
   - $\alpha_4$：沿设计锚固长度内焊接横向钢筋的影响 [Ref-4]
   - $\alpha_5$：横向压力的影响 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]
   - 最小锚固长度限制（$l_{b,min}$） [Ref-4]

其次，分析搭接长度（Lap length）的影响因素：
1. 搭接长度基于基本锚固长度计算，因此受上述所有基本锚固长度因素的影响 [Ref-3, Ref-7]

   - 搭接钢筋的间距/净距（如净距 > 4$\phi$ 时需要增加搭接长度） [Ref-9, 图10.6说明]

1. 直接结论：概述锚固长度和搭接长度受钢筋自身属性、混凝土性能、构造细节及受力状态等多方面因素影响。

3. 横向钢筋约束（$\alpha_3$）：非焊接横向钢筋（如箍筋）提供的约束作用 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
4. 焊接横向钢筋（$\alpha_4$）：沿锚固长度内存在的焊接横向钢筋的影响 [Ref-4]。
5. 横向压力（$\alpha_5$）：垂直于劈裂面的横向压力影响 [Ref-4, Ref-9, Ref-11]。
此外，设计锚固长度还必须满足最小锚固长度（$l_{b,min}$）的限值要求 [Ref-4]。

三、 搭接长度的特有影响因素
搭接长度基于基本锚固长度计算，因此受上述所有基本因素的影响 [Ref-3, Ref-7]。此外，还受以下搭接特有因素影响：
1. 同一截面搭接钢筋比例（$\alpha_6$）：同一截面（包含两侧 $0.65l_0$ 范围内）搭接钢筋面积占总钢筋面积的比例（$\rho_1$）。当比例大于 50% 时，搭接长度需乘以 1.0 至 1.5 的放大系数 [Ref-3, Ref-7]。
2. 搭接钢筋的净距：当搭接钢筋之间的净距大于 4倍钢筋直径（$4\phi$）时，搭接长度需要增加，增加量等于净距超出 $4\phi$ 的部分 [Ref-9]。

四、 依据位置汇总
（列出引用的 Ref 编号）

- 每一个关键结论绑定出处：是的。

- 指南文档只能作为补充：是的，DG 文档作为补充说明。

细化国家附录提示：
在提到大直径钢筋折减时，补充说明：欧洲规范规定 $\phi > 32$ mm 时进行折减，但在英国国家附录（UK National Annex）中，大直径钢筋被定义为大于 40 mm，且折减公式有所不同 [Ref-2, Ref-11]。

In EN 1992-1-1 the parameter $l _ { \mathrm { b , r e q d } }$ (basic anchorage length) is used in the calculation of design anchorage and lap lengths:



where $\phi$ is the diameter of the bar, $\sigma _ { \mathrm { s d } }$ is the stress in the bar and $f _ { \mathrm { b d } }$ is the design value of ultimate bond stress. The axial force in the bar is assumed to be distributed uniformly over this length through bond stress between the reinforcement and concrete.

The ultimate bond stress basically depends upon the tensile strength of concrete and the location of the bar within the concrete. The latter is referred to as ‘bond condition’. EN 1992- 1-1 defines ‘good’ and ‘poor’ bond conditions, and these are shown in Fig. 10.2. There is also test evidence to show that the ultimate bond stress has some dependence on the size of the bar. EN 1992-1-1 de-rates the bond stress for large-diameter bars. In the UK National Annex it is defined as bars larger than 40 mm. The above factors are reflected in the expression for the ultimate stress:



where $\eta _ { 1 }$ is 1.0 for ‘good’ bond conditions and 0.7 for ‘poor’ bond conditions and $\eta _ { 2 } = 1 . 0$ for bar $\phi \leq 3 2$ mm and $( 1 3 2 - \phi ) / 1 0 0$ for bar $\phi > 3 2$ mm. In the UK this expression should strictly be $( 1 4 0 - \phi ) / 1 0 0$

Table 10.2 shows the ultimate bond stress for different grades of concrete together with values of basic anchorage lengths assuming full design stress in the bars.

As the length of reinforcement bars is generally likely to be less than the length of the structure, lapping (or splicing) of bars will be necessary in most structural elements. At laps, forces are transmitted from one bar to another. This can be achieved through the concrete surrounding the lapping bars or by welding of the bars or by mechanical couplers.

Lapped bars should comply with the arrangement shown in Fig. 10.6.

Design lap length is calculated by modifying the basic anchorage length (see Section 10.2.4 above) by applying multipliers:



where $\alpha _ { 1 } , \alpha _ { 2 } , \alpha _ { 3 }$ and $\alpha _ { 5 }$ are as discussed for anchorage and $\alpha _ { 6 }$ allows for the effect of the amount of reinforcement that is lapped at one section:



with values in the range $1 . 0 \mathrm { - } 1 . 5 \left( \mathrm { f o r } \ \rho _ { 1 } > 5 0 \% \right)$ . The amount of reinforcement lapped at one section includes any laps occurring within $0 . 6 5 l _ { 0 }$ on either side of the section.

sources.original_text:
The basic anchorage length can be modified to allow for such effects as the shape of the bars, the size of the concrete cover, confinement offered by transverse reinforcement or transverse pressure. In EN 1992-1-1, the design anchorage length is obtained by multiplying the basic anchorage length by a number of factors:



for anchorage in tension and



for anchorage in compression; the product $\alpha _ { 2 } \alpha _ { 3 } \alpha _ { 5 }$ should be $\geq 0 . 7$ . Values of the different multipliers together with the conditions that should be met are given in the code and are not reproduced here. However, the applicability of these in practice are discussed below.

The following applies to bars in tension:

$\alpha _ { 1 }$ allows for the shape of the bars. For straight bars, $\alpha _ { 1 } = 1 . 0$ . For curved bars, $\alpha _ { 1 }$ may be taken as 0.7, provided that the lesser of the side cover to the bars or half the clear spacing between bars i $\mathfrak { s } \geq 3 \phi$ . It will be difficult to meet this condition in all but a few practical cases.

$\alpha _ { 2 }$ allows for the effect of the size of concrete cover. For straight bars in tension, some reduction will be possible when the parameter $c _ { \mathrm { d } }$ is between $\phi$ and $3 \phi ,$ where $c _ { \mathrm { d } }$ is the least of the side or bottom cover or half the clear spacing between the bars. In the case of curved bars this benefit does not accrue until $c _ { \mathrm { d } }$ is larger than $3 \phi .$ Again, advantage can be taken of this reduction only in a limited number of practical cases.

$\alpha _ { 3 }$ allows for the effect of confinement offered by transverse reinforcement, which is not welded to main bars. The transverse reinforcement should be placed between the concrete surface and the bar that is being anchored. The reduction will be enhanced if the transverse reinforcement is in the form of links. Even so, the reduction that can be achieved in beams will only be 0.925 when $\sum { A _ { \mathrm { s t } } } = 1 . 0 A _ { \mathrm { s t } }$ s .

In clause 8.4.1, EN 1992-1-1 states that transverse reinforcement should be provided if necessary. There is no other direct guidance. In the section dealing with design anchorage length there are references to transverse reinforcement. This could be interpreted to mean that there is no specific requirement for transverse reinforcement. This is unlike the requirements in the ENV, which still appear to be prudent, and are repeated here:

In beams, transverse reinforcement should be provided for anchorage in tension, if there is no transverse compression due to support reaction (e.g. indirect supports); and for all compression anchorage.

The minimum total area of the transverse reinforcement (the area of the legs parallel to the plane of the longitudinal reinforcement) is 25% of the area of one anchored bar. (Fig. 10.4).

The transverse reinforcement should be distributed evenly along the anchorage length, and at least one bar should be placed in the region of the hook, bend or loop of any curved bars.

For bars in compression, transverse reinforcement should surround the bars, being concentrated at the end of the anchorage and extend beyond it to a distance of at least four times the diameter of the anchored bar. This is a precaution against bursting forces that are likely to arise due to the ‘pin effect’ at the end of the bar.

In clause 8.4.1, EN 1992-1-1 states that transverse reinforcement should be provided if necessary. There is no other direct guidance. In the section dealing with design anchorage length there are references to transverse reinforcement. This could be interpreted to mean that there is no specific requirement for transverse reinforcement. This is unlike the requirements in the ENV, which still appear to be prudent, and are repeated here:

In beams, transverse reinforcement should be provided for anchorage in tension, if there is no transverse compression due to support reaction (e.g. indirect supports); and for all compression anchorage.

The minimum total area of the transverse reinforcement (the area of the legs parallel to the plane of the longitudinal reinforcement) is 25% of the area of one anchored bar. (Fig. 10.4).

The transverse reinforcement should be distributed evenly along the anchorage length, and at least one bar should be placed in the region of the hook, bend or loop of any curved bars.

For bars in compression, transverse reinforcement should surround the bars, being concentrated at the end of the anchorage and extend beyond it to a distance of at least four times the diameter of the anchored bar. This is a precaution against bursting forces that are likely to arise due to the ‘pin effect’ at the end of the bar.
