sources.section: Prestressed concrete > 11.7. Prestress losses
sources.original_text:
The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to allow for losses of prestress when calculating the design forces in tendons at the various stages considered in the design. The causes of these losses are listed in EN 1992-1-1. Because of the uncertainty in estimating such losses, it is suggested that values are taken from European technical approval documents where these are available. In the absence of such data, EN 1992-1-1 suggests values for the various parameters that can be used for design.

Loss of prestressing force due to friction in the jack and anchorages is not mentioned in EN 1992-1-1. It is not generally a problem for the designer, because the design is normally based on the tendon force on the concrete member side of the jack. However, it does need to be allowed for in calibration of the actual jack used for stressing.

EN 1992-1-1 specifies the standard formula for calculating the force lost in overcoming duct friction when the tendon is stressed. This separates the loss into two parts:

(1) that caused by the tendon and duct following the specified profile (2) that caused by slight variations in the actual line of the duct, which may cause additional points of contact between the tendon and the duct wall.

The losses are calculated in terms of the coefficient of friction µ and an unintentional Clause 5.10.5.2(2)angular displacement per metre length k. Values of µ for a range of internal tendons which fill about 50% of the duct and for a range of external unbonded tendons in different ducts are Clause 5.10.5.2(3)given in EN 1992-1-1, which also suggests that k should be taken between 0.005 and Clause 5.10.5.2(4)0.01 rad/m. The loss of prestress due to unintentional angular displacements may be ignored Clause 5.10.5.2(1)for external tendons. Rather than using these values, it is generally better to refer to European technical approval documents or test results produced by the manufacturers of prestressing components; EN 1992-1-1 allows the designer to adopt this approach.

The method specified for the calculation of losses due to the immediate elastic deformation of the concrete when the prestressing force is applied follows normal procedures.

Clause 6.3.1(2)

EN 1992-1-1 mentions this cause of loss of prestressing force, but does not specify the values to be used. Appropriate values can be obtained from European technical approval documents and from the anchorage manufacturers, and should be checked on site, particularly if the member is short, when the loss due to this cause can be critical.

The loss due to anchorage draw-in, $\Delta P$ is given by



where



$E _ { \mathrm { p } }$ is the modulus of elasticity of tendons

$A _ { \mathrm { p s } }$ is the area of prestressing tendons

$\delta$ is the anchorage draw-in

$m$ is the rate of change of prestressing force due to friction, which may be taken as $P _ { 0 } \mu ( \alpha + k )$

$\mu$ is the coefficient of friction

$\alpha$ is the angular deviation per unit length

k is the unintentional angular deviation per unit length
[-> Formula]
[-> Formula]

Time-dependent losses are those due to relaxation of the prestressing tendons and shrinkage and creep of the concrete. EN 1992-1-1 considers the loss due to each effect, as if that effect were acting alone, and then combines them taking 80% of the relaxation loss to account for the effect of creep and shrinkage reducing the stress in the tendon. The formula given in EN 1992-1-1 further reduces the combined loss to allow for the reduction in compressive stress in the concrete as the prestress force reduces with time.

The method specified for the calculation of losses due to the immediate elastic deformation of the concrete when the prestressing force is applied follows normal procedures.

Clause 6.3.1(2)

EN 1992-1-1 mentions this cause of loss of prestressing force, but does not specify the values to be used. Appropriate values can be obtained from European technical approval documents and from the anchorage manufacturers, and should be checked on site, particularly if the member is short, when the loss due to this cause can be critical.

(1) The losses due to friction $\Delta P _ { \mu } ( x )$ in post-tensioned tendons may be estimated from:



where:

$\theta$ is the sum of the angular displacements over a distance x (irrespective of direction or sign)   
$\mu$ is the coefficient of friction between the tendon and its duct   
$k$ is an unintentional angular displacement for internal tendons (per unit length)   
$\mathsf { \pmb X }$ is the distance along the tendon from the point where the prestressing force is equal to $P _ { \mathrm { { m a x } } }$ (the force at the active end during tensioning)

The values $\mu$ and $k$ are given in the relevant European Technical Approval. The value $\mu$ depends on the surface characteristics of the tendons and the duct, on the presence of rust, on the elongation of the tendon and on the tendon profile.

The value $k$ for unintentional angular displacement depends on the quality of workmanship, on the distance between tendon supports, on the type of duct or sheath employed, and on the degree of vibration used in placing the concrete.

(2) In the absence of data given in a European Technical Approval the values for $\mu$ given in Table 5.1 may be assumed, when using Expression (5.45).

(4) For external tendons, the losses of prestress due to unintentional angles may be ignored.

sources.original_text:
(1)P The properties of prestressing steel are given in EN 10138, Parts 2 to 4 or European Technical Approval.

(2)P The prestressing tendons (wires, strands and bars) shall be classified according to:

(i) Strength, denoting the value of the $0 , 1 \%$ proof stress $( f _ { \mathsf { p } 0 , 1 \mathsf { k } } )$ and the value of the ratio of tensile strength to proof strength $( f _ { \mathrm { p k } } / f _ { \mathrm { p 0 } , 1 \mathrm { k } } )$ and elongation at maximum load $\left( \varepsilon _ { \mathsf { U k } } \right)$   
(ii) Class, indicating the relaxation behaviour   
(iii) Size   
(iv) Surface characteristics.

(3)P The actual mass of the prestressing tendons shall not differ from the nominal mass by more than the limits specified in EN 10138 or given in an appropriate European Technical Approval.

(4)P In this Eurocode, three classes of relaxation are defined:

Class 1: wire or strand - ordinary relaxation Class 2: wire or strand - low relaxation Class 3: hot rolled and processed bars

Note: Class 1 is not covered by EN 10138.

(5) The design calculations for the losses due to relaxation of the prestressing steel should be based on the value of $\rho _ { 1 0 0 0 }$ , the relaxation loss (in $\%$ ) at 1000 hours after tensioning and at a mean temperature of ${ 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } C }$ (see EN 10138 for the definition of the isothermal relaxation test).

Note: The value of $\rho _ { 1 0 0 0 }$ is expressed as a percentage ratio of the initial stress and is obtained for an initial stress equal to $0 , 7 f _ { \mathrm { p } }$ , where $f _ { \mathfrak { p } }$ is the actual tensile strength of the prestressing steel samples. For design calculations, the characteristic tensile strength $( f _ { \mathsf { p k } } )$ is used and this has been taken into account in the following expressions.

(6) The values for $\rho _ { 1 0 0 0 }$ can be either assumed equal to $8 \%$ for Class 1, $2 { , } 5 \%$ for Class 2, and $4 \%$ for Class 3, or taken from the certificate.

(7) The relaxation loss may be obtained from the manufacturers test certificates or defined as the percentage ratio of the variation of the prestressing stress over the initial prestressing stress, should be determined by applying one of the Expressions below. Expressions (3.28) and (3.29) apply for wires or strands for ordinary prestressing and low relaxation tendons respectively, whereas Expression (3.30) applies for hot rolled and processed bars.

Class 1

Class 2



Class 3

Where

$\Delta \sigma _ { \mathsf { p r } }$ is absolute value of the relaxation losses of the prestress

For post-tensioning $\sigma _ { \mathsf { p i } }$ is the absolute value of the initial prestress $\sigma _ { \mathsf { p i } } = \sigma _ { \mathsf { p m } 0 }$ (see also 5.10.3 (2));

For pre-tensioning $\sigma _ { \mathsf { p i } }$ is the maximum tensile stress applied to the tendon minus the immediate losses occurred during the stressing process see 5.10.4 (1) (i)   
$t$ is the time after tensioning (in hours)   
$\mu$ $= \sigma _ { \mathsf { p i } } / f _ { \mathsf { p k } }$ ，where $\pmb { f } _ { \mathsf { p k } }$ is the characteristic value of the tensile strength of the prestressing steel   
$\rho _ { 1 0 0 0 }$ is the value of relaxation loss $( \mathrm { i n ~ } \% )$ ),at 1000 hours after tensioning and at a mean temperature of $\scriptstyle 2 0 ^ { \circ } \complement$ .

Note: Where the relaxation losses are calculated for different time intervals (stages) and greater accuracy is required, reference should be made to Annex D.

(8) The long term (final) values of the relaxation losses may be estimated for a time t equal to 500 000 hours (i.e. around 57 years).

(9) Relaxation losses are very sensitive to the temperature of the steel. Where heat treatment is applied (e.g. by steam), 10.3.2.2 applies. Otherwise where this temperature is greater than $5 0 \textdegree$ the relaxation losses should be verified.

(1)P The prestress considered in this Standard is that applied to the concrete by stressed tendons.

(2) The effects of prestressing may be considered as an action or a resistance caused by prestrain and precurvature. The bearing capacity should be calculated accordingly.

(3) In general prestress is introduced in the action combinations defined in EN 1990 as part of the loading cases and its effects should be included in the applied internal moment and axial force.

(4) Following the assumptions of (3) above, the contribution of the prestressing tendons to the resistance of the section should be limited to their additional strength beyond prestressing. This may be calculated assuming that the origin of the stress/strain relationship of the tendons is displaced by the effects of prestressing.

(5)P Brittle failure of the member caused by failure of prestressing tendons shall be avoided.

(6) Brittle failure should be avoided by one or more of the following methods:

Method A: Provide minimum reinforcement in accordance with 9.2.1.

Method B: Provide pretensioned bonded tendons.

Method C: Provide easy access to prestressed concrete members in order to check and control the condition of tendons by non-destructive methods or by monitoring.

Method D: Provide satisfactory evidence concerning the reliability of the tendons.

Method E: Ensure that if failure were to occur due to either an increase of load or a reduction of prestress under the frequent combination of actions, cracking would occur before the ultimate capacity would be exceeded, taking account of moment redistribution due to cracking effects.

Note: The selection of Methods to be used in a Country may be found in its National Annex.

sources.original_text:
The design of anchorage zones, or end blocks, in post-tensioned members is a very important area of design, but one that is rarely well-treated in codes of practice. EN 1992-1-1 is no exception, although it does draw attention to this important area and outlines the principles of the design.

The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to consider bearing stresses behind the anchorage, overall equilibrium and transverse tensile forces, i.e. bursting and spalling forces. The design is carried out at the ultimate limit state, and is based on $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p } } ~ ( = 1 . 2 )$ times the prestressing force. No check of crack widths is required when reinforcement stresses are limited to 300 MPa. Bearing stresses under anchorage plates should be checked in accordance with the relevant European technical approval. In practice, this means that the designer should check with the supplier the minimum concrete strength and reinforcement required adjacent to the anchorage. It is suggested that overall equilibrium be checked using a strut-and-tie method, and guidance is given on this and on the angle of dispersion of the prestressing force into the concrete section. Formulae are also given for determining the bursting forces behind an anchorage. This is of benefit to the designer. However, no guidance is given on how to design against spalling forces.

The designer should give particular attention to anchorage zones that have a cross-section of different shape from that of the general cross-section of the member.

For more information on the design and detailing of anchorage zones in prestressed concrete, the designer is referred to the excellent documents produced by CIRIA14 and the Institution of Structural Engineers.15

Guidance is provided in EN 1992-1-1 for estimating the transmission lengths in pretensioned members. A distinction is drawn between the transmission length over which the prestressing force is fully transmitted to the concrete $l _ { \mathrm { p t } } \mathrm { ; }$ the dispersion length over which the concrete stresses gradually disperse to a distribution compatible with plane sections remaining plane $l _ { \mathrm { d i s p } } ;$ and the anchorage length over which the tendon force at the ultimate limit state is fully transmitted to the concrete $l _ { \mathrm { b p d } } .$ The designer will find that this distinction helps to clarify the distribution of forces within the anchorage zone. Typical transmission and anchorage lengths for good bond conditions are given in Table 11.10.

The anchorage of pretensioned tendons at the ultimate limit state need only be checked if the concrete tensile stress in the anchorage zone exceeds $f _ { \mathrm { c t 0 . 0 5 k } }$ . The tendon force to be used should be calculated assuming a cracked cross-section and include the effect of shear.

Often pretensioned tendons are well distributed across the cross-section of the member so that forces induced by transfer of the prestressing force from the tendon positions to a linear distribution are low. In slabs these forces can often be resisted by the concrete alone without the need for ordinary reinforcement, whilst in beams it is generally satisfactory to reduce the stirrup spacing to approximately 75 mm throughout the transmission length. Where this is not the case, reinforcement to maintain overall equilibrium and carry any spalling forces should be provided as described in Section 11.8.2.

(1)P This clause applies to wires, bars and strands used as prestressing tendons in concrete structures.

(2)P Prestressing tendons shall have an acceptably low level of susceptibility to stress corrosion.

(3) The level of susceptibility to stress corrosion may be assumed to be acceptably low if the prestressing tendons comply with the criteria specified in EN 10138 or given in an appropriate European Technical Approval.

(4) The requirements for the properties of the prestressing tendons are for the materials as placed in their final position in the structure. Where the methods of production, testing and attestation of conformity for prestressing tendons are in accordance with EN 10138 or given in an appropriate European Technical Approval it may be assumed that the requirements of this Eurocode are met.

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these te…

sources.section: Prestressed concrete
sources.original_text:
In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The principles and methods given in EN 1992-1-1 are, in general, applicable to the full range of reinforced concrete construction. This chapter covers the aspects of design and detailing that are particular to prestressed concrete; those that apply equally to reinforced concrete are covered in other chapters of this guide.

EN 1992-1-1 covers the design of prestressed concrete members in which the prestress is applied by tendons; the tendons may be embedded in the concrete and may be pretensioned and bonded or post-tensioned and bonded or unbonded. The tendons may also be external to the structure with points of contact occurring at deviators and anchorages. It should be noted that second-order moments can be induced in prestressed members with external tendons if their points of contact with the concrete are sufficiently far apart.

The main clauses relating to the design of prestressed concrete in EN 1992-1-1 are summarized in Table 11.1.

Steel reinforcement and prestressing tendons are protected against corrosion by complying with EN 1992-1-1 requirements on stress levels, crack widths and concrete cover. EN 1992-1-1 specifies a ‘minimum’ cover, based on the greater of the requirements for bond or durability, to which a construction tolerance of 10 mm must be added.

For post-tensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should not be less than the duct diameter (for circular ducts), or the greater of the smaller dimension or half the larger dimension (for rectangular ducts). In no case does it need to be greater than 80 mm. Although EN 1992-1-1 specifies requirements for the minimum cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature for curved reinforcing bars, it does not specify similar requirements for curved prestressing tendons. This is an unfortunate omission, and the designer is recommended to refer to other codes, e.g. BS 8110, where specific requirements are stated for the prevention of bursting of the cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature. The requirements of BS 8110 are given in Table 11.2.

For pretensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should be not less than 1.5 the tendon diameter, or 2.5 times the diameter when indented wires are used. The minimum cover is not related to the aggregate size, but this will probably not be a problem in practice when the construction tolerance is taken into account.

The minimum cover to prestressing tendons and concrete strengths for durability requirements are given in Tables 4.3N, 4.5N and E.1N. The UK National Annex replaces these tables with two tables specifying minimum covers and concrete strengths, maximum water/cement ratios, minimum cement content, cement/combination types and equivalent designated concrete for different exposure classes and for intended working lives of 50 and

100 years (see Chapter 9). The tables are limited to exposure classes XC, XD and XS for a working life of 50 years and exposure class XC for a working life of 100 years because there is insufficient data to make recommendations for members exposed to other conditions. For selecting the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, the designer is referred to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

The UK tables allow a greater range of concrete strengths and covers and take advantage of the improved durability of blended cements to reduce minimum concrete strengths and increase water/cement ratios for the same cover. As far as the minimum cover to ensure durability is concerned, the UK Annex does not distinguish between normal reinforcement and prestressing tendons. EN 1992-1-1, on the other hand, suggests that greater covers should be provided to prestressing steel. Presumably this is because it is generally believed that the risks posed to prestressing tendons from the breakdown of the protection provided by the concrete are greater. In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The principles and methods given in EN 1992-1-1 are, in general, applicable to the full range of reinforced concrete construction. This chapter covers the aspects of design and detailing that are particular to prestressed concrete; those that apply equally to reinforced concrete are covered in other chapters of this guide.

EN 1992-1-1 covers the design of prestressed concrete members in which the prestress is applied by tendons; the tendons may be embedded in the concrete and may be pretensioned and bonded or post-tensioned and bonded or unbonded. The tendons may also be external to the structure with points of contact occurring at deviators and anchorages. It should be noted that second-order moments can be induced in prestressed members with external tendons if their points of contact with the concrete are sufficiently far apart.

chunks.content:
(1) The following losses occurring during pre-tensioning should be considered:

(i) during the stressing process: loss due to friction at the bends (in the case of curved wires or strands) and losses due to wedge draw-in of the anchorage devices.

(ii) before the transfer of prestress to concrete: loss due to relaxation of the pretensioning tendons during the period which elapses between the tensioning of the tendons and prestressing of the concrete.

Note: In case of heat curing, losses due to shrinkage and relaxation are modified and should be assessed accordingly; direct thermal effect should also be considered (see Annex D)

(iii) at the transfer of prestress to concrete: loss due to elastic deformation of concrete as the result of the action of pre-tensioned tendons when they are released from the anchorages.

chunks.title: DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2
chunks.section: Prestressed concrete > 11.7. Prestress losses
chunks.content:
The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to allow for losses of prestress when calculating the design forces in tendons at the various stages considered in the design. The causes of these losses are listed in EN 1992-1-1. Because of the uncertainty in estimating such losses, it is suggested that values are taken from European technical approval documents where these are available. In the absence of such data, EN 1992-1-1 suggests values for the various parameters that can be used for design.

Loss of prestressing force due to friction in the jack and anchorages is not mentioned in EN 1992-1-1. It is not generally a problem for the designer, because the design is normally based on the tendon force on the concrete member side of the jack. However, it does need to be allowed for in calibration of the actual jack used for stressing.

EN 1992-1-1 specifies the standard formula for calculating the force lost in overcoming duct friction when the tendon is stressed. This separates the loss into two parts:

(1) that caused by the tendon and duct following the specified profile (2) that caused by slight variations in the actual line of the duct, which may cause additional points of contact between the tendon and the duct wall.

The losses are calculated in terms of the coefficient of friction µ and an unintentional Clause 5.10.5.2(2)angular displacement per metre length k. Values of µ for a range of internal tendons which fill about 50% of the duct and for a range of external unbonded tendons in different ducts are Clause 5.10.5.2(3)given in EN 1992-1-1, which also suggests that k should be taken between 0.005 and Clause 5.10.5.2(4)0.01 rad/m. The loss of prestress due to unintentional angular displacements may be ignored Clause 5.10.5.2(1)for external tendons. Rather than using these values, it is generally better to refer to European technical approval documents or test results produced by the manufacturers of prestressing components; EN 1992-1-1 allows the designer to adopt this approach.

The method specified for the calculation of losses due to the immediate elastic deformation of the concrete when the prestressing force is applied follows normal procedures.

Clause 6.3.1(2)

Appropriate values can be obtained from European technical approval documents and from the anchorage manufacturers, and should be checked on site, particularly if the member is short, when the loss due to this cause can be critical.

$m$ is the rate of change of prestressing force due to friction, which may be taken as $P _ { 0 } \mu ( \alpha + k )$

[-> Formula]

Time-dependent losses are those due to relaxation of the prestressing tendons and shrinkage and creep of the concrete. EN 1992-1-1 considers the loss due to each effect, as if that effect were acting alone, and then combines them taking 80% of the relaxation loss to account for the effect of creep and shrinkage reducing the stress in the tendon. The formula given in EN 1992-1-1 further reduces the combined loss to allow for the reduction in compressive stress in the concrete as the prestress force reduces with time.

(1)P The prestress considered in this Standard is that applied to the concrete by stressed tendons.

(2) The effects of prestressing may be considered as an action or a resistance caused by prestrain and precurvature. The bearing capacity should be calculated accordingly.

(3) In general prestress is introduced in the action combinations defined in EN 1990 as part of the loading cases and its effects should be included in the applied internal moment and axial force.

(4) Following the assumptions of (3) above, the contribution of the prestressing tendons to the resistance of the section should be limited to their additional strength beyond prestressing. This may be calculated assuming that the origin of the stress/strain relationship of the tendons is displaced by the effects of prestressing.

(5)P Brittle failure of the member caused by failure of prestressing tendons shall be avoided.

(6) Brittle failure should be avoided by one or more of the following methods:

Method A: Provide minimum reinforcement in accordance with 9.2.1.

Method B: Provide pretensioned bonded tendons.

Method C: Provide easy access to prestressed concrete members in order to check and control the condition of tendons by non-destructive methods or by monitoring.

Method D: Provide satisfactory evidence concerning the reliability of the tendons.

Method E: Ensure that if failure were to occur due to either an increase of load or a reduction of prestress under the frequent combination of actions, cracking would occur before the ultimate capacity would be exceeded, taking account of moment redistribution due to cracking effects.

Note: The selection of Methods to be used in a Country may be found in its National Annex.

chunks.content:
The design of anchorage zones, or end blocks, in post-tensioned members is a very important area of design, but one that is rarely well-treated in codes of practice. EN 1992-1-1 is no exception, although it does draw attention to this important area and outlines the principles of the design.

The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to consider bearing stresses behind the anchorage, overall equilibrium and transverse tensile forces, i.e. bursting and spalling forces. The design is carried out at the ultimate limit state, and is based on $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p } } ~ ( = 1 . 2 )$ times the prestressing force. No check of crack widths is required when reinforcement stresses are limited to 300 MPa. Bearing stresses under anchorage plates should be checked in accordance with the relevant European technical approval. In practice, this means that the designer should check with the supplier the minimum concrete strength and reinforcement required adjacent to the anchorage. It is suggested that overall equilibrium be checked using a strut-and-tie method, and guidance is given on this and on the angle of dispersion of the prestressing force into the concrete section. Formulae are also given for determining the bursting forces behind an anchorage. This is of benefit to the designer. However, no guidance is given on how to design against spalling forces.

The designer should give particular attention to anchorage zones that have a cross-section of different shape from that of the general cross-section of the member.

For more information on the design and detailing of anchorage zones in prestressed concrete, the designer is referred to the excellent documents produced by CIRIA14 and the Institution of Structural Engineers.15

Guidance is provided in EN 1992-1-1 for estimating the transmission lengths in pretensioned members. A distinction is drawn between the transmission length over which the prestressing force is fully transmitted to the concrete $l _ { \mathrm { p t } } \mathrm { ; }$ the dispersion length over which the concrete stresses gradually disperse to a distribution compatible with plane sections remaining plane $l _ { \mathrm { d i s p } } ;$ and the anchorage length over which the tendon force at the ultimate limit state is fully transmitted to the concrete $l _ { \mathrm { b p d } } .$ The designer will find that this distinction helps to clarify the distribution of forces within the anchorage zone. Typical transmission and anchorage lengths for good bond conditions are given in Table 11.10.

The anchorage of pretensioned tendons at the ultimate limit state need only be checked if the concrete tensile stress in the anchorage zone exceeds $f _ { \mathrm { c t 0 . 0 5 k } }$ . The tendon force to be used should be calculated assuming a cracked cross-section and include the effect of shear.

Often pretensioned tendons are well distributed across the cross-section of the member so that forces induced by transfer of the prestressing force from the tendon positions to a linear distribution are low. In slabs these forces can often be resisted by the concrete alone without the need for ordinary reinforcement, whilst in beams it is generally satisfactory to reduce the stirrup spacing to approximately 75 mm throughout the transmission length. Where this is not the case, reinforcement to maintain overall equilibrium and carry any spalling forces should be provided as described in Section 11.8.2.

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these te…

In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The principles and methods given in EN 1992-1-1 are, in general, applicable to the full range of reinforced concrete construction. This chapter covers the aspects of design and detailing that are particular to prestressed concrete; those that apply equally to reinforced concrete are covered in other chapters of this guide.

EN 1992-1-1 covers the design of prestressed concrete members in which the prestress is applied by tendons; the tendons may be embedded in the concrete and may be pretensioned and bonded or post-tensioned and bonded or unbonded. The tendons may also be external to the structure with points of contact occurring at deviators and anchorages. It should be noted that second-order moments can be induced in prestressed members with external tendons if their points of contact with the concrete are sufficiently far apart.

The main clauses relating to the design of prestressed concrete in EN 1992-1-1 are summarized in Table 11.1.

Steel reinforcement and prestressing tendons are protected against corrosion by complying with EN 1992-1-1 requirements on stress levels, crack widths and concrete cover. EN 1992-1-1 specifies a ‘minimum’ cover, based on the greater of the requirements for bond or durability, to which a construction tolerance of 10 mm must be added.

For post-tensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should not be less than the duct diameter (for circular ducts), or the greater of the smaller dimension or half the larger dimension (for rectangular ducts). In no case does it need to be greater than 80 mm. Although EN 1992-1-1 specifies requirements for the minimum cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature for curved reinforcing bars, it does not specify similar requirements for curved prestressing tendons. This is an unfortunate omission, and the designer is recommended to refer to other codes, e.g. BS 8110, where specific requirements are stated for the prevention of bursting of the cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature. The requirements of BS 8110 are given in Table 11.2.

For pretensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should be not less than 1.5 the tendon diameter, or 2.5 times the diameter when indented wires are used. The minimum cover is not related to the aggregate size, but this will probably not be a problem in practice when the construction tolerance is taken into account.

The minimum cover to prestressing tendons and concrete strengths for durability requirements are given in Tables 4.3N, 4.5N and E.1N. The UK National Annex replaces these tables with two tables specifying minimum covers and concrete strengths, maximum water/cement ratios, minimum cement content, cement/combination types and equivalent designated concrete for different exposure classes and for intended working lives of 50 and

The tables are limited to exposure classes XC, XD and XS for a working life of 50 years and exposure class XC for a working life of 100 years because there is insufficient data to make recommendations for members exposed to other conditions. For selecting the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, the designer is referred to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

The UK tables allow a greater range of concrete strengths and covers and take advantage of the improved durability of blended cements to reduce minimum concrete strengths and increase water/cement ratios for the same cover. As far as the minimum cover to ensure durability is concerned, the UK Annex does not distinguish between normal reinforcement and prestressing tendons. EN 1992-1-1, on the other hand, suggests that greater covers should be provided to prestressing steel. Presumably this is because it is generally believed that the risks posed to prestressing tendons from the breakdown of the protection provided by the concrete are greater. parent_chunks.content:
(1)P The prestress considered in this Standard is that applied to the concrete by stressed tendons.

(2) The effects of prestressing may be considered as an action or a resistance caused by prestrain and precurvature. The bearing capacity should be calculated accordingly.

(3) In general prestress is introduced in the action combinations defined in EN 1990 as part of the loading cases and its effects should be included in the applied internal moment and axial force.

(4) Following the assumptions of (3) above, the contribution of the prestressing tendons to the resistance of the section should be limited to their additional strength beyond prestressing. This may be calculated assuming that the origin of the stress/strain relationship of the tendons is displaced by the effects of prestressing.

(5)P Brittle failure of the member caused by failure of prestressing tendons shall be avoided.

(6) Brittle failure should be avoided by one or more of the following methods:

Method A: Provide minimum reinforcement in accordance with 9.2.1.

Method B: Provide pretensioned bonded tendons.

Method C: Provide easy access to prestressed concrete members in order to check and control the condition of tendons by non-destructive methods or by monitoring.

Method D: Provide satisfactory evidence concerning the reliability of the tendons.

Method E: Ensure that if failure were to occur due to either an increase of load or a reduction of prestress under the frequent combination of actions, cracking would occur before the ultimate capacity would be exceeded, taking account of moment redistribution due to cracking effects.

guide_chunks.section: Prestressed concrete > 11.7. Prestress losses
guide_chunks.content:
The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to allow for losses of prestress when calculating the design forces in tendons at the various stages considered in the design. The causes of these losses are listed in EN 1992-1-1. Because of the uncertainty in estimating such losses, it is suggested that values are taken from European technical approval documents where these are available. In the absence of such data, EN 1992-1-1 suggests values for the various parameters that can be used for design.

Loss of prestressing force due to friction in the jack and anchorages is not mentioned in EN 1992-1-1. It is not generally a problem for the designer, because the design is normally based on the tendon force on the concrete member side of the jack. However, it does need to be allowed for in calibration of the actual jack used for stressing.

EN 1992-1-1 specifies the standard formula for calculating the force lost in overcoming duct friction when the tendon is stressed. This separates the loss into two parts:

(1) that caused by the tendon and duct following the specified profile (2) that caused by slight variations in the actual line of the duct, which may cause additional points of contact between the tendon and the duct wall.

The losses are calculated in terms of the coefficient of friction µ and an unintentional Clause 5.10.5.2(2)angular displacement per metre length k. Values of µ for a range of internal tendons which fill about 50% of the duct and for a range of external unbonded tendons in different ducts are Clause 5.10.5.2(3)given in EN 1992-1-1, which also suggests that k should be taken between 0.005 and Clause 5.10.5.2(4)0.01 rad/m. The loss of prestress due to unintentional angular displacements may be ignored Clause 5.10.5.2(1)for external tendons. Rather than using these values, it is generally better to refer to European technical approval documents or test results produced by the manufacturers of prestressing components; EN 1992-1-1 allows the designer to adopt this approach.

The method specified for the calculation of losses due to the immediate elastic deformation of the concrete when the prestressing force is applied follows normal procedures.

Clause 6.3.1(2)

EN 1992-1-1 mentions this cause of loss of prestressing force, but does not specify the values to be used. Appropriate values can be obtained from European technical approval documents and from the anchorage manufacturers, and should be checked on site, particularly if the member is short, when the loss due to this cause can be critical.

The loss due to anchorage draw-in, $\Delta P$ is given by



where

$A _ { \mathrm { p s } }$ is the area of prestressing tendons

$\delta$ is the anchorage draw-in

$m$ is the rate of change of prestressing force due to friction, which may be taken as $P _ { 0 } \mu ( \alpha + k )$

$\mu$ is the coefficient of friction

$\alpha$ is the angular deviation per unit length

k is the unintentional angular deviation per unit length
[-> Formula]

Time-dependent losses are those due to relaxation of the prestressing tendons and shrinkage and creep of the concrete. EN 1992-1-1 considers the loss due to each effect, as if that effect were acting alone, and then combines them taking 80% of the relaxation loss to account for the effect of creep and shrinkage reducing the stress in the tendon. The formula given in EN 1992-1-1 further reduces the combined loss to allow for the reduction in compressive stress in the concrete as the prestress force reduces with time.

guide_chunks.title: DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2
guide_chunks.section: Prestressed concrete > 11.8. Anchorage zones > 11.8.2. Post-tensioned members
guide_chunks.content:
The design of anchorage zones, or end blocks, in post-tensioned members is a very important area of design, but one that is rarely well-treated in codes of practice. EN 1992-1-1 is no exception, although it does draw attention to this important area and outlines the principles of the design.

The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to consider bearing stresses behind the anchorage, overall equilibrium and transverse tensile forces, i.e. bursting and spalling forces. The design is carried out at the ultimate limit state, and is based on $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p } } ~ ( = 1 . 2 )$ times the prestressing force. No check of crack widths is required when reinforcement stresses are limited to 300 MPa. Bearing stresses under anchorage plates should be checked in accordance with the relevant European technical approval. In practice, this means that the designer should check with the supplier the minimum concrete strength and reinforcement required adjacent to the anchorage. It is suggested that overall equilibrium be checked using a strut-and-tie method, and guidance is given on this and on the angle of dispersion of the prestressing force into the concrete section. Formulae are also given for determining the bursting forces behind an anchorage. This is of benefit to the designer. However, no guidance is given on how to design against spalling forces.

The designer should give particular attention to anchorage zones that have a cross-section of different shape from that of the general cross-section of the member.

For more information on the design and detailing of anchorage zones in prestressed concrete, the designer is referred to the excellent documents produced by CIRIA14 and the Institution of Structural Engineers.15

metadata.normalized_answer:
根据欧洲规范 EN 1992-1-1 及其相关设计指南，后张法（post-tensioning）预应力损失的计算分为**瞬时损失**和**随时间变化的损失**两大类。以下是具体的计算步骤、适用公式及参数取值说明。

### 1. 瞬时损失 (Immediate losses)
瞬时损失 $\Delta P_i(x)$ 发生在张拉和锚固过程中或刚完成时，主要包括以下四项 [Ref-1]：

#### (1) 摩擦引起的损失 $\Delta P_\mu(x)$
后张法预应力筋在管道中张拉时，由于管道偏差和曲线线形会产生摩擦损失 [Ref-6]。
* **计算公式** [Ref-17]：
  $$ \Delta P_\mu(x) = P_{max} \left( 1 - e^{-\mu(\theta + kx)} \right) $$
* **参数说明与取值** [Ref-6]：
  * $P_{max}$：张拉端施加的最大张拉力。
  * $\theta$：从张拉端到计算截面距离 $x$ 内，预应力筋角度变化的总和（不考虑方向或符号）。
  * $\mu$：预应力筋与管道之间的摩擦系数。**优先采用欧洲技术批准（ETA）或制造商提供的数据**；若无数据，可查规范表 5.1 取值。
  * $k$：内部预应力筋的无意角度偏差（每单位长度）。若无 ETA 数据，一般取 $0.005 < k < 0.01 \text{ rad/m}$。
  * $x$：从张拉端沿预应力筋的距离。
  * **适用条件限制**：对于**外部预应力筋**（external tendons），由无意角度偏差（即 $k$ 项）引起的预应力损失可以忽略 [Ref-6]。

#### (2) 锚具回缩/滑移引起的损失 $\Delta P_{sl}$
* **计算说明**：规范正文未直接指定具体计算数值，要求从 ETA 文件或锚具制造商处获取回缩量，并在现场进行核实（特别是对于短构件，该损失可能起控制作用） [Ref-4], [Ref-21]。
* **指南参考参数**：设计指南指出，锚具回缩损失 $\Delta P$ 的计算依赖于以下参数 [Ref-21]：
  * $\delta$：锚具回缩量（draw-in）。
  * $E_p$：预应力筋弹性模量；$A_{ps}$：预应力筋截面积。
  * $m$：由摩擦引起的预应力变化率，可近似取 $m = P_0 \mu (\alpha + k)$（其中 $\alpha$ 为单位长度的角度偏差）。

#### (3) 混凝土弹性变形引起的损失 $\Delta P_{el}$
* **计算说明**：由于后张法通常是逐根张拉，先张拉的钢筋会因后续钢筋张拉导致混凝土发生弹性压缩而产生损失。计算方法遵循常规结构力学程序，根据混凝土在预应力作用下的弹性应变进行计算 [Ref-1], [Ref-4]。

#### (4) 短期松弛损失 $\Delta P_r$
* 发生在张拉过程与锚固完成之间的短暂时间段内的钢筋松弛损失 [Ref-1]。

---

### 2. 随时间变化的损失 (Time-dependent losses)
随时间变化的损失 $\Delta P_{c+s+r}(x)$ 是由混凝土的收缩、徐变以及预应力钢筋的长期松弛共同引起的 [Ref-1]。规范提供了一个考虑这三者相互作用的简化综合计算公式。

#### (1) 综合损失计算公式
* **计算公式 (5.46)** [Ref-15], [Ref-18]：
  $$ \Delta P_{c+s+r} = A_p \Delta \sigma_{p,c+s+r} = A_p \frac{\varepsilon_{cs} E_p + 0.8 \Delta \sigma_{pr} + \frac{E_p}{E_{cm}} \varphi(t, t_0) \sigma_{c,QP}}{1 + \frac{E_p}{E_{cm}} \frac{A_p}{A_c} \left(1 + \frac{A_c}{I_c} z_{cp}^2\right) \left[1 + 0.8 \varphi(t, t_0)\right]} $$
  *(注：证据原文中准永久组合下的混凝土应力符号识别为 $\sigma_{c,op}$，实际应为 $\sigma_{c,QP}$)*
* **参数说明** [Ref-15]：
  * $\varepsilon_{cs}$：混凝土收缩应变估计值的绝对值（按规范 3.1.4(6) 计算）。
  * $E_p, E_{cm}$：分别为预应力钢和混凝土的弹性模量。
  * $\varphi(t, t_0)$：混凝土徐变系数。
  * $\sigma_{c,QP}$：在初始预应力和准永久作用组合下，预应力筋重心处的混凝土应力。
  * $A_p, A_c$：预应力筋和混凝土的截面积；$I_c$：混凝土截面惯性矩；$z_{cp}$：预应力筋重心至混凝土截面重心的距离。
  * $\Delta \sigma_{pr}$：由于预应力钢松弛引起的应力变化绝对值。
  * **相互作用折减**：公式中的系数 **0.8** 是为了考虑混凝土徐变和收缩会降低钢筋应力，从而相应减少钢筋松弛损失的交互影响 [Ref-15]。

#### (2) 钢筋松弛损失 $\Delta \sigma_{pr}$ 的计算
松弛损失需根据预应力筋的松弛类别（Class 1, 2, 3）单独计算 [Ref-7]。
* **初始应力取值**：对于后张法，计算松弛时的初始应力 $\sigma_{pi}$ 取锚固后的初始预应力绝对值，即 $\sigma_{pi} = \sigma_{pm0}$ [Ref-3], [Ref-7]。
* **计算公式 (以 Class 1 普通松弛钢丝/钢绞线为例，公式 3.28)** [Ref-16]：
  $$ \frac{\Delta \sigma_{pr}}{\sigma_{pi}} = 5.39 \rho_{1000} e^{6.7\mu} \left(\frac{t}{1000}\right)^{0.75(1-\mu)} 10^{-5} $$
* **参数说明** [Ref-3], [Ref-7]：
  * $\rho_{1000}$：张拉后 1000 小时、平均温度 20°C 时的松弛损失百分比。若无测试证书，可假定：Class 1 取 8%，Class 2（低松弛）取 2.5%，Class 3（热轧及加工钢筋）取 4%。
  * $\mu = \sigma_{pi} / f_{pk}$，其中 $f_{pk}$ 为预应力钢抗拉强度特征值。
  * $t$：张拉后的时间（小时）。**长期（最终）松弛损失**可按 $t = 500,000$ 小时（约 57 年）进行估算 [Ref-3], [Ref-7]。

sources_summary.highlight_text:
The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to allow for losses of prestress when calculating the design forces in tendons at the various stages considered in the design. The causes of these losses are listed in EN 1992-1-1. Because of the uncertainty in estimating such losses, it is suggested that values are taken from European technical approval documents where these are available. In the absence of such data, EN 1992-1-1 suggests values for the various parameters that can be used for design.

Loss of prestressing force due to friction in the jack and anchorages is not mentioned in EN 1992-1-1. It is not generally a problem for the designer, because the design is normally based on the tendon force on the concrete member side of the jack. However, it does need to be allowed for in calibration of the actual jack used for stressing.

EN 1992-1-1 specifies the standard formula for calculating the force lost in overcoming duct friction when the tendon is stressed. This separates the loss into two parts:

(1) that caused by the tendon and duct following the specified profile (2) that caused by slight variations in the actual line of the duct, which may cause additional points of contact between the tendon and the duct wall.

sources_summary.locator_text: The design of anchorage zones, or end blocks, in post-tensioned members is a very important area of design, but one that is rarely well-treated in codes of practice. EN 1992-1-1 is no exception, although it does draw attention to this
sources_summary.highlight_text:
The design of anchorage zones, or end blocks, in post-tensioned members is a very important area of design, but one that is rarely well-treated in codes of practice. EN 1992-1-1 is no exception, although it does draw attention to this important area and outlines the principles of the design.

The designer’s attention is drawn to the need to consider bearing stresses behind the anchorage, overall equilibrium and transverse tensile forces, i.e. bursting and spalling forces. The design is carried out at the ultimate limit state, and is based on times the prestressing force. No check of crack widths is required when reinforcement stresses are limited to 300 MPa. Bearing stresses under anchorage plates should be checked in accordance with the relevant European technical approval. In practice, this means that the designer should check with the supplier the minimum concrete strength and reinforcement required adjacent to the anchorage. It is suggested that overall equilibrium be checked using a strut-and-tie method, and guidance is given on this and on the angle of dispersion of the prestressing force into the concrete section. Formulae are also given for determining the bursting forces behind an anchorage. This is of benefit to the designer. However, no guidance is given on how to design against spalling forces.

The designer should give particular attention to anchorage zones that have a cross-section of different shape from that of the general cross-section of the member.

For more information on the design and detailing of anchorage zones in prestressed concrete, the designer is referred to the excellent documents produced by CIRIA14 and the Institution of Structural Engineers.15

sources_summary.highlight_text:
Guidance is provided in EN 1992-1-1 for estimating the transmission lengths in pretensioned members. A distinction is drawn between the transmission length over which the prestressing force is fully transmitted to the concrete the dispersion length over which the concrete stresses gradually disperse to a distribution compatible with plane sections remaining plane and the anchorage length over which the tendon force at the ultimate limit state is fully transmitted to the concrete The designer will find that this distinction helps to clarify the distribution of forces within the anchorage zone. Typical transmission and anchorage lengths for good bond conditions are given in Table 11.10.

The anchorage of pretensioned tendons at the ultimate limit state need only be checked if the concrete tensile stress in the anchorage zone exceeds . The tendon force to be used should be calculated assuming a cracked cross-section and include the effect of shear.

Often pretensioned tendons are well distributed across the cross-section of the member so that forces induced by transfer of the prestressing force from the tendon positions to a linear distribution are low. In slabs these forces can often be resisted by the concrete alone without the need for ordinary reinforcement, whilst in beams it is generally satisfactory to reduce the stirrup spacing to approximately 75 mm throughout the transmission length. Where this is not the case, reinforcement to maintain overall equilibrium and carry any spalling forces should be provided as described in Section 11.8.2.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). – as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

sources_summary.highlight_text:
In EN 1992-1-1, prestressed concrete is treated as part of a much wider material group known as reinforced concrete, which covers normal reinforced concrete through partially prestressed concrete to fully prestressed concrete. The principles and methods given in EN 1992-1-1 are, in general, applicable to the full range of reinforced concrete construction. This chapter covers the aspects of design and detailing that are particular to prestressed concrete; those that apply equally to reinforced concrete are covered in other chapters of this guide.

EN 1992-1-1 covers the design of prestressed concrete members in which the prestress is applied by tendons; the tendons may be embedded in the concrete and may be pretensioned and bonded or post-tensioned and bonded or unbonded. The tendons may also be external to the structure with points of contact occurring at deviators and anchorages. It should be noted that second-order moments can be induced in prestressed members with external tendons if their points of contact with the concrete are sufficiently far apart.

The main clauses relating to the design of prestressed concrete in EN 1992-1-1 are summarized in Table 11.1.

Steel reinforcement and prestressing tendons are protected against corrosion by complying with EN 1992-1-1 requirements on stress levels, crack widths and concrete cover. EN 1992-1-1 specifies a ‘minimum’ cover, based on the greater of the requirements for bond or durability, to which a construction tolerance of 10 mm must be added.

For post-tensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should not be less than the duct diameter (for circular ducts), or the greater of the smaller dimension or half the larger dimension (for rectangular ducts). In no case does it need to be greater than 80 mm. Although EN 1992-1-1 specifies requirements for the minimum cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature for curved reinforcing bars, it does not specify similar requirements for curved prestressing tendons. This is an unfortunate omission, and the designer is recommended to refer to other codes, e.g. BS 8110, where specific requirements are stated for the prevention of bursting of the cover perpendicular to the plane of curvature. The requirements of BS 8110 are given in Table 11.2.

For pretensioned members, the minimum cover for bond requirements should be not less than 1.5 the tendon diameter, or 2.5 times the diameter when indented wires are used. The minimum cover is not related to the aggregate size, but this will probably not be a problem in practice when the construction tolerance is taken into account.

The minimum cover to prestressing tendons and concrete strengths for durability requirements are given in Tables 4.3N, 4.5N and E.1N. The tables are limited to exposure classes XC, XD and XS for a working life of 50 years and exposure class XC for a working life of 100 years because there is insufficient data to make recommendations for members exposed to other conditions. For selecting the quality of concrete subject to freeze-thaw and concrete in aggressive ground conditions, the designer is referred to Annex A of BS 8500-1.

The UK tables allow a greater range of concrete strengths and covers and take advantage of the improved durability of blended cements to reduce minimum concrete strengths and increase water/cement ratios for the same cover. As far as the minimum cover to ensure durability is concerned, the UK Annex does not distinguish between normal reinforcement and prestressing tendons. EN 1992-1-1, on the other hand, suggests that greater covers should be provided to prestressing steel. Presumably this is because it is generally believed that the risks posed to prestressing tendons from the breakdown of the protection provided by the concrete are greater. items.question: 预应力在各类极限状态下的影响是什么
items.category: 复杂场景与多参数耦合层
items.answer:
基于欧洲规范 EN 1992-1-1 及其相关设计指南，预应力在承载能力极限状态（ULS）和正常使用极限状态（SLS）下的影响及设计考虑存在显著差异。以下为具体分类说明：

### 一、 承载能力极限状态 (ULS) 下的影响与设计
1. **分项系数取值**：在大多数情况下，预应力是有利影响，ULS 验证时应使用有利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,fav}$ [Ref-1, Ref-4, Ref-6]。EN 1992-1-1 推荐 $\gamma_{p,fav} = 1.0$，不利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,unfav} = 1.3$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
   *注意：英国国家附录 (UK NA) 将其修改为 $\gamma_{p,fav} = 0.9$ 和 $\gamma_{p,unfav} = 1.1$ [Ref-1, Ref-5]。*
2. **特殊情况的 ULS 验证**：
   - 对于外部预应力的整体稳定性极限状态，若预应力增加会产生不利影响，应使用 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$（推荐值 1.3）[Ref-6, Ref-16]。
   - 对于局部效应（如锚固区），也应使用 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$（推荐值 1.2）[Ref-6, Ref-16]。
3. **截面设计中的应变计算**：ULS 下需考虑初始应变 $\varepsilon_{p0}$ 乘以分项系数，并加上应变增量 $\Delta\varepsilon_p$ [Ref-1, Ref-5]。
   - **有粘结预应力筋**：应变增量等于预应力筋水平处混凝土的应变增量 [Ref-1, Ref-5]。
   - **无粘结和外部预应力筋**：应变增量需基于构件变形计算，或假定应力增加 100 N/mm² [Ref-1, Ref-5]。若使用平均属性计算变形，应力增量需乘以 $\gamma_{\Delta p}$（有利取 0.8，不利取 1.2）；若使用未开裂截面进行线性分析，则取 $\gamma_{\Delta p} = 1.0$ [Ref-1, Ref-5]。

### 二、 正常使用极限状态 (SLS) 下的影响与设计
1. **预应力特征值上下限**：SLS 下荷载和材料属性的分项系数通常为 1.0 [Ref-7, Ref-13, Ref-16]。预应力采用上限 ($r_{sup}$) 或下限 ($r_{inf}$) 特征值，取对设计更不利的值 [Ref-5]。
   - 先张或无粘结筋：上限 1.05，.05，下限 0.95（乘以平均值）[Ref-2, Ref-5]。
   - 后张有粘结筋：上限 1.1，下限 0.9 [Ref-2, Ref-5]。
   - *注意：英国国家附录 (UK NA) 简化采用单一值 1.0 [Ref-2, Ref-5]；对于受剪设计，EN 和 UK 均取 1.0 [Ref-2]。*
2. **裂缝控制**：SLS 需考虑特征、频遇和准永久三种荷载组合 [Ref-5, Ref-7]。根据暴露类别和预应力筋类型，裂缝宽度限制如下 [Ref-3]：
   - **无粘结筋**（准永久荷载）：所有暴露类别限制为 0.3 mm [Ref-3]。
   - **有粘结筋**（频遇荷载）：X0、XC1 及 XC2~XC4 类别限制为 0.2 mm；XD、XS 类别要求消压 (Decompression) [Ref-3]。
   - **有粘结筋**（准永久荷载）：XC2~XC4 类别要求消压 [Ref-3]。
3. **混凝土应力限制与徐变**：
   - 在侵蚀性环境（XD, XF, XS）中，建议将 SLS 下的混凝土压应力限制在 $0.6 f_{ck}$，或采取增加保护层/横向约束等措施 [Ref-13]。
   - 若准永久组合下压应力超过 $0.45 f_{ck}$，应考虑非线性徐变的影响 [Ref-13]。

### 三、 疲劳及其他时间依存效应
1. **疲劳极限状态**：疲劳验证时，预应力的有利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,fav}$ 推荐值同样可取 1.0 [Ref-4, Ref-6]。
2. **徐变、收缩与温度效应**：
   - **SLS**：必须考虑徐变和收缩的影响 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。徐变效应应在准永久组合下评估，通常使用永久荷载和预应力平均值 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。温度效应也应在 SLS 中予以考虑 [Ref-10]。
   - **ULS**：仅当这些时间依存效应显著时（例如二阶效应重要的稳定性验证）才需考虑；若构件具有足够的延性和转动能力，通常可忽略 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。

### 四、 依据位置
- [Ref-1] DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2, 11.5.1. Ultimate limit state, pp. 216-217
- [Ref-2] DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2, Table 11.6, pp. 216-217
- [Ref-3] DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2, Table 11.7, pp. 216-217
- [Ref-4] EN1992-1-1 2004, 2.4.2.2, p. 23
- [Ref-5] DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2, 11.5. Design of sections for flexure and axial load, pp. 216-217
- [Ref-6] EN1992-1-1_2004, 2.4.2.2, pp. 23-24
- [Ref-7] DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2, 8.1. General, pp. 139-140
- [Ref-9] EN1992-1-1 2004, 2.3.2.2, p. 22
- [Ref-10] EN1992-1-1_2004, 2.3.1.1~2.3.1.3, pp. 20-23
- [Ref-13] DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2, Serviceability limit states, pp. 139-192
- [Ref-16] EN199 EN1992-1-1_2004, 2.4.2.1~2.4.2.3, pp. 23-25
items.reasoning:
用户的问题是：“预应力在各类极限状态下的影响是什么”。
需要回答预应力（prestress）在各类极限状态（limit states，包括承载能力极限状态 ULS 和正常使用极限状态 SLS）下的影响、设计考虑、分项系数等。

首先，梳理提供的证据：
1. **承载能力极限状态 (ULS)**:
   - 预应力在大多数情况下是有利影响（favourable effect），因此 ULS 验证时通常使用有利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,fav}$ [Ref-1, Ref-4, Ref-5, Ref-6, Ref-15, Ref-16]。
   - EN 1992-1-1 推荐的 $\gamma_{p,fav} = 1.0$，$\gamma_{p,unfav} = 1.3$ [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-15]。
   - 英国国家附录 (UK NA) 修改为 $\gamma_{p,fav} = 0.9$，$\gamma_{p,unfav} = 1.1$ [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-15]。
   - 对于外部预应力的稳定性极限状态验证，如果预应力增加是不利的，应使用 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$（推荐值 1.3）[Ref-6, Ref-16]。
   - 对于局部效应（如锚固区），也应使用 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$（推荐值 1.2）[Ref-6, Ref-16]。
   - 在截面设计中，考虑初始应变 $\varepsilon_{p0}$ 乘以分项系数 $\gamma_p$，加上 ULS 下的应变增量 $\Delta\varepsilon_p$ [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-15]。
     - 有粘结预应力筋：应变增量等于预应力筋水平处混凝土的应变增量 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-15]。
     - 无粘结和外部预应力筋：应变增量需基于混凝土构件变形计算，或假定应力增加 100 N/mm²。使用平均属性计算变形时，应力增量需乘以 $\gamma_{\Delta p}$（有利取0.8，不利取1.2）；或使用未开裂截面属性的线性分析，取 $\gamma_{\Delta p} = 1.0$ [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-15]。
   - Table 11.6 给出了 ULS 下的分项系数：
     - 受弯 (Flexure): 先张或无粘结 (EN: max 1.3, min 1.0; UK: max 1.1, min 0.9)；后张有粘结 (EN: max 1.3, min 1.0; UK: max 1.1, min 0.9) [Ref-2]。
     - 受剪 (Shear): EN (max 1.3, min 1.0); UK (max 1.1, min 0.9) [Ref-2]。

2. **正常使用极限状态 (SLS)**:
   - SLS   - SLS 下，荷载的分项系数通常为 1.0 [Ref-7, Ref-12, Ref-13]。
   - 材料属性的分项系数通常也为 1.0 [Ref-7, Ref-13, Ref-16]。
   - 预应力在 SLS 下采用上限或下限特征值 ($r_{sup}$ 和 $r_{inf}$)，取对设计更不利的值 [Ref-5]。
     - 先张或无粘结筋：上限 1.05，下限 0.95 乘以平均值 [Ref-5]。
     - 后张有粘结筋：上限 1.1，下限 0.9 乘以平均值 [Ref-5]。
     - 英国国家附录 (UK NA) 采用单一值 1.0 [Ref-5]。
   - Table 11.6 给出了 SLS 下的分项系数（即 $r_{sup}$ 和 $r_{inf}$）：
     - 受弯：先张/无粘结 (EN: max 1.05, min 0.95; UK: 1.0, 1.0)；后张有粘结 (EN: max 1.1, min 0.9; UK: 1.0, 1.0) [Ref-2]。
     - 受剪：EN 和 UK 均为 1.0 [Ref-2]。
   - SLS 需要考虑三种荷载组合：特征组合 (Characteristic)、频遇组合 (Frequent)、准永久组合 (Quasi-permanent) [Ref-5, Ref-7, Ref-12, Ref-13]。
   - 裂缝控制 (Table 11.7)：
     - 无粘结筋在准永久荷载下：所有暴露类别限制为 0.3 mm [Ref-3]。
     - 有粘结筋在频遇荷载下：X0, XC1 为 0.2 mm；XC2-4 为 0.2 mm；XD, XS 类为消压 (Decompression) [Ref-3]。
     - 有粘结筋在准永久荷载下：XC2-4 为消压；XD, XS 类无具体数值限制（或根据具体情况）[Ref-3]。
   - 徐变和收缩的影响：通常必须在 SLS 验证中考虑 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。当考虑徐变时，其设计效应应在准永久组合下评估，通常使用永久荷载和预应力平均值 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。
   - 应力限制：SLS 下可能需要限制混凝土压应力（如避免微裂缝或过度徐变）。在侵蚀性环境（XD, XF, XS）中，建议将应力限制在 $0.6 f_{ck}$，或采取其他措施 [Ref-13]。如果准永久组合下压应力超过 $0.45 f_{ck}$，应考虑非线性徐变 [Ref-13]。

3. **疲劳极限状态 (Fatigue)**:
   - 疲劳验证时，预应力的有利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,fav}$ 推荐值也可取 1.0 [Ref-4, Ref-6, Ref-16]。

4. **其他影响（如温度、沉降）**：
   - 温度、收缩和徐变引起的变形后果应在设计中考虑 [Ref-10]。
   - 在 ULS 中，只有当徐变、收缩、温度或差异沉降的影响显著时（例如二阶效应重要的稳定性验证），才需要考虑它们；否则，只要构件具有足够的延性和转动能力，可不考虑 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。

组织回答结构：
1. **直接结论/概述**：预应力在承载能力极限状态（ULS）和正常使用极限状态（SLS）下的影响和设计原则不同。ULS 主要关注预应力作为有利或不利作用的分项系数及应变增量；SLS 主要关注预应力的特征值上下限、裂缝控制、应力限制及徐变收缩效应。
2. **承载能力极限状态 (ULS) 下的影响与设计**：
   - 分项系数取值（有利 vs 不利，不利，EN 与 UK NA 对比）。
   - 局部效应与稳定性。
   - 截面设计中的应变计算（有粘结 vs 无粘结/外部）。
3. **正常使用极限状态 (SLS) 下的影响与设计**：
   - 预应力特征值上下限（$r_{sup}$ 和 $r_{inf}$）。
   - 荷载组合与裂缝控制要求。
   - 混凝土应力限制与徐变影响。
4. **疲劳及其他极限状态**：
   - 疲劳验证的分项系数。
   - 徐变、收缩和温度在 ULS 和 SLS 中的考虑原则。
5. **依据位置**：列出引用的 Ref。

检查细节：
- ULS 分项系数：EN 1992-1-1 推荐 $\gamma_{p,fav}=1.0$, $\gamma_{p,unfav}=1.3$ [Ref-1, Ref-4, Ref-6]。UK NA 修改为 0.9 和 1.1 [Ref-1, Ref-5]。
- 局部效应 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$ 推荐 1.2 [Ref-6, Ref-16]。外部预应力稳定性 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$ 推荐 1.3 [Ref-6, Ref-16]。
- SLS 预应力上下限：先张/无粘结 1.05/0.95；后张有粘结 1.1/0.9 [Ref-5]。UK NA 统一为 1.0 [Ref-5]。
- 裂缝控制：Table 11.7 [Ref-3]。
- 无粘结/外部筋 ULS 应变增量：假定 100 MPa，乘以 $\gamma_{\Delta p}$ (0.8 或 1.2) 或线性分析取 1.0 [Ref-1, Ref-5, Ref-15]。

语言要求：中文，专业，简洁，不编造，严格绑定 [Ref-N]。

撰写草稿：
**一、 承载能力极限状态 (ULS) 下的影响与设计**
1. **分项系数取值**：在大多数情况下，预应力是有利影响，ULS 验证时应使用有利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,fav}$ [Ref-1, Ref-4, Ref-6]。EN 1992-1-1 推荐 $\gamma_{p,fav} = 1.0$，不利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,unfav} = 1.3$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。英国国家附录 (UK NA) 将其修改为 $\gamma_{p,fav} = 0.9$ 和 $\gamma_{p,unfav} = 1.1$ [Ref-1, Ref-5]。
2. **特殊情况的 ULS 验证**：
   - 对于外部预应力的整体稳定性极限状态，若预应力增加会产生不利影响，应使用 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$（推荐值 1.3）[Ref-6, Ref-16]。
   - 对于局部效应（如锚固区），也应使用 $\gamma_{p,unfav}$（推荐值 1.2）[Ref-6, Ref-16]。
3. **截面设计中的应变计算**：ULS 下需考虑初始应变 $\varepsilon_{p0}$ 乘以分项系数，并加上应变增量 $\Delta\varepsilon_p$ [Ref-1, Ref-5]。
   - **有粘结预应力筋**：应变增量等于预应力筋水平处混凝土的应变增量 [Ref-1, Ref-5]。
   - **无粘结和外部预应力筋**：应变增量需基于构件变形计算，或假定应力增加 100 N/mm² [Ref-1, Ref-5]。若使用平均属性计算变形，应力增量需乘以 $\gamma_{\Delta p}$（有利取 0.8，不利取 1.2）；若使用未开裂截面进行线性分析，则取 $\gamma_{\Delta p} = 1.0$ [Ref-1, Ref-5]。

**二、 正常使用极限状态 (SLS) 下的影响与设计**
1. **预应力特征值上下限**：SLS 下荷载和材料分项系数通常为 1.0 [Ref-7, Ref-13, Ref-16]。预应力采用上限 ($r_{sup}$sup}$) 或下限 ($r_{inf}$) 特征值，取对设计更不利的值 [Ref-5]。
   - 先张或无粘结筋：上限 1.05，下限 0.95（乘以平均值）[Ref-2, Ref-5]。
   - 后张有粘结筋：上限 1.1，下限 0.9 [Ref-2, Ref-5]。
   - *注：英国国家附录 (UK NA) 简化采用单一值 1.0 [Ref-5]。*
2. **裂缝控制**：SLS 需考虑特征、频遇和准永久三种荷载组合 [Ref-5, Ref-7]。根据暴露类别和预应力筋类型，裂缝宽度限制如下 [Ref-3]：
   - **无粘结筋**（准永久荷载）：所有暴露类别限制为 0.3 mm [Ref-3]。
   - **有粘结筋**（频遇荷载）：X0/XC1/XC2-XC4 类别限制为 0.2 mm；XD/XS 类别要求消压 (Decompression) [Ref-3]。
   - **有粘结筋**（准永久荷载）：XC2-XC4 类别要求消压 [Ref-3]。
3. **混凝土应力限制与徐变**：
   - 在侵蚀性环境（XD, XF, XS）中，建议将 SLS 下的混凝土压应力限制在 $0.6 f_{ck}$，或采取增加保护层/横向约束等措施 [Ref-13]。
   - 若准永久组合下压应力超过 $0.45 f_{ck}$，应考虑非线性徐变的影响 [Ref-13]。

**三、 疲劳及其他时间依存效应**
1. **疲劳极限状态**：疲劳验证时，预应力的有利分项系数 $\gamma_{p,fav}$ 推荐值同样可取 1.0 [Ref-4, Ref-6]。
2. **徐变、收缩与温度效应**：
   - **SLS**：必须考虑徐变和收缩的影响 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。徐变效应应在准永久组合下评估，通常使用永久荷载和预应力平均值 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。温度效应也应在 SLS 中考虑 [Ref-10]。
   - **ULS**：仅当这些时间依存效应显著时（例如二阶效应重要的稳定性验证）才需考虑；若构件具有足够的延性和转动能力，通常可忽略 [Ref-9, Ref-10]。

EN 1992-1-1 specifies two partial safety factors for prestress when considering overall analysis and the design of sections: $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p , f a v } } = 1 . 0$ and $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p , u n f a v } } = 1 . 3$ . However, the UK National Annex specifies modified values of $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p , f a v } } = 0 . 9$ and $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p , u n f a v } } = 1 . 1$ . In most cases, prestressing is a favourable effect, and $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p , f a v } }$ should be used.

In the design of sections, the initial strain in the tendons, $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p 0 } } ,$ multiplied by the partial factor, $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p } } ,$ is taken into account together with the increase in strain at the ultimate limit state, $\Delta \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } } .$ The increase in strain at the ultimate limit state is determined as follows:

For bonded tendons, the increase in strain in the tendon is equal to the increase in strain in the concrete above zero at the level of the tendon (Fig. 11.2).



  
$\varepsilon _ { \mathsf { p } 0 }$ = the initial strain in the tendon at a section (i.e. allowing only for losses due to friction and draw-in) $+ \Delta \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p 0 } }$  
$\Delta \varepsilon _ { \scriptscriptstyle { \mathsf { p } 0 } }$ = 0, for pretensioned members

= t he strain in the concrete due to stressing the tendon (or to stressing the first tendon when a number of tendons are stressed successively), for post-tensioned members

p = the force in the prestressing tendons at the ultimate limit state



Fig. 11.2. Strain in bonded prestressing tendons at the ultimate limit state

Clause



\* For X0, XC1 exposure classes, crack width has no influence on durability and this limit state is set to guarantee acceptable appearance. In the absence of appearance conditions this limit may be relaxed.

For unbonded and external tendons, the increase in strain has to be calculated based on the deformation of the concrete member. Alternatively, an increase in stress of 100 N/mm2 may be assumed. When the deformation is calculated using mean values of the member properties, the increase in stress should be multiplied by a partial factor, $\gamma _ { \Delta \mathrm { p } } \cdot \gamma _ { \Delta \mathrm { p } }$ should be taken as 0.8 or 1.2, depending on whether the increase in stress is a beneficial or adverse effect. Alternatively, a linear analysis using uncracked section properties can be used with $\gamma _ { \Delta \mathfrak { p } } = 1 . 0 .$

In most cases, prestressing is a favourable effect, and $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p , f a v } }$ should be used.

In the design of sections, the initial strain in the tendons, $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p 0 } } ,$ multiplied by the partial factor, $\gamma _ { \mathrm { p } } ,$ is taken into account together with the increase in strain at the ultimate limit state, $\Delta \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } } .$ The increase in strain at the ultimate limit state is determined as follows:

For bonded tendons, the increase in strain in the tendon is equal to the increase in strain in the concrete above zero at the level of the tendon (Fig. 11.2).



  
$\varepsilon _ { \mathsf { p } 0 }$ = the initial strain in the tendon at a section (i.e. allowing only for losses due to friction and draw-in) $+ \Delta \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p 0 } }$  
$\Delta \varepsilon _ { \scriptscriptstyle { \mathsf { p } 0 } }$ = 0, for pretensioned members

= t he strain in the concrete due to stressing the tendon (or to stressing the first tendon when a number of tendons are stressed successively), for post-tensioned members

p = the force in the prestressing tendons at the ultimate limit state

Clause



\* For X0, XC1 exposure classes, crack width has no influence on durability and this limit state is set to guarantee acceptable appearance. In the absence of appearance conditions this limit may be relaxed.

For unbonded and external tendons, the increase in strain has to be calculated based on the deformation of the concrete member. Alternatively, an increase in stress of 100 N/mm2 may be assumed. When the deformation is calculated using mean values of the member properties, the increase in stress should be multiplied by a partial factor, $\gamma _ { \Delta \mathrm { p } } \cdot \gamma _ { \Delta \mathrm { p } }$ should be taken as 0.8 or 1.2, depending on whether the increase in stress is a beneficial or adverse effect. EN 1992-1-1 distinguishes between three serviceability load combinations, i.e. characteristic, frequent and quasi-permanent. All are relevant to the design of prestressed concrete members, but their relative magnitude depends on the loads applied and the type of structure being designed.

EN 1992-1-1 also adopts an upper or lower characteristic value $( r _ { \mathrm { s u p } }$ and $r _ { \mathrm { i n f } } )$ for the prestressing force (whichever is more critical) at the serviceability limit state. The upper and lower characteristic values are taken as 1.05 and 0.95 times the mean value of the prestress respectively for pretensioned or unbonded tendons, and as 1.1 and 0.9 for post-tensioned bonded tendons. sources.title: EN1992-1-1 2004
sources.section: 2.3.2.2 Shrinkage and creep
sources.original_text:
(1) Shrinkage and creep are time-dependent properties of concrete. Their effects should generally be taken into account for the verification of serviceability limit states.

(2) The effects of shrinkage and creep should be considered at ultimate limit states only where their effects are significant, for example in the verification of ultimate limit states of stability where second order effects are of importance. In other cases these effects need not be considered for ultimate limit states, provided that ductility and rotation capacity of the elements are sufficient.

(3) When creep is taken into account its design effects should be evaluated under the quasipermanent combination of actions irrespective of the design situation considered i.e. persistent, transient or accidental.

Note: In most cases the effects of creep may be evaluated under permanent loads and the mean value of prestress.
