Section 5 of EN 1992-1-2 sets out minimum dimensions and axis distances (cover plus half the diameter of the reinforcement bar) for different types of structural element for fire exposure periods of 30, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min. Some detailing requirements are also given. The member types covered are columns, load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls, beams (simply supported and continuous) and slabs (simply supported and continuous boundary conditions, one- and two-way spanning slabs, solid and ribbed slabs, and flat slabs).

The table values apply to concrete made with siliceous aggregates and with a density in the range 2000-2600 $\mathrm { k g } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ . If calcareous or lightweight aggregate is used, the table values for minimum dimensions for slabs and beams may be reduced by 10%.

When using tabulated data, no further checks are required for shear, torsion, anchorage details and explosive spalling of concrete (spalling related to the moisture content of the concrete). However, the code requires surface reinforcement when the axis distance in a member exceeds 70 mm to prevent falling off of the cover concrete.

Rather than repeating the data tabulated in the code here, this guide discusses the basis of the tables and some of the limitations.

The tables have been developed on an empirical basis, general experience in Europe and theoretical evaluation of tests. In particular, the data for method A for columns are based on recent tests in Belgium and Canada. The data for the more common types of structural elements are derived making approximate and conservative assumptions.

Structural fire design is covered in EN 1991-1-2. Under fire conditions, a structure will be required to fulfil load bearing and/or separating function. The code provides guidance for satisfying the above requirements and this chapter of the manual discusses the salient features. Building regulations normally specify the fire rating for the building. It can also be calculated from first principles using EN 1991-1-2 (Actions on Structures Exposed to Fire).

The structure is required to comply with criteria R, I and E as appropriate:

Criterion R is assumed to be satisfied if the structure maintains adequate mechanical resistance for the required duration of fire exposure.

Criterion I is the insulation criterion, which also applies to members fulfilling separating function. It is deemed to be satisfied if the average rise in temperature on the nonexposed surface does not exceed 140 K and the maximum rise does not exceed 180 K.

Criterion E applies to elements required to fulfil separating function, and will be satisfied if the integrity of the structure is maintained for the required duration such that the spread of flames, hot gases and excessive heat is avoided.

The designer has a wide choice of methods. The method for verifying the fire resistance in a project should be chosen on the basis of acceptability to regulatory authorities. The design can be based on thermal actions given by either nominal fire exposure or those calculated using the physical parameters of the building. The former is the most common method, and the latter should only be undertaken by designers with adequate appreciation of all aspects of fire engineering.

In both procedures it is further permitted to base the design on (1) member analysis (2) analysis of parts of the structure or (3) analysis of the whole structure.

In member analysis - which includes tabulated data - only the effects of thermal gradients across the cross-section is considered; the effects of axial or in plane thermal expansions are neglected. Also, the boundary conditions are assumed to remain unchanged throughout the fire exposure.

In the analysis of a part of the structure, a section of the structure is isolated such that stationary boundary conditions could be prescribed in the analysis. Within the part that is isolated, the relevant failure mode in fire exposure, temperature-dependent material properties and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations should be taken into account in the analysis.

In the analysis of the whole structure, none of the approximations noted above are used, and the global analysis is undertaken accounting for the temperature-dependent material properties, member stiffness and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations.

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

sources.original_text:
Annex D (clause D8.2.1) gives a standard procedure for the assessment of a characteristic value based on the following assumptions:

Clause D8.2.1

a) the resistance function is a function of a number of independent variables X;

b) a sufficient number of test results is available;

c) all relevant geometrical and material properties are measured;

d ) there is no correlation (statistical dependence) between the variables in the resistance function;

e) all variables follow either a Normal or a log-normal distribution.

This procedure is detailed in clauses D8.2.2.1 to D8.2.2.7. The procedure is presented in Table 10.2, and illustrated by an example. The selected example is the resistance function for bolts in bearing. Some additional comments follow the table.

Table 10.2. Standard evaluation procedure: method (a)

Steps

Example

Step 1

Develop a design model (clause D8.2.2.1)







X the vector of basic variables

Compare theoretical and experimental values For bolt i:

(clause D8.2.2.2):



Plot $r _ { \mathrm { e } }$ against $r _ { t }$



The causes of any systematic deviation from the line $\theta = \pi / 4$ should be investigated to check whether this indicates errors in the test procedures or in the resistance function

Table 10.2. Continued

Steps

Step 3

Estimate the mean value correction factor b (clause D8.2.2.3):

Corrected resistance: $r = b r _ { t \delta }$

Calculate: $b = \frac { \sum r _ { \mathrm { e } } r _ { t } } { \sum r _ { t } ^ { 2 } }$



Step 4

Estimate the coefficient of variation $V _ { \delta }$ of the errors (clause D8.2.2.4):

Calculate: $\delta _ { i } = \frac { r _ { \mathrm { e } i } } { b r _ { t i } }$

(1)P For the verification of the shear resistance the following symbols are defined:

$V _ { \sf R d , c }$ is the design shear resistance of the member without shear reinforcement.

$V _ { \sf R d , s }$ is the design value of the shear force which can be sustained by the yielding shear reinforcement.

$V _ { \sf R d , m a x }$ is the design value of the maximum shear force which can be sustained by the member, limited by crushing of the compression struts.

In members with inclined chords the following additional values are defined (see Figure 6.2):

$V _ { \mathsf { c c d } }$ is the design value of the shear component of the force in the compression area, in the case of an inclined compression chord.

$V _ { \mathrm { { t d } } }$ is the design value of the shear component of the force in the tensile reinforcement, in the case of an inclined tensile chord.

  
Figure 6.2: Shear component for members with inclined chords

(2) The shear resistance of a member with shear reinforcement is equal to:



(3) In regions of the member where $V _ { \sf E d } \leq V _ { \sf R d , c }$ no calculated shear reinforcement is necessary. $V _ { \mathsf { E d } }$ is the design shear force in the section considered resulting from external loading and prestressing (bonded or unbonded).

(4) When, on the basis of the design shear calculation, no shear reinforcement is required, minimum shear reinforcement should nevertheless be provided according to 9.2.2. The minimum shear reinforcement may be omitted in members such as slabs (solid, ribbed or hollow core slabs) where transverse redistribution of loads is possible. Minimum reinforcement may also be omitted in members of minor importance (e.g. lintels with span ≤ 2 m) which do not contribute significantly to the overall resistance and stability of the structure.

(5) In regions where $V _ { \sf E d } > V _ { \sf R d , c }$ according to Expression (6.2), sufficient shear reinforcement should be provided in order that $V _ { \sf E d } \leq V _ { \sf R d }$ (see Expression (6.8)).

$V _ { \sf R d , s }$ is the design value of the shear force which can be sustained by the yielding shear reinforcement.

$V _ { \sf R d , m a x }$ is the design value of the maximum shear force which can be sustained by the member, limited by crushing of the compression struts.

In members with inclined chords the following additional values are defined (see Figure 6.2):

$V _ { \mathsf { c c d } }$ is the design value of the shear component of the force in the compression area, in the case of an inclined compression chord.

$V _ { \mathrm { { t d } } }$ is the design value of the shear component of the force in the tensile reinforcement, in the case of an inclined tensile chord.

  
Figure 6.2: Shear component for members with inclined chords

(2) The shear resistance of a member with shear reinforcement is equal to:



(3) In regions of the member where $V _ { \sf E d } \leq V _ { \sf R d , c }$ no calculated shear reinforcement is necessary. $V _ { \mathsf { E d } }$ is the design shear force in the section considered resulting from external loading and prestressing (bonded or unbonded).

(4) When, on the basis of the design shear calculation, no shear reinforcement is required, minimum shear reinforcement should nevertheless be provided according to 9.2.2. The minimum shear reinforcement may be omitted in members such as slabs (solid, ribbed or hollow core slabs) where transverse redistribution of loads is possible. Minimum reinforcement may also be omitted in members of minor importance (e.g. lintels with span $\leq 2 \mathsf { m }$ ) which do not contribute significantly to the overall resistance and stability of the structure.

(5) In regions where $V _ { \sf E d } > V _ { \sf R d , c }$ according to Expression (6.2), sufficient shear reinforcement should be provided in order that $V _ { \sf E d } \leq V _ { \sf R d }$ (see Expression (6.8)).

(6) The sum of the design shear force and the contributions of the flanges, $V _ { \mathsf { E d } } - V _ { \mathsf { c c d } } - V _ { \mathsf { t d } }$ , should not exceed the permitted maximum value $V _ { \sf R d , m a x }$ (see 6.2.3), anywhere in the member.

(7) The longitudinal tension reinforcement should be able to resist the additional tensile force caused by shear (see 6.2.3 (7)).

(8) For members subject to predominantly uniformly distributed loading the design shear force need not to be checked at a distance less than $d$ from the face of the support. Any shear reinforcement required should continue to the support. In addition it should be verified that the shear at the support does not exceed $V _ { \sf R d , m a x }$ (see also 6.2.2 (6) and 6.2.3 (8).

(9) Where a load is applied near the bottom of a section, sufficient vertical reinforcement to carry the load to the top of the section should be provided in addition to any reinforcement required to resist shear.

chunks.content:
(1) The simplified procedure for continuous beams and continuous one way spanning slabs is based on the rotation capacity of beam/slab zones over a length of approximately 1,2 times the depth of section. It is assumed that these zones undergo a plastic deformation (formation of yield hinges) under the relevant combination of actions. The verification of the plastic rotation in the ultimate limit state is considered to be fulfilled, if it is shown that under the relevant combination of actions the calculated rotation, $\theta _ { \mathsf { s } }$ , is less than or equal to the allowable plastic rotation (see Figure 5.5).

  
Figure 5.5: Plastic rotation $\pmb { \theta _ { \lessgtr } }$ of reinforced concrete sections for continuous beams and continuous one way spanning slabs.

(2) In regions of yield hinges, $x _ { \mathrm { u } } / d$ shall not exceed the value 0,45 for concrete strength classes less than or equal to C50/60, and 0,35 for concrete strength classes greater than or equal to C55/67.

(3) The rotation $\theta _ { \mathsf { s } }$ should be determined on the basis of the design values for actions and materials and on the basis of mean values for prestressing at the relevant time.

(4) In the simplified procedure, the allowable plastic rotation may be determined by multiplying the basic value of allowable rotation, $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ , by a correction factor $k _ { \lambda }$ that depends on the shear slenderness.

Note: Values of $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended values for steel Classes B and C (the use of Class A steel is not recommended for plastic analysis) and concrete strength classes less than or equal to C50/60 and C90/105 are given in Figure 5.6N.

The values for concrete strength classes C 55/67 to $\complement 9 0 / 1 0 5$ may be interpolated accordingly. The values apply for a shear slenderness $\lambda = 3 { , } 0$ . parent_chunks.title: DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2
parent_chunks.section: Structural fire design
parent_chunks.content:
Structural fire design is covered in EN 1991-1-2. Under fire conditions, a structure will be required to fulfil load bearing and/or separating function. The code provides guidance for satisfying the above requirements and this chapter of the manual discusses the salient features. Building regulations normally specify the fire rating for the building. It can also be calculated from first principles using EN 1991-1-2 (Actions on Structures Exposed to Fire).

The structure is required to comply with criteria R, I and E as appropriate:

Criterion R is assumed to be satisfied if the structure maintains adequate mechanical resistance for the required duration of fire exposure.

Criterion I is the insulation criterion, which also applies to members fulfilling separating function. It is deemed to be satisfied if the average rise in temperature on the nonexposed surface does not exceed 140 K and the maximum rise does not exceed 180 K.

Criterion E applies to elements required to fulfil separating function, and will be satisfied if the integrity of the structure is maintained for the required duration such that the spread of flames, hot gases and excessive heat is avoided.

The designer has a wide choice of methods. The method for verifying the fire resistance in a project should be chosen on the basis of acceptability to regulatory authorities. The design can be based on thermal actions given by either nominal fire exposure or those calculated using the physical parameters of the building. The former is the most common method, and the latter should only be undertaken by designers with adequate appreciation of all aspects of fire engineering.

In both procedures it is further permitted to base the design on (1) member analysis (2) analysis of parts of the structure or (3) analysis of the whole structure.

In member analysis - which includes tabulated data - only the effects of thermal gradients across the cross-section is considered; the effects of axial or in plane thermal expansions are neglected. Also, the boundary conditions are assumed to remain unchanged throughout the fire exposure.

In the analysis of a part of the structure, a section of the structure is isolated such that stationary boundary conditions could be prescribed in the analysis. Within the part that is isolated, the relevant failure mode in fire exposure, temperature-dependent material properties and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations should be taken into account in the analysis.

In the analysis of the whole structure, none of the approximations noted above are used, and the global analysis is undertaken accounting for the temperature-dependent material properties, member stiffness and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations.

The code gives only limited guidance for methods 2 and 3 above.

Where calculations are undertaken, the load combination to be used in fire conditions is given in EN 1990 (Basis of Structural Design). It is



where $A _ { \mathrm { d } }$ is the design value of the accidental action (in this case actions caused by fire), $Q _ { \mathrm { k } } ,$ is the leading variable action and $Q _ { \mathrm { k , \ell } }$ i represents other accompanying actions, if applicable.

For member analysis, where the effects of thermal deformation are neglected and where there is only one variable action, the action effect under fire conditions may be taken as $\eta _ { \mathrm { f i } }$ times the value of action effect used in normal temperature design. The value of $\eta _ { \mathrm { f i } }$ depends on the ratio of variable and permanent loads and the use of the building. EN 1992-1-2 provides a figure to arrive at the value. A value of 0.7 may be used as a safe approximation in all cases.

Section 5 of EN 1992-1-2 sets out minimum dimensions and axis distances (cover plus half the diameter of the reinforcement bar) for different types of structural element for fire exposure periods of 30, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min. Some detailing requirements are also given. The member types covered are columns, load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls, beams (simply supported and continuous) and slabs (simply supported and continuous boundary conditions, one- and two-way spanning slabs, solid and ribbed slabs, and flat slabs).

The table values apply to concrete made with siliceous aggregates and with a density in the range 2000-2600 $\mathrm { k g } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ . If calcareous or lightweight aggregate is used, the table values for minimum dimensions for slabs and beams may be reduced by 10%.

When using tabulated data, no further checks are required for shear, torsion, anchorage details and explosive spalling of concrete (spalling related to the moisture content of the concrete). However, the code requires surface reinforcement when the axis distance in a member exceeds 70 mm to prevent falling off of the cover concrete.

Rather than repeating the data tabulated in the code here, this guide discusses the basis of the tables and some of the limitations.

The tables have been developed on an empirical basis, general experience in Europe and theoretical evaluation of tests. In particular, the data for method A for columns are based on recent tests in Belgium and Canada. The data for the more common types of structural elements are derived making approximate and conservative assumptions.

When the thickness of walls and slabs complies with the minimum dimensions, the integrity and insulation criteria (see Section 12.4.1 above for definition) for the separating function may be assumed to be satisfied.

For the load-bearing function, the following assumptions apply:

$E _ { \mathrm { d , f i } } / R _ { \mathrm { d , f i } } { \leq } 1 . 0$ , where $E _ { \mathrm { d , f i } }$ is the design effect of actions under fire conditions and $R _ { \mathrm { d , f i } }$ is the design resistance of the element under fire conditions.

Unless otherwise noted, it is assumed that $\eta _ { \mathrm { f i } } = E _ { \mathrm { d , f i } } / E _ { \mathrm { d } } = 0 . 7$ , where $E _ { \mathrm { d } }$ is the design effect of actions in normal temperature design.

The critical temperature of reinforcement $( \theta _ { \mathrm { c r } } )$ (i.e. the temperature of reinforcement at which the failure of the member is expected to occur under fire conditions for a given level of steel stress) is 500°C. This assumes that the stress leve $1 = \sigma _ { \mathrm { s , f i } } / f _ { \mathrm { y k } } = 0 . 6 , \eta _ { \mathrm { f i } } = 0 . 7$ and $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } = 1 . 1 5$

For prestressing tendons, $\theta _ { \mathrm { c r } } = 4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and for prestressing wires and strands $\theta _ { \mathrm { c r } } = 3 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ The stress level for both is taken as 0.55.

The thickness of slabs in the tables is to ensure adequacy for the separating function, and may include the thickness of any non-combustible floor finishes in addition to the thickness of the structural floor.

根据欧洲规范 EN 1992-1-1（混凝土结构设计），剪应力（剪力）的验证程序主要分为**一般剪切（梁、板等构件）**和**冲切（板柱节点、基础）** 两类。以下是基于规范条文整理的标准化验证步骤：

### 一、 一般剪切验证程序（梁、板等构件）
一般剪切验证基于桁架模型，核心是对比设计剪力与构件的抗剪承载力。

**1. 确定设计剪力 $V_{Ed}$**
计算由外部荷载和预应力（粘结或无粘结）在目标截面引起的设计剪力 $V_{Ed}$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。

**2. 验算无抗剪钢筋的抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd,c}$**
*   **若 $V_{Ed} \le V_{Rd,c}$**：理论上无需通过计算配置抗剪钢筋，但仍需按规范第9.2.2节配置**最小抗剪钢筋** [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
    *   *豁免条件*：对于能够横向重分布荷载的板（如实心板、肋形板或空心板），或不显著影响结构整体抗力和稳定性的次要构件（如跨度 $\le 2\text{ m}$ 的过梁），可省略最小抗剪钢筋 [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
*   **若 $V_{Ed} > V_{Rd,c}$**：必须配置足够的抗剪钢筋，进入步骤4 [Ref-1, Ref-6]。

**3. 验算截面最大抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd,max}$（防止混凝土压杆压碎）**
在构件的任何部位，设计剪力（扣除倾斜弦杆的贡献后，即 $V_{Ed} - V_{ccd} - V_{td}$）均不得超过由混凝土压杆压碎控制的极限值 $V_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。

**4. 计算所需抗剪钢筋**
当需要配置抗剪钢筋时，构件的总抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd}$ 应满足 $V_{Ed} \le V_{Rd}$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
*   总承载力公式：$V_{Rd} = V_{Rd,s} + V_{ccd} + V_{td}$ [Ref-2, Ref-6]。
*   抗剪钢筋提供的承载力（公式6.8）：$V_{Rd,s} = \frac{A_{sw}}{s} z f_{ywd} \cot\theta$ [Ref-3]。
    *(注：$A_{sw}$ 为抗剪钢筋截面积，$s$ 为间距，$z$ 为内力臂，$f_{ywd}$ 为抗剪钢筋设计屈服强度，$\theta$ 为混凝土压杆倾角)*。

**5. 纵向钢筋附加拉力验算**
纵向受拉钢筋必须具备足够的锚固和截面积，以抵抗由剪力引起的附加拉力 [Ref-6]。

**6. 支座附近的特殊规定**
对于主要承受均布荷载的构件，距支座边缘小于有效高度 $d$ 的范围内无需验算设计剪力，但抗剪钢筋必须延伸至支座，且支座边缘处的剪力仍不得超过 $V_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-6]。

---

### 二、 冲切验证程序（板柱节点、基础）
冲切验证主要针对集中荷载或支座反力作用在相对较小区域的情况，验证基于控制截面上的剪应力进行。

**1. 确定控制截面**
验证应在**柱周边（或加载区域周边）**以及**基本控制周长 $u_1$**（通常距加载区域 $2.0d$）处进行 [Ref-4, Ref-8, Ref-10, Ref-14]。

**2. 计算设计冲切剪应力 $v_{Ed}$**
*   若支座反力对控制周长存在偏心，最大剪应力需乘以放大系数 $\beta$。
*   计算公式（公式6.38）：$v_{Ed} = \beta \frac{V_{Ed}}{u_i d}$ [Ref-10, Ref-17]。

**3. 验算最大冲切剪应力（防局部压碎）**
在柱周边或加载区域周边，设计冲切剪应力不得超过最大限值：$v_{Ed} \le v_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10]。

**4. 验算是否需要冲切钢筋**
*   **若 $v_{Ed} \le v_{Rd,c}$**（无冲切钢筋的板抗力）：无需配置冲切钢筋 [Ref-4, Ref-10]。
*   **若 $v_{Ed} > v_{Rd,c}$**：必须配置冲切钢筋，并需向外扩展计算，找到不再需要冲切钢筋的外围控制周长 $u_{out,ef}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10, Ref-14]。

---

### 三、 适用条件与注意事项提醒
1. **国家附录（National Annex）参数**：规范中涉及的诸多关键参数（如 $C_{Rd,c}$、$v_{min}$、$k_1$、$\cot\theta$ 的限值范围等）均允许各国自行规定。工程师在实际计算时，**必须查阅项目所在国的国家附录**以获取准确数值 [Ref-13, Ref-14]。
2. **倾斜弦杆构件**：对于具有倾斜受压或受拉弦杆的变截面构件，必须计算并计入混凝土受压区剪力分量 $V_{ccd}$ 和受拉钢筋剪力分量 $V_{td}$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
3. **底部加载情况**：若荷载作用在截面底部附近（如牛腿或悬挂荷载），除常规抗剪钢筋外，还需配置足够的竖向钢筋将荷载直接传递至截面顶部 [Ref-6]。

### 四、 依据位置
*   **一般剪切验证程序**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 第6.2.1节 (1)P~(9) [Ref-1, Ref-6]；第6.2.3节 公式(6.8) [Ref-3]。
*   **冲切验证程序**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 第6.4.1节 [Ref-8]；第6.4.3节 (1)P~(3) 及公式(6.38) [Ref-4, Ref-10, Ref-17]。
*   **参数与国家附录说明**：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 第6.2.2节及6.4.4节 [Ref-13, Ref-14]。
metadata.thinking:
用户询问的是“剪应力一般验证程序是怎样的”。
根据提供的证据，主要涉及EN 1992-1-1（欧洲规范2：混凝土结构设计）中的剪切（Shear）和冲切（Punching shear）的验证程序。
需要区分“一般剪切（Shear）”和“冲切（Punching shear）”，因为规范中这两者的验证程序有所不同，但都属于广义的“剪应力/剪力验证”。

首先，梳理一般剪切（Shear）的验证程序（EN 1992-1-1 第6.2.1节 General verification procedure）：
1. 确定设计剪力 $V_{Ed}$。
2. 计算无抗剪钢筋的构件抗剪承载力设计值 $V_{Rd,c}$。
3. 比较 $V_{Ed}$ 和 $V_{Rd,c}$：
   - 如果 $V_{Ed} \le V_{Rd,c}$，则不需要计算抗剪钢筋，但仍需按9.2.2节配置最小抗剪钢筋（某些板或次要构件可豁免）[Ref-1, Ref-6, Ref-13]。
   - 如果 $V_{Ed} > V_{Rd,c}$，则需要配置足够的抗剪钢筋，使得 $V_{Ed} \le V_{Rd}$ [Ref-1, Ref-6, Ref-13]。
4. 计算有抗剪钢筋的构件抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd}$：
   $V_{Rd} = V_{Rd,s} + V_{ccd} + V_{td}$ [Ref-1, Ref-2, Ref-6]。
   其中 $V_{Rd,s}$ 是屈服抗剪钢筋能承受的剪力设计值，公式为 $V_{Rd,s} = \frac{A_{sw}}{s} z f_{ywd} \cot\theta$ [Ref-3]。
5. 验证最大抗剪承载力（防止混凝土压杆压碎）：
   构件任何部位的 $V_{Ed} - V_{ccd} - V_{td}$ 不得超过允许的最大值 $V_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-6]。
6. 纵向受拉钢筋需能抵抗由剪力引起的附加拉力 [Ref-6]。
7. 对于主要承受均布荷载的构件，距支座边缘小于 $d$ 的距离内无需验算设计剪力，但抗剪钢筋需延伸至支座，且支座处的剪力不得超过 $V_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-6]。

其次，梳理冲切（Punching shear）的验证程序（EN 1992-1-1 第6.4.3节 Punching shear calculation）：
1. 确定控制截面（柱周边和基本控制周长 $u_1$）[Ref-4, Ref-8, Ref-10, Ref-14]。
2. 计算设计冲切剪应力 $v_{Ed}$。如果支座反力对控制周长有偏心，最大剪应力为 $v_{Ed} = \beta \frac{V_{Ed}}{u_i d}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10, Ref-17]。
3. 验证柱周边或加载区域周边的最大冲切剪应力：$v_{Ed} \le v_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10]。
4. 验证是否需要冲切钢筋：
   - 如果 $v_{Ed} \le v_{Rd,c}$，则不需要冲切钢筋 [Ref-4, Ref-10]。
   - 如果 $v_{Ed} > v_{Rd,c}$，则需要按6.4.5节配置冲切钢筋，并找到不需要冲切钢筋的外围周长 $u_{out,ef}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10, Ref-14]。

组织回答结构：
1. 直接结论：剪应力（剪力）验证程序在EN 1992-1-1中分为**一般剪切（梁/板等构件）**和**冲切（板柱节点/基础）** 两类。
2. 一般剪切验证程序（基于桁架模型）：
   - 步骤1：计算设计剪力 $V_{Ed}$。
   - 步骤2：验算无抗剪钢筋的抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd,c}$。
   - 步骤3：验算最大抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd,max}$（防压杆压碎）。
   - 步骤4：计算所需抗剪钢筋（若 $V_{Ed} > V_{Rd,c}$）。
   - 步骤5：纵向钢筋的附加拉力验算。
3. 冲切验证程序：
   - 步骤1：确定控制周长。
   - 步骤2：计算设计冲切剪应力 $v_{Ed}$（考虑偏心放大系数 $\beta$）。
   - 步骤3：验算最大冲切剪应力 $v_{Rd,max}$。
   - 步骤4：验算是否需要冲切钢筋（对比 $v_{Rd,c}$）。
4. 适用条件与注意事项（如国家附录参数、最小配筋率豁免等）。
5. 依据位置。

检查证据细节：
- 一般剪切：
  - $V_{Rd} = V_{Rd,s} + V_{ccd} + V_{td}$ [Ref-2]
  - $V_{Rd,s} = \frac{A_{sw}}{s} z f_{ywd} \cot\theta$ (Expression 6.8) [Ref-3]
  - 最小抗剪钢筋要求及豁免（板、次要构件）[Ref-1, Ref-6]
  - 均布荷载靠近支座的豁免（距离 $<d$）[Ref-6]
- 冲切：
  - 控制截面：柱面和 $u_1$ [Ref-4, Ref-10]
  - 偏心影响：$v_{Ed} = \beta \frac{V_{Ed}}{u_i d}$ (Expression 6.38) [Ref-10, Ref-17]
  - 判断条件：$v_{Ed} < v_{Rd,max}$ 和 $v_{Ed} < v_{Rd,c}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10]

语言要求：中文，专业，清晰，绑定[Ref-N]。不编造。

开始撰写回答。
一、一般剪切（梁、板等构件）验证程序
1. 确定设计剪力 $V_{Ed}$：由外部荷载和预应力引起 [Ref-1]。
2. 验算无抗剪钢筋的抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd,c}$：
   - 若 $V_{Ed} \le V_{Rd,c}$，理论上无需计算抗剪钢筋，但仍需按规范9.2.2节配置最小抗剪钢筋 [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
   - 豁免情况：对于能够横向重分布荷载的板（实心板、肋形板或空心板），或不显著影响结构整体抗力和稳定性的次要构件（如跨度≤2m的过梁），可省略最小抗剪钢筋 [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
3. 验算截面最大抗剪承载力 $V_{Rd,max}$（防止混凝土压杆压碎）：
   - 构件任何部位的设计剪力（扣除翼缘贡献后，即 $V_{Ed} - V_{ccd} - V_{td}$）不得超过最大允许值 $V_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
4. 计算抗剪钢筋（当 $V_{Ed} > V_{Rd,c}$ 时）：
   - 需配置足够的抗剪钢筋，使 $V_{Ed} \le V_{Rd}$ [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
   - 有抗剪钢筋构件的抗剪承载力公式为：$V_{Rd} = V_{Rd,s} + V_{ccd} + V_{td}$ [Ref-1, Ref-2, Ref-6]。
   - 其中，抗剪钢筋提供的承载力 $V_{Rd,s} = \frac{A_{sw}}{s} z f_{ywd} \cot\theta$ （公式6.8）[Ref-3]。
5. 纵向钢筋验算：纵向受拉钢筋必须能够抵抗由剪力引起的附加拉力 [Ref-6]。
6. 支座附近的特殊规定：对于主要承受均布荷载的构件，距支座边缘小于有效高度 $d$ 的范围内无需验算设计剪力，但抗剪钢筋必须延伸至支座，且支座处的剪力不得超过 $V_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-6]。

二、冲切（板柱节点、基础）验证程序
1. 确定控制截面：验证应在柱周边（或加载区域周边）以及基本控制周长 $u_1$（通常距加载区域2.0d）处进行 [Ref-4, Ref-8, Ref-10, Ref-14]。
2. 计算设计冲切剪应力 $v_{Ed}$：
   - 若支座反力对控制周长存在偏心，最大剪应力需乘以放大系数 $\beta$，计算公式为：$v_{Ed} = \beta \frac{V_{Ed}}{u_i d}$ （公式6.38）[Ref-4, Ref-10, Ref-17]。
3. 验算最大冲切剪应力：在柱周边或加载区域周边，设计冲切剪应力不得超过最大值，即 $v_{Ed} \le v_{Rd,max}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10]。
4. 验算是否需要冲切钢筋：
   - 若 $v_{Ed} \le v_{Rd,c}$（无冲切钢筋的抗力），则无需配置冲切钢筋 [Ref-4, Ref-10]。
   - 若 $v_{Ed} > v_{Rd,c}$，则需配置冲切钢筋，并需进一步计算找到不再需要冲切钢筋的外围控制周长 $u_{out,ef}$ [Ref-4, Ref-10, Ref-14]。

三、注意事项与适用条件
1. 国家附录（National Annex）：公式中的诸多参数（如 $C_{Rd,c}$、$v_{min}$、$k_1$、$\cot\theta$ 的限值等）的具体取值可能因国家而异，需查阅项目所在国的国家附录 [Ref-13, Ref-14]。
2. 倾斜弦杆构件：对于具有倾斜受压或受拉弦杆的构件，必须考虑混凝土受压区剪力分量 $V_{ccd}$ 和受拉钢筋剪力分量 $V_{td}$ 的影响 [Ref-1, Ref-6]。
3. 底部加载：若荷载作用在截面底部附近，除抗剪钢筋外，还需提供足够的竖向钢筋将荷载传递至截面顶部 [Ref-6]。

四、依据位置
- 一般剪切验证程序：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 第6.2.1节 (1)P~(9) [Ref-1, Ref-6]；第6.2.3节 公式(6.8) [Ref-3]。
- 冲切验证程序：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 第6.4.1节 [Ref-8]；第6.4.3节 (1)P~(3) 及公式(6.38) [Ref-4, Ref-10, Ref-17]。
- 参数与国家附录说明：EN 1992-1-1:2004, 第6.2.2节及6.4.4节 [Ref-13, Ref-14]。

逻辑清晰，没有编造，完全基于证据。直接输出。

(5) In regions where $V _ { \sf E d } > V _ { \sf R d , c }$ according to Expression (6.2), sufficient shear reinforcement should be provided in order that $V _ { \sf E d } \leq V _ { \sf R d }$ (see Expression (6.8)).

(6) The sum of the design shear force and the contributions of the flanges, $V _ { \mathsf { E d } } - V _ { \mathsf { c c d } } - V _ { \mathsf { t d } }$ , should not exceed the permitted maximum value $V _ { \sf R d , m a x }$ (see 6.2.3), anywhere in the member.

(7) The longitudinal tension reinforcement should be able to resist the additional tensile force caused by shear (see 6.2.3 (7)).

(8) For members subject to predominantly uniformly distributed loading the design shear force need not to be checked at a distance less than $d$ from the face of the support. Any shear reinforcement required should continue to the support. In addition it should be verified that the shear at the support does not exceed $V _ { \sf R d , m a x }$ (see also 6.2.2 (6) and 6.2.3 (8).

(9) Where a load is applied near the bottom of a section, sufficient vertical reinforcement to carry the load to the top of the section should be provided in addition to any reinforcement required to resist shear.

sources_summary.highlight_text:
Structural fire design is covered in EN 1991-1-2. Under fire conditions, a structure will be required to fulfil load bearing and/or separating function. The code provides guidance for satisfying the above requirements and this chapter of the manual discusses the salient features. Building regulations normally specify the fire rating for the building. It can also be calculated from first principles using EN 1991-1-2 (Actions on Structures Exposed to Fire).

The structure is required to comply with criteria R, I and E as appropriate:

Criterion R is assumed to be satisfied if the structure maintains adequate mechanical resistance for the required duration of fire exposure.

Criterion I is the insulation criterion, which also applies to members fulfilling separating function. It is deemed to be satisfied if the average rise in temperature on the nonexposed surface does not exceed 140 K and the maximum rise does not exceed 180 K.

Criterion E applies to elements required to fulfil separating function, and will be satisfied if the integrity of the structure is maintained for the required duration such that the spread of flames, hot gases and excessive heat is avoided.

The designer has a wide choice of methods. The method for verifying the fire resistance in a project should be chosen on the basis of acceptability to regulatory authorities. The design can be based on thermal actions given by either nominal fire exposure or those calculated using the physical parameters of the building. The former is the most common method, and the latter should only be undertaken by designers with adequate appreciation of all aspects of fire engineering.

In both procedures it is further permitted to base the design on (1) member analysis (2) analysis of parts of the structure or (3) analysis of the whole structure.

In member analysis - which includes tabulated data - only the effects of thermal gradients across the cross-section is considered; the effects of axial or in plane thermal expansions are neglected. Also, the boundary conditions are assumed to remain unchanged throughout the fire exposure.

In the analysis of a part of the structure, a section of the structure is isolated such that stationary boundary conditions could be prescribed in the analysis. Within the part that is isolated, the relevant failure mode in fire exposure, temperature-dependent material properties and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations should be taken into account in the analysis.

In the analysis of the whole structure, none of the approximations noted above are used, and the global analysis is undertaken accounting for the temperature-dependent material properties, member stiffness and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations.

The code gives only limited guidance for methods 2 and 3 above.

Where calculations are undertaken, the load combination to be used in fire conditions is given in EN 1990 (Basis of Structural Design). It is

For member analysis, where the effects of thermal deformation are neglected and where there is only one variable action, the action effect under fire conditions may be taken as times the value of action effect used in normal temperature design. The value of depends on the ratio of variable and permanent loads and the use of the building. EN 1992-1-2 provides a figure to arrive at the value. A value of 0.7 may be used as a safe approximation in all cases.

Section 5 of EN 1992-1-2 sets out minimum dimensions and axis distances (cover plus half the diameter of the reinforcement bar) for different types of structural element for fire exposure periods of 30, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min. Some detailing requirements are also given. The member types covered are columns, load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls, beams (simply supported and continuous) and slabs (simply supported and continuous boundary conditions, one- and two-way spanning slabs, solid and ribbed slabs, and flat slabs).

The table values apply to concrete made with siliceous aggregates and with a density in the range 2000-2600 . If calcareous or lightweight aggregate is used, the table values for minimum dimensions for slabs and beams may be reduced by 10%.

When using tabulated data, no further checks are required for shear, torsion, anchorage details and explosive spalling of concrete (spalling related to the moisture content of the concrete). However, the code requires surface reinforcement when the axis distance in a member exceeds 70 mm to prevent falling off of the cover concrete.

The tables have been developed on an empirical basis, general experience in Europe and theoretical evaluation of tests. In particular, the data for method A for columns are based on recent tests in Belgium and Canada. Within the part that is isolated, the relevant failure mode in fire exposure, temperature-dependent material properties and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations should be taken into account in the analysis.

In the analysis of the whole structure, none of the approximations noted above are used, and the global analysis is undertaken accounting for the temperature-dependent material properties, member stiffness and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations.

The code gives only limited guidance for methods 2 and 3 above.

For member analysis, where the effects of thermal deformation are neglected and where there is only one variable action, the action effect under fire conditions may be taken as $\eta _ { \mathrm { f i } }$ times the value of action effect used in normal temperature design. The value of $\eta _ { \mathrm { f i } }$ depends on the ratio of variable and permanent loads and the use of the building. EN 1992-1-2 provides a figure to arrive at the value. A value of 0.7 may be used as a safe approximation in all cases.

Section 5 of EN 1992-1-2 sets out minimum dimensions and axis distances (cover plus half the diameter of the reinforcement bar) for different types of structural element for fire exposure periods of 30, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min. Some detailing requirements are also given. The member types covered are columns, load-bearing and non-load-bearing walls, beams (simply supported and continuous) and slabs (simply supported and continuous boundary conditions, one- and two-way spanning slabs, solid and ribbed slabs, and flat slabs).

The table values apply to concrete made with siliceous aggregates and with a density in the range 2000-2600 $\mathrm { k g } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ . If calcareous or lightweight aggregate is used, the table values for minimum dimensions for slabs and beams may be reduced by 10%.

When using tabulated data, no further checks are required for shear, torsion, anchorage details and explosive spalling of concrete (spalling related to the moisture content of the concrete). This assumes that the stress leve $1 = \sigma _ { \mathrm { s , f i } } / f _ { \mathrm { y k } } = 0 . 6 , \eta _ { \mathrm { f i } } = 0 . 7$ and $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } = 1 . 1 5$

For prestressing tendons, $\theta _ { \mathrm { c r } } = 4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and for prestressing wires and strands $\theta _ { \mathrm { c r } } = 3 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ The stress level for both is taken as 0.55.

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . items.question: 单向板的设计步骤包括哪些
items.category: 构件极限状态计算层
items.answer:
基于欧洲规范 EN 1992-192-1-1 及其相关指南，单向板（One-way spanning slab）的设计步骤可系统归纳为结构判定、内力分析、极限状态验算及构造细部设计等核心环节。以下为可直接使用的设计步骤及核查要点：

### 1. 结构判定与建模
*   **单向板界定**：对于主要承受均布荷载的板，若满足以下任一条件，可视为单向板进行设计 [Ref-3]：
    1. 具有两个自由（无支撑）且大致平行的边缘；
    2. 为四边支撑的矩形板的中心部分，且长跨与短跨之比大于 2。

### 2. 荷载布置与内力分析
*   **荷载组合布置**：需考虑交替跨加载（设计可变荷载+永久荷载）与相邻跨加载等不同布置方式，以获取弯矩和剪力的包络图 [Ref-22]。
*   **支座弯矩简化与调整**（无论采用何种分析方法均适用） [Ref-5], [Ref-7]：
    *   **无转动约束支座**（如墙体）：连续板的设计支座弯矩可减小 $F_{Ed,supp} t / 8$（$F_{Ed,supp}$ 为支座反力，$t$ 为支座宽度）。
    *   **整体浇筑支座**：临界设计弯矩可取支座边缘处的弯矩。
    *   **刚性支座**：支座边缘的设计弯矩不得小于假定完全固定时计算值的 65%。
*   **指南简化计算（可选）**：若满足以下条件，可直接使用指南提供的弯矩和剪力系数表（如指南表3.3）进行计算，但**不允许**进行弯矩重分布 [Ref-18], [Ref-23]：
    1. 特征可变荷载不超过特征永久荷载；
    2. 荷载主要为均布且跨越三个或更多跨；
    3. 跨度变化不超过最长跨的 15%；
    4. 端柱与板的刚度比不超过 1.0。

### 3. 承载能力极限状态 (ULS) 设计
*   **受弯配筋计算**：根据内力包络图计算主受力方向的受弯钢筋面积。对于脆性破坏风险较小的板，最小配筋面积 $A_{s,min}$ 可取 ULS 验算所需面积的 1.2 倍 [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
*   **塑性分析限制**：若采用塑性分析（弯矩重分布），必须验证转动能力，或满足以下**免算转动能力**的条件 [Ref-6]：
    1. 受压区高度限制：$x_u/d \le 0.25$（混凝土 $\le$ C50/60）或 $x_u/d \le 0.15$（混凝土 $\ge$ C55/67）；
    2. 钢筋必须为 B 级或 C 级（不推荐使用 A 级）；
    3. 中间支座弯矩与跨中弯矩之比在 0.5 到 2 之间。
    *(注：若进行显式转动能力验算，屈服铰区域的 $x_u/d$ 不得超过 0.45 或 0.35 [Ref-1], [Ref-2]。)*

### 4. 正常使用极限状态 (SLS) 验算
*   **挠度控制**：通常可通过限制**跨高比（span/effective depth）** 来免除详细的挠度计算。根据规范表 7.4N，无轴压钢筋混凝土单向板的基本跨高比系数 $K$ 为 [Ref-9]：
    *   简支单向板：$K = 1.0$
    *   连续单向板端跨：$K = 1.3$
    *   连续单向板内部跨：$K = 1.5$
    *(注：需根据实际配筋率 $\rho$ 查表获取具体限值，并乘以 $K$ 值。)*

### 5. 构造与细部设计 (Detailing)
*   **横向分布钢筋**：单向板必须提供不小于主受力钢筋面积 **20%** 的次要横向钢筋。但在支座附近若无横向弯矩，则顶部主筋无需配置横向钢筋 [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
*   **钢筋间距限制**：需符合国家附录（NDP）规定。规范推荐的最大间距 $s_{max,slabs}$ 为 [Ref-4], [Ref-12]：
    *   一般区域：主筋 $3h \le 400\text{ mm}$，次筋 $3.5h \le 450\text50\text{ mm}$（$h$ 为板厚）；
    *   集中荷载或最大弯矩区域：主筋 $2h \le 250\text{ mm}$，次筋 $3h \le 400\text{ mm}$。
*   **支座锚固与截断** [Ref-4], [Ref-12]：
    *   **简支板**：至少一半的计算跨中钢筋应延伸至支座并按规范锚固。
    *   **部分固定边缘**（分析中未考虑固定作用时）：顶部钢筋需能承受相邻跨最大弯矩的至少 **25%**（端支座可减至 **15%**），并从支座边缘延伸至少 **0.2 倍**相邻跨长。
*   **自由边缘**：沿无支撑的自由边缘，必须配置纵向和横向的边缘钢筋（U型或闭合箍筋形式） [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。

### 6. 防火设计 (如适用)
*   **单向板界定**：若板不满足四边支撑条件，在防火设计中必须按单向板处理 [Ref-8]。
*   **连续板支座配筋要求**：对于连续单向板，若出现以下情况之一，中间支座处必须提供至少 **0.5% $A_c$** 的顶部钢筋 [Ref-8]：
    1. 使用冷加工钢筋；
    2. 端支座无固定或未按照 EN 1992-1-1 进行细部设计；
    3. 荷载效应无法在横向进行分布。
*   **截面尺寸与保护层**：需根据目标耐火极限（如 R60, R90），查规范表格确定最小楼板厚度及钢筋轴线距离（保护层厚度 + 钢筋半径），以满足承载力(R)和隔热性(I)要求 [Ref-11]。

---

### ⚠️ 工程师注意事项（适用条件与国家附录）
1. **国家附录 (NDP) 差异**：钢筋最大间距限值 [Ref-4]、塑性分析的基本允许转动角 $\theta_{pl,d}$ [Ref-1] 等参数，各国国家附录可能采用与规范推荐值不同的数值，设计时必须查阅项目所在国的 National Annex。
2. **支撑构件设计**：在评估支撑单向连续板的构件（如梁、墙）上的荷载时，可假定支座无转动约束；但在设计支撑构件（如柱子）本身时，必须考虑板连续性带来的弯矩传递效应 [Ref-5], [Ref-7]。
3. **指南参考说明**：上述步骤 2 中提及的“指南表 3.3 弯矩系数”属于非矛盾性补充信息（指南 DG_EN1992-1-1），可大幅简化手算过程，但前提是必须严格满足其 4 项前置假设条件 [Ref-18], [Ref-23]。

用户询问的是“单向板的设计步骤包括哪些”。
我需要根据提供的证据，整理出单向板（one-way spanning slab）的设计步骤。

首先，分析提供的证据：
[Ref-3] 5.3.1 (5) 单向板的定义：主要承受均布荷载的板，如果具有两个自由（无支撑）且大致平行的边缘，或者它是四边支撑的矩形板的中心部分且长跨与短跨之比大于2，则可视为单向板。
[Ref-4], [Ref-12] 9.3.1 实体板的受弯钢筋（包括单向板）：
- 最小和最大配筋率（9.2.1.1）。
- 单向板应提供不小于主筋20%的次要横向钢筋。在支座附近如果没有横向弯矩，则不需要主顶部钢筋的横向钢筋。
- 钢筋间距不应超过 $s_{max,slabs}$。
- 简支板中，一半的计算跨中钢筋应延伸至支座并锚固。
- 部分固定边缘的顶部钢筋应能承受相邻跨最大弯矩的至少25%（端支座可减至15%），延伸至少0.2倍相邻跨长。
- 自由边缘的纵向和横向钢筋。
[Ref-5], [Ref-7] 弯矩传递和简化：
- 支撑无转动约束时，连续板的设计支座弯矩可减小 $F_{Ed,supp} t / 8$。
- 整体浇筑时，临界弯矩可取支座边缘处的弯矩。
- 刚性支座边缘的设计弯矩不应小于假定完全固定时计算的支座弯矩的65%。
- 支撑单向连续板的构件上的荷载可假定支撑无转动约束来评估。
[Ref-9] -9] 7.4.2 挠度控制（免算挠度的条件）：
- 表7.4N给出了跨高比的基本值。简支单向板K=1.0；连续单向板端跨K=1.3，内部跨K=1.5。
[Ref-18] 表3.3 单向连续板的极限弯矩和剪力系数（指南）。
[Ref-22] 荷载组合和布置：
- 交替跨加载设计可变和永久荷载，其他跨仅设计永久荷载。
[Ref-23] 单向板和连续梁的简化（指南）：
- 使用弯矩系数（如表3.3）的条件：特征可变荷载不超过特征永久荷载；荷载主要为均布且跨越三个或更多跨；跨度变化不超过最长跨的15%。端柱与板的刚度比不超过1.0。不允许弯矩重分布。
[Ref-1], [Ref-2], [Ref-6] 5.6 塑性分析：
- 连续单向板可使用塑性分析（简化程序基于转动能力）。
- 屈服铰区域 $x_u/d$ 限制（C50/60及以下为0.45，C55/67及以上为0.35）。
- 如果不直接检查转动能力，需满足：$x_u/d \le 0.25$ (或0.15)，钢筋为B或C级，中间支座与跨中弯矩比在0.5到2之间。
[Ref-8], [Ref-11] 防火设计：
- 单向板如果不符合四边支撑，则按单向板处理。连续板的厚度与简支板相同，但如果常温设计的弯矩重分布不超过15%且中间支座顶部钢筋满足要求，轴线距离可减少。中间支座需提供至少0.5% $A_c$ 的顶部钢筋（特定条件下）。

整理设计步骤：
由于规范并没有直接给出一个名为“单向板设计步骤”的1234列表，我需要根据规范中关于单向板分析、设计、构造的条款，逻辑性地归纳出设计步骤。
步骤大致如下：
1. **结构建模与判定**：确认板是否满足单向板的定义（长宽比>2或两自由边）[Ref-3]。
2. **荷载与内力分析**：
   - 确定荷载组合与布置（如交替跨布置）[Ref-22]。
   - 计算弯矩和剪力。可使用弹性分析、塑性分析（需满足转动能力或特定条件）[Ref-6]，或使用简化弯矩系数（如指南中的表3.3，需满足特定条件）[Ref-18], [Ref-23]。
   - 支座弯矩的简化与调整（如考虑支座宽度、取支座边缘弯矩、刚性支座最小弯矩限制）[Ref-5], [Ref-7]。
3. **截面设计与配筋计算（ULS）**：
   - 受弯承载力计算，确定主筋面积。
   - 若采用塑性分析，需验算转动能力或满足免算条件（如 $x_u/d$ 限制，钢筋延性要求）[Ref-1], [Ref-6]。
4. **正常使用极限状态（SLS）验算**：
   - 挠度控制：可通过限制跨高比（span/effective depth）来免除详细计算，查表7.4N获取基本跨高比（简支K=1.0，连续端跨K=1.3，内跨K=1.5）[Ref-9]。
   - 裂缝控制（虽然证据中未详细展开板的裂缝，但属于SLS常规步骤，可略提或依据现有证据说明）。
5. **构造与 detailing（细部设计）**：
   - 最小/最大配筋率要求[Ref-4]。
   - 横向分布钢筋：单向板需提供不小于主筋20%的次要横向钢筋[Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
   - 钢筋间距 - 钢筋间距限制（主筋和次筋的最大间距）[Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
   - 支座锚固与截断：简支板一半跨中钢筋伸入支座；部分固定边缘需配置承受25%（端部15%）跨中最大弯矩的顶部钢筋，延伸0.2倍跨度[Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
   - 自由边缘钢筋配置[Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
6. **防火设计（如适用）**：
   - 确定板厚和钢筋轴线距离以满足耐火极限（R, E, I 准则），注意连续板中间支座的顶部钢筋要求（如至少0.5% $A_c$）[Ref-8], [Ref-11]。

检查证据是否支持上述步骤：
- 步骤1：[Ref-3] 5.3.1(5) 支持。
- 步骤2：[Ref-22] 荷载布置；[Ref-6] 塑性分析；[Ref-18], [Ref-23] 简化系数；[Ref-5], [Ref-7] 支座弯矩调整。支持。
- 步骤3：[Ref-1], [Ref-2], [Ref-6] 塑性分析的 $x_u/d$ 限制。支持。
- 步骤4：[Ref-9] 表7.4N 挠度控制跨高比。支持。
- 步骤5：[Ref-4], [Ref-12] 9.3.1 实体板配筋构造（横向钢筋20%，间距，支座锚固，部分固定边缘25%顶部钢筋，自由边缘）。支持。
- 步骤6：[Ref-8], [Ref-11] 防火设计板厚、轴线距离、连续板支座顶部钢筋0.5%。支持。

组织回答结构：
- **直接结论**：概述单向板设计的核心流程（判定、分析、ULS、SLS、构造、防火）。
- **详细步骤说明**：
  1. 结构判定与建模
  2. 内力分析与计算
  3. 承载能力极限状态 (ULS) 设计
  4. 正常使用极限状态 (SLS) 验算
  5. 构造与细部设计 (Detailing)
  6. 防火设计 (如适用)
- **依据位置**：列出引用的 Ref 编号。

注意：
- 严格依据证据，不编造。
- 指出国家附录（NDP）可能影响某些参数（如钢筋间距限值、塑性分析基本转动角等）。
- 指南内容（如表3.3弯矩系数）作为补充说明，明确其适用条件。

细化各步骤内容：
**1. 结构判定与建模**
- 判定条件：主要承受均布荷载的板，若具有两个自由且大致平行的边缘，或为四边支撑矩形板的中心部分且长跨与短跨之比大于2，可视为单向板 [Ref-3]。

**2. 内力分析与计算**
- 荷载布置：需考虑交替跨加载（设计可变+永久荷载）与相邻跨加载等组合，以获取内力包络图 [Ref-22]。
- 分析方法：可采用弹性分析或塑性分析 [Ref-6]。
- 简化计算（指南参考）：若满足特定条件（如可变荷载不超过永久荷载、至少三跨均布荷载、跨度变化≤15%、端柱与板刚度比≤1.0），可使用简化弯矩和剪力系数（如指南表3.3），但此时不允许进行弯矩重分布 [Ref-18], [Ref-23]。
- 支座弯矩调整：
  - 若支座无转动约束（如墙），连续板的设计支座弯矩可减小 $F_{Ed,supp} t / 8$ [Ref-5], [Ref-7]。
  - 整体浇筑时，临界弯矩可取支座边缘处的弯矩 [Ref-5], [Ref-7]。
  - 刚性支座边缘的设计弯矩不应小于假定完全固定时计算值的65% [Ref-5], [Ref-7]。

**3. **3. 承载能力极限状态 (ULS) 设计**
- 若采用塑性分析，需验证转动能力，或满足免算转动能力的条件：$x_u/d \le 0.25$（≤C50/60）或 $0.15$（≥C55/67），钢筋为B或C级，中间支座与跨中弯矩比在0.5~2之间 [Ref-6]。
- 若进行转动能力验算，屈服铰区域 $x_u/d$ 不得超过 0.45（≤C50/60）或 0.35（≥C55/67） [Ref-1], [Ref-2]。

**4. 正常使用极限状态 (SLS) 验算**
- 挠度控制：可通过限制跨高比（span/effective depth）免除详细计算。根据表7.4N，简支单向板K=1.0，连续单向板端跨K=1.3，内部跨K=1.5 [Ref-9]。

**5. 构造与细部设计 (Detailing)**
- 横向钢筋：单向板必须提供不小于主筋面积20%的次要横向钢筋（支座附近无横向弯矩时，顶部主筋无需横向钢筋） [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
- 钢筋间距：主筋和次筋的最大间距需符合国家附录规定（推荐值：主筋 $3h \le 400$ mm，次筋 $3.5h \le 450$ mm；集中荷载或最大弯矩区更严） [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
- 支座锚固与截断：
  - 简支板：一半计算跨中钢筋应延伸至支座并锚固 [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
  - 部分固定边缘（分析中未考虑固定）：顶部钢筋需能承受相邻跨最大弯矩的至少25%（端支座可减至15%），并从支座边缘延伸至少0.2倍相邻跨长 [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。
- 自由边缘：需配置纵向和横向边缘钢筋 [Ref-4], [Ref-12]。

**6. 防火设计 (如适用)**
- 若板不满足四边支撑，必须按单向板进行防火设计 [Ref-8]。
- 连续单向板在中间支座处需提供至少 0.5% $A_c$ 的顶部钢筋（在使用冷加工钢筋、端支座无固定或未按要求细部设计、或荷载效应无法横向分布时） [Ref-8]。
- 需满足规范表格对板厚和钢筋轴线距离（保护层+半根钢筋直径）的要求，以保证隔热性(I)和承载力(R) [Ref-11]。

检查是否有遗漏或错误：
- 证据中提到的 $A_{s,min}$ 可取 ULS 计算面积的 1.2 倍（脆性破坏风险小的板）[Ref-4], [Ref-12]。可以补充到 ULS 或构造中。
- 指南中的表3.3是“Ultimate bending moment and shear forces in one-way spanning slabs”，非常切题，作为指南参考案例/补充说明很合适。
- 国家附录（NDP）提示：钢筋间距限值、塑性分析基本转动角 $\theta_{pl,d}$ 等可能因国家而异，需提醒用户 [Ref-1], [Ref-4]。

语言风格：
专业、清晰、分点列出，使用 [Ref-N] 标注。

调整结构，使其更符合“计算/设计步骤”的逻辑：
1. 结构判定
2. 荷载与内力分析
3. 截面承载力设计 (ULS)
4. 正常使用极限状态验算 (SLS)
5. 构造与细部设计
6. 防火设计 (特定工况)

撰写具体内容，确保每个结论都有 [Ref-N]。
- 结构判定：[Ref-3]
- 荷载布置：[Ref-22]
- 支座弯矩调整：[Ref-5], [Ref-7]
- 塑性分析条件：[Ref-6], [Ref-1], [Ref-2]
- 挠度控制：[Ref-9]
- 构造要求：[Ref-4], [Ref-12]
- 防火：[Ref-8], [Ref-11]
- 指南简化系数：[Ref-18], [Ref-23]

确认无误后输出。

sources.original_text:
(1) The simplified procedure for continuous beams and continuous one way spanning slabs is based on the rotation capacity of beam/slab zones over a length of approximately 1,2 times the depth of section. It is assumed that these zones undergo a plastic deformation (formation of yield hinges) under the relevant combination of actions. The verification of the plastic rotation in the ultimate limit state is considered to be fulfilled, if it is shown that under the relevant combination of actions the calculated rotation, $\theta _ { \mathsf { s } } ,$ , is less than or equal to the allowable plastic rotation (see Figure 5.5).

  
Figure 5.5: Plastic rotation $\pmb { \theta _ { \lessgtr } }$ of reinforced concrete sections for continuous beams and continuous one way spanning slabs.

(2) In regions of yield hinges, $x _ { \mathrm { u } } / d$ shall not exceed the value 0,45 for concrete strength classes less than or equal to C50/60, and 0,35 for concrete strength classes greater than or equal to C55/67.

(3) The rotation $\theta _ { \mathsf { s } }$ should be determined on the basis of the design values for actions and materials and on the basis of mean values for prestressing at the relevant time.

(4) In the simplified procedure, the allowable plastic rotation may be determined by multiplying the basic value of allowable rotation, $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ , by a correction factor $k _ { \lambda }$ that depends on the shear slenderness.

Note: Values of $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended values for steel Classes B and C (the use of Class A steel is not recommended for plastic analysis) and concrete strength classes less than or equal to C50/60 and C90/105 are given in Figure 5.6N.

The values for concrete strength classes C 55/67 to C 90/105 may be interpolated accordingly. The values apply for a shear slenderness $\lambda = 3 { , } 0$ . For different values of shear slenderness $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ should be multiplied by $k _ { \lambda }$



Where  is the ratio of the distance between point of zero and maximum moment after redistribution and effective depth, d.

As a simplification  may be calculated for the concordant design values of the bending moment and shear :



  
Figure 5.6N: Basic value of allowable rotation, $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } } ,$ of reinforced concrete sections for Class B and C reinforcement. The values apply for a shear slenderness  = 3,0

sources.title: EN1992-1-1 2004
sources.section: 5.3.1 Structural models for overall analysis
sources.original_text:
(1)P The elements of a structure are classified, by consideration of their nature and function, as beams, columns, slabs, walls, plates, arches, shells etc. Rules are provided for the analysis of the commoner of these elements and of structures consisting of combinations of these elements.

(2) For buildings the following provisions (3) to (7) are applicable:   
(3) A beam is a member for which the span is not less than 3 times the overall section depth.   
Otherwise it should be considered as a deep beam.   
(4) A slab is a member for which the minimum panel dimension is not less than 5 times the   
overall slab thickness.   
(5) A slab subjected to dominantly uniformly distributed loads may be considered to be one  
way spanning if either: - it possesses two free (unsupported) and sensibly parallel edges, or - it is the central part of a sensibly rectangular slab supported on four edges with a ratio of the longer to shorter span greater than 2.

(6) Ribbed or waffle slabs need not be treated as discrete elements for the purposes of analysis, provided that the flange or structural topping and transverse ribs have sufficient torsional stiffness. This may be assumed provided that:

- the rib spacing does not exceed $1 5 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$   
- the depth of the rib below the flange does not exceed 4 times its width.   
- the depth of the flange is at least 1/10 of the clear distance between ribs or $5 0 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ , whichever is the greater.   
- transverse ribs are provided at a clear spacing not exceeding 10 times the overall depth of the slab.

The minimum flange thickness of $5 0 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ may be reduced to $4 0 \mathsf { m m }$ where permanent blocks are incorporated between the ribs.

(7) A column is a member for which the section depth does not exceed 4 times its width and the height is at least 3 times the section depth. Otherwise it should be considered as a wall.

sources.original_text:
For the design of beams, the bending moment coefficients given in Fig. 3.20 or Table 3.3 may be used, noting the conditions to be complied with, which are discussed in Section 3.8.1.

EN 1992-1-1 permits the following simplifications regardless of the method of analysis used:

(1) At a support assumed to offer no restraint to rotation (e.g. over walls), a beam or a slab which is continuous over it may be designed for a support moment which is less than the moment theoretically calculated on the centre line of the support. The permitted reduction in moment is then ${ \cal F } _ { \mathrm { E d , s u p p } } t / 8 ,$ , where $F _ { \mathrm { E d , s u p p } }$ is the design support reaction and t is the breadth of the support. This recognizes the effect of the width of support and arbitrarily rounds off the peak in the bending moment diagram.

(2) Where a beam or a slab is cast monolithically into its supports, the critical moment may be taken as that at the face of the supports (but see also (3) below). This provision is quite reasonable, as failure cannot occur within the support.

(3) The design moment at the faces of rigid supports should not be less than 65% of the support moment calculated assuming full fixity at the faces of support. This ensures a minimum design value for the support moment, particularly in the case of wide supports.

(4) Loads on members supporting one-way-spanning continuous slabs (solid and ribbed) and beams (including T beams) may be assessed on the assumption that supports offer no rotational restraint. This is reasonable; but the effect of continuity should be considered when designing the support such as columns or walls.

(1)P Methods based on plastic analysis shall only be used for the check at ULS.

(2)P The ductility of the critical sections shall be sufficient for the envisaged mechanism to be formed.

(3)P The plastic analysis should be based either on the lower bound (static) method or on the upper bound (kinematic) method.

Note: A Country’s National Annex Guidance may refer to non-contradictory complementary information.

(4) The effects of previous applications of loading may generally be ignored, and a monotonic increase of the intensity of actions may be assumed.

(1)P Plastic analysis without any direct check of rotation capacity may be used for the ultimate limit state if the conditions of 5.6.1 (2)P are met.

(2) The required ductility may be deemed to be satisfied without explicit verification if all the following are fulfilled:

i) the area of tensile reinforcement is limited such that, at any section

$x _ { \mathrm { u } } / d \leq 0 , 2 5$ for concrete strength classes ≤ C50/60

$x _ { \mathrm { u } } / d \le 0 , 1 5$ for concrete strength classes ≥ C55/67

ii) reinforcing steel is either Class B or C

iii) the ratio of the moments at intermediate supports to the moments in the span should be between 0,5 and 2.

(3) Columns should be checked for the maximum plastic moments which can be transmitted by connecting members. For connections to flat slabs this moment should be included in the punching shear calculation.

(4) When plastic analysis of slabs is carried out account should be taken of any non-uniform reinforcement, corner tie down forces, and torsion at free edges.

(5) Plastic methods may be extended to non-solid slabs (ribbed, hollow, waffle slabs) if their response is similar to that of a solid slab, particularly with regard to the torsional effects.

(1) The simplified procedure for continuous beams and continuous one way spanning slabs is based on the rotation capacity of beam/slab zones over a length of approximately 1,2 times the depth of section. It is assumed that these zones undergo a plastic deformation (formation of yield hinges) under the relevant combination of actions. The verification of the plastic rotation in the ultimate limit state is considered to be fulfilled, if it is shown that under the relevant combination of actions the calculated rotation, $\theta _ { \mathsf { s } } ,$ , is less than or equal to the allowable plastic rotation (see Figure 5.5).

  
Figure 5.5: Plastic rotation $\pmb { \theta _ { \lessgtr } }$ of reinforced concrete sections for continuous beams and continuous one way spanning slabs.

(2) In regions of yield hinges, $x _ { \mathrm { u } } / d$ shall not exceed the value 0,45 for concrete strength classes less than or equal to C50/60, and 0,35 for concrete strength classes greater than or equal to C55/67.

(3) The rotation $\theta _ { \mathsf { s } }$ should be determined on the basis of the design values for actions and materials and on the basis of mean values for prestressing at the relevant time.

(4) In the simplified procedure, the allowable plastic rotation may be determined by multiplying the basic value of allowable rotation, $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ , by a correction factor $k _ { \lambda }$ that depends on the shear slenderness.

Note: Values of $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended values for steel Classes B and C (the use of Class A steel is not recommended for plastic analysis) and concrete strength classes less than or equal to C50/60 and C90/105 are given in Figure 5.6N.

The values for concrete strength classes C 55/67 to C 90/105 may be interpolated accordingly. The values apply for a shear slenderness $\lambda = 3 { , } 0$ . For different values of shear slenderness $\theta _ { \mathsf { p l } , \mathsf { d } }$ should be multiplied by $k _ { \lambda }$

(1) Strut and tie models may be used for design in ULS of continuity regions (cracked state of beams and slabs, see 6.1 - 6.4) and for the design in ULS and detailing of discontinuity regions (see 6.5). In general these extend up to a distance h (section depth of member) from the discontinuity. Strut and tie models may also be used for members where a linear distribution within the cross section is assumed, e.g. plane strain.

(2) Verifications in SLS may also be carried out using strut-and-tie models, e.g. verification of steel stresses and crack width control, if approximate compatibility for strut-and-tie models is ensured (in particular the position and direction of important struts should be oriented according to linear elasticity theory)

(3) Strut-and-tie models consist of struts representing compressive stress fields, of ties representing the reinforcement, and of the connecting nodes. The forces in the elements of a strut-and-tie model should be determined by maintaining the equilibrium with the applied loads in the ultimate limit state. The elements of strut-and-tie models should be dimensioned according to the rules given in 6.5.

(4) The ties of a strut-and-tie model should coincide in position and direction with the corresponding reinforcement.

(5) Possible means for developing suitable strut-and-tie models include the adoption of stress trajectories and distributions from linear-elastic theory or the load path method. All strut-and-tie models may be optimised by energy criteria.

sources.section: Introduction > Moment transfer at edge columns > 3.8.5. Simplifications
sources.original_text:
EN 1992-1-1 permits the following simplifications regardless of the method of analysis used:

(1) At a support assumed to offer no restraint to rotation (e.g. over walls), a beam or a slab which is continuous over it may be designed for a support moment which is less than the moment theoretically calculated on the centre line of the support. The permitted reduction in moment is then ${ \cal F } _ { \mathrm { E d , s u p p } } t / 8 ,$ , where $F _ { \mathrm { E d , s u p p } }$ is the design support reaction and t is the breadth of the support. This recognizes the effect of the width of support and arbitrarily rounds off the peak in the bending moment diagram.

(2) Where a beam or a slab is cast monolithically into its supports, the critical moment may be taken as that at the face of the supports (but see also (3) below). This provision is quite reasonable, as failure cannot occur within the support.

(3) The design moment at the faces of rigid supports should not be less than 65% of the support moment calculated assuming full fixity at the faces of support. This ensures a minimum design value for the support moment, particularly in the case of wide supports.

(4) Loads on members supporting one-way-spanning continuous slabs (solid and ribbed) and beams (including T beams) may be assessed on the assumption that supports offer no rotational restraint. This is reasonable; but the effect of continuity should be considered when designing the support such as columns or walls.

sources.title: DG_EN1992-1-1__-1-2
sources.section: Structural fire design > Slabs
sources.original_text:
The data for two-way spanning slabs are applicable only to slabs supported on all four edges.   
If this is not met, the slab should be treated as one-way spanning.

The thickness of the slab for continuous slabs is the same as for simply supported slabs. But some reduction in the axis distance will apply to continuous slabs if the redistribution of bending moments for normal-temperature design does not exceed 15% and top reinforcement over intermediate supports complies with the requirements mentioned for beams.

There is also a requirement to provide top reinforcement of at least 0.5% A over intermediate supports if any of the following apply: (1) use of cold worked reinforcement; (2) the end supports in a continuous slab do not have fixity or are not detailed in accordance with EN 1992-1-1; or (3) the load effects cannot be distributed laterally.

In flat slabs, redistribution of bending moment for normal-temperature design should not exceed 15%. For fire ratings of 90 min and above, top reinforcement should be provided over the full span in the column strips. The area of reinforcement should be at least 20% of the total top reinforcement required over intermediate supports.

sources.original_text:
Structural fire design is covered in EN 1991-1-2. Under fire conditions, a structure will be required to fulfil load bearing and/or separating function. The code provides guidance for satisfying the above requirements and this chapter of the manual discusses the salient features. Building regulations normally specify the fire rating for the building. It can also be calculated from first principles using EN 1991-1-2 (Actions on Structures Exposed to Fire).

The structure is required to comply with criteria R, I and E as appropriate:

Criterion R is assumed to be satisfied if the structure maintains adequate mechanical resistance for the required duration of fire exposure.

Criterion I is the insulation criterion, which also applies to members fulfilling separating function. It is deemed to be satisfied if the average rise in temperature on the nonexposed surface does not exceed 140 K and the maximum rise does not exceed 180 K.

Criterion E applies to elements required to fulfil separating function, and will be satisfied if the integrity of the structure is maintained for the required duration such that the spread of flames, hot gases and excessive heat is avoided.

The designer has a wide choice of methods. The method for verifying the fire resistance in a project should be chosen on the basis of acceptability to regulatory authorities. The design can be based on thermal actions given by either nominal fire exposure or those calculated using the physical parameters of the building. The former is the most common method, and the latter should only be undertaken by designers with adequate appreciation of all aspects of fire engineering.

In both procedures it is further permitted to base the design on (1) member analysis (2) analysis of parts of the structure or (3) analysis of the whole structure.

In member analysis - which includes tabulated data - only the effects of thermal gradients across the cross-section is considered; the effects of axial or in plane thermal expansions are neglected. Also, the boundary conditions are assumed to remain unchanged throughout the fire exposure.

In the analysis of a part of the structure, a section of the structure is isolated such that stationary boundary conditions could be prescribed in the analysis. Within the part that is isolated, the relevant failure mode in fire exposure, temperature-dependent material properties and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations should be taken into account in the analysis.

In the analysis of the whole structure, none of the approximations noted above are used, and the global analysis is undertaken accounting for the temperature-dependent material properties, member stiffness and the effects of thermal expansions and deformations.

The code gives only limited guidance for methods 2 and 3 above.

For member analysis, where the effects of thermal deformation are neglected and where there is only one variable action, the action effect under fire conditions may be taken as $\eta _ { \mathrm { f i } }$ times the value of action effect used in normal temperature design. The value of $\eta _ { \mathrm { f i } }$ depends on the ratio of variable and permanent loads and the use of the building. EN 1992-1-2 provides a figure to arrive at the value. A value of 0.7 may be used as a safe approximation in all cases.

For prestressing tendons, $\theta _ { \mathrm { c r } } = 4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and for prestressing wires and strands $\theta _ { \mathrm { c r } } = 3 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ The stress level for both is taken as 0.55.

This European Standard EN 1992, Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures: General rules and rules for buildings, has been prepared by Technical Committee CEN/TC250 « Structural Eurocodes », the Secretariat of which is held by BSI. CEN/TC250 is responsible for all Structural Eurocodes.

This European Standard shall be given the status of a National Standard, either by publication of an identical text or by endorsement, at the latest by June 2005, and conflicting National Standards shall be withdrawn at latest by March 2010.

This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

According to the CEN-CENELEC Internal Regulations, the National Standard Organisations of the following countries are bound to implement these European Standard: Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary,

Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and United Kingdom.

In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.

Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.

For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.

In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

The Structural Eurocode programme comprises the following standards generally consisting of a number of Parts:

EN 1990 Eurocode 0: Basis of Structural Design

EN 1991 Eurocode 1: Actions on structures

EN 1992 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures

EN 1993 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures

EN 1994 Eurocode 4: Design of composite steel and concrete structures

EN 1995 Eurocode 5: Design of timber structures

EN 1996 Eurocode 6: Design of masonry structures

EN 1997 Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design

EN 1998 Eurocode 8: Design of structures for earthquake resistance

EN 1999 Eurocode 9: Design of aluminium structures

Eurocode standards recognise the responsibility of regulatory authorities in each Member State and have safeguarded their right to determine values related to regulatory safety matters at national level where these continue to vary from State to State.

The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :

– as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential requirements of Council Directive 89/106/EEC, particularly Essential Requirement N°1 – Mechanical resistance and stability – and Essential Requirement N°2 – Safety in case of fire;

– as a basis for specifying contracts for construction works and related engineering services;

– as a framework for drawing up harmonised technical specifications for construction products (ENs and ETAs)

The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3 . Therefore, technical aspects arising from the Eurocodes work need to be adequately considered by CEN Technical Committees and/or EOTA Working Groups working on product standards with a view to achieving full compatibility of these te…

(1) Restraining moments may be resisted by top reinforcement placed in the topping or in plugs in open cores of hollow core units. In the former case the horizontal shear in the connection should be checked according to 6.2.5. In the latter case the transfer of force between the in situ concrete plug and the hollow core unit should be verified according to 6.2.5. The length of the top reinforcement should be in accordance with 9.2.1.3.

(2) Unintended restraining effects at the supports of simply supported slabs should be considered by special reinforcement and/or detailing.

(1) In wall elements installed over floor slabs, reinforcement should normally be provided for possible eccentricities and concentrations of the vertical load at the end of the wall. For floor elements see 10.9.1 (2).

the diaphragm should form part of a realistic structural model, taking into account the deformation compatibility with bracing units,

the diaphragm should be reinforced for the tensile forces assumed in the structural model,

stress concentrations at openings and connections should be taken into account in the detailing of reinforcement.
